# Syntomic cycle classes and prismatic Poincaré duality

**Authors:** Longke Tang

## Abstract

We introduce $F$ -gauges over a prism, construct syntomic cycle classes, and prove the prismatic Poincaré duality for proper smooth schemes.

#### Contents

- 1 Introduction

- 2 $F$ -gauges over a prism

- 3 Weighted homotopy invariance of cohomologies

- 4 Thom classes

- 5 Cycle classes

- 6 Poincaré duality

- References

## 1. Introduction

### 1.1. Goal

Poincaré duality is one of the most classical theorems in algebraic topology, saying that if $X$ is a compact oriented manifold of dimension $d$ , then its singular cohomologies with coefficient in a field $k$ satisfy

$$ \mathrm{H}^{i}(X,k)^{\vee}\cong\mathrm{H}^{d-i}(X,k), $$

where $-^{\vee}$ denotes dual $k$ -vector spaces.

If $X$ is now a projective complex manifold of dimension $d$ , then the Hodge decomposition theorem states that

$$ \mathrm{H}^{i}(X,\mathbb{Z})\otimes{Z}\mathbb{C}\cong\bigoplus_{p+q=i}\mathrm{H}^{q}(X,\Omega^{p}_{X/\mathbb{C}}), $$

where $\Omega^{p}_{X/\mathbb{C}}$ is the sheaf of holomorphic $p$ -forms on $X$ , and $\mathrm{H}^{q}(X,-)$ means the sheaf cohomology. From the proof of the above isomorphism, it is straightforward to see that the Poincaré duality on the left and the Serre duality on the right intertwine. Therefore, in terms of Hodge structures, one can write the duality as

$$ \mathrm{R}\Gamma(X,\mathbb{Z})^{\vee}\cong\mathrm{R}\Gamma(X,\mathbb{Z})(d)[2d], $$

where $-^{\vee}$ denotes the dual functor $\RHom(-,\mathbb{Z})$ in the derived category of Hodge structures. See for example [Cat+14, Example 3.1.5, Theorem 3.1.17].

An important consequence of the Poincaré duality is the cycle class, which associates a cohomology class $\mathrm{Cl}_{Y/X}\in\mathrm{H}^{r}(X,\mathbb{Z})$ to a compact oriented submanifold $Y$ of codimension $r$ in a compact oriented manifold $X$ .

If $X$ is again a projective complex manifold and $Y$ is its closed submanifold of complex codimension $r$ , then the above cycle class, after tensoring with $\mathbb{C}$ , actually lies in the direct summand $\mathrm{H}^{r}(X,\Omega^{r}_{X/\mathbb{C}})$ in the Hodge decomposition. See for example [Cat+14, Lemma 3.1.27]. In terms of Hodge structures, this amounts to saying that the cycle class defines a map of Hodge structures

$$ \mathrm{Cl}_{Y/X}\colon\mathbb{Z}\to\mathrm{H}^{2r}(X,\mathbb{Z})(r). $$

This paper aims to tell the above story for integral $p$ -adic Hodge theory.

### 1.2. Results

In their remarkable paper [BS22], Bhatt and Scholze defined the prismatic cohomology for schemes over a $p$ -adic base, which specializes to various $p$ -adic cohomologies known before, including étale, de Rham, and crystalline, also generalizing their previous works [BMS18] and [BMS19] joint with Morrow.

As its name suggests, prismatic cohomology is based on prisms, which are roughly triples $(A,I,\varphi)$ , where $A$ is a ring, $I$ is an invertible ideal, $\varphi\colon A\to A$ is a Frobenius lift, $A$ is $(p,I)$ -complete, and finally $p\in(I,\varphi(I))$ . See [BS22, Definition 3.2] for a precise definition. Given such a structure, prismatic cohomology associates to every $A/I$ -scheme $X$ a complex $\mathrm{R}\Gamma_{{\mathbbl{\Delta}}}(X/A)\in\mathsf{D}(A)$ , along with a $\varphi$ -semilinear Frobenius $F\colon\mathrm{R}\Gamma_{{\mathbbl{\Delta}}}(X/A)\to\mathrm{R}\Gamma_{{\mathbbl{\Delta}}}(X/A)$ and a so-called Nygaard filtration $\fil^{\bullet}\varphi^{*}\mathrm{R}\Gamma_{{\mathbbl{\Delta}}}(X/A)$ , from which one can recover the étale, de Rham, and crystalline cohomologies of $X$ ; see [BS22, Theorem 1.8, Theorem 1.16].

Given the above construction, the reader might have noticed that, in the $p$ -adic setting, prismatic cohomology should play the role of singular cohomology with a Hodge structure, and the outputs of prismatic cohomology should play the role of Hodge structures. This is indeed the case. The structures in these outputs are summarized in §2 as follows:

#### Definition 1.1 (Definitions 2.25, 2.30, 2.31, 2.32; Examples 2.29, 2.33).

An $F$ -gauge over a prism $(A,I)$ is a triple $(M,\fil^{\bullet}\varphi^{*}M,F)$ where $\fil^{\bullet}\varphi^{*}M$ is a filtration on $\varphi^{*}M$ and $F\colon\fil^{\bullet}\varphi^{*}M\to I^{\bullet}M$ exhibits $I^{\bullet}M$ as a filtered base change of $\fil^{\bullet}\varphi^{*}M$ along $A\to A[1/I]$ . The category of $F$ -gauges over $(A,I)$ is denoted ${F\text{-}\mathsf{Gauge}}(A,I)$ .

The outputs of prismatic cohomology are $F$ -gauges, and there are various specialization functors from ${F\text{-}\mathsf{Gauge}}(A,I)$ , corresponding to Hodge–Tate, de Rham, and étale specializations of prismatic cohomology. In addition, there are Breuil–Kisin twists $A\{n\}$ of $F$ -gauges for all $n\in\mathbb{Z}$ that are analogous to Tate twists $\mathbb{Z}(n)$ of complex Hodge structures.

With $F$ -gauges in hand, one can now easily write down the $p$ -adic analog of the isomorphism (1), the prismatic Poincaré duality:

#### Theorem 1.2 (Theorem 6.4).

For a proper smooth $A/I$ -scheme $X$ of dimension $d$ , there is a canonical isomorphism of $F$ -gauges

$$ \mathrm{R}\Gamma_{{\mathbbl{\Delta}}}(X/A)^{\vee}\cong\mathrm{R}\Gamma_{{\mathbbl{\Delta}}}(X/A)\{d\}[2d]. $$

To prove the above theorem is not as easy as to state it. In the case of étale cohomology, with the help of its 6-functor formalism, one essentially localizes, factorizes, and finally treats $\mathbb{A}^{1}$ . While it might be possible, we choose not to develop a prismatic 6-functor formalism here. In the case of de Rham cohomology, [Stacks, 0FW3] tried hard and managed to construct a trace map $\mathrm{R}\Gamma_{\mathrm{dR}}(X/k)\to k$ that induces a perfect pairing after the cup product; we are not sure whether this method will work here, either. Instead, we follow and improve the method of the recent lecture notes [Cla21], which first constructed the de Rham cycle class, then applied it to the diagonal, obtaining a copairing

$$ k\to\mathrm{R}\Gamma_{\mathrm{dR}}(X/k)\otimes\mathrm{R}\Gamma_{\mathrm{dR}}(X/k)[2d], $$

and finally proved its perfectness by reduction to the Hodge case. Note that the logical order here is reverse to that in classical algebraic topology, where one constructs the cycle class using the Poincaré duality.

As suggested by the map (2) in the complex case, the prismatic cycle class should actually be an $F$ -gauge map

$$ \mathrm{Cl}_{Y/X}^{{\mathbbl{\Delta}}}\colon A\to\mathrm{R}\Gamma_{{\mathbbl{\Delta}}}(X/A)\{r\}[2r], $$

instead of merely an element of $\mathrm{H}^{2r}_{{\mathbbl{\Delta}}}(X/A)$ . This brings us to consider the following:

#### Definition 1.3 (Proposition 2.35, cf. [AKN22, §4]).

For an $A/I$ -scheme $X$ , its $n$ th syntomic cohomology relative to $A$ , denoted $\mathbb{Z}_{p}(n)(X/A)$ , is the complex

$$ \RHom_{{F\text{-}\mathsf{Gauge}}(A,I)}(A,\mathrm{R}\Gamma_{{\mathbbl{\Delta}}}(X/A)\{n\})\in\mathsf{D}(\mathbb{Z}_{p}). $$

While the relative syntomic cohomology seems hard to control, its absolute counterpart has long been considered by $K$ -theorists as the $p$ -adic motivic cohomology, cf. [Niz06], and has recently been redefined using the absolute prismatic cohomology by [BMS19] and [BL22]. Since the absolute syntomic cohomology naturally maps to the relative one, construction of the relative syntomic cycle class boils down to that of the absolute one, which is another main result of this paper:

#### Theorem 1.4 (Definitions 5.26, 5.32; Remarks 5.28, 5.29).

There is a unique functorial way to associate a syntomic cohomology class $\mathrm{Cl}_{Y/X}^{\mathrm{syn}}\in\mathrm{H}^{2r}_{\mathrm{syn}}(X,\mathbb{Z}_{p}(r))$ to every regular immersion $Y\to X$ of codimension $r$ , satifying:

For regular immersions $Y\to X$ and $Y^{\prime}\to X^{\prime}$ , we have $\mathrm{Cl}_{Y/X}^{\mathrm{syn}}\boxtimes\mathrm{Cl}_{Y^{\prime}/X^{\prime}}^{\mathrm{syn}}=\mathrm{Cl}_{(Y\times Y^{\prime})/(X\times X^{\prime})}^{\mathrm{syn}}$ .

In codimension one, $\mathrm{Cl}_{Y/X}^{\mathrm{syn}}=c_{1}(\mathcal{O}(Y))$ is the first Chern class defined in [BL22, §7.5, §8.4].

Moreover, the syntomic cycle class can be upgraded to a syntomic Gysin map

$$ \mathrm{R}\Gamma_{\mathrm{syn}}(Y,\mathbb{Z}_{p}(n))\to\mathrm{R}\Gamma_{\mathrm{syn}}(X,\mathbb{Z}_{p}(n+r))[2r]. $$

We also relate the syntomic Gysin map above to the pushforward map in $K$ -theory via the motivic filtration. In the following theorem, let $K$ denote the $p$ -completed étale $K$ -theory, which is motivic filtered by $\mathbb{Z}_{p}(n)$ by [BMS19, §7.4].

#### Theorem 1.5 (Theorem 5.38).

There is a unique way to enhance the pushforward $K(Y)\to K(X)$ to a motivic filtered map $\fil^{\bullet}K(Y)\to\fil^{\bullet+r}K(X)$ functorially for all regular immersions $Y\to X$ of codimension $r$ of $p$ -formal stacks. Moreover, its associated graded map coincides with the map (3).

#### Remark 1.6.

The functoriality in the above two theorems is with respect to only pullbacks of regular immersions rather than compositions of them. We are not going to pursue the latter functoriality in this work, but we hope to address it in a future project, where a more general Gysin map construction based on the $\mathbb{P}^{1}$ -motivic homotopy theory developed in [AHI24] will be given.

### 1.3. Conventions

Fix a prime $p$ throughout. By “rings” we mean commutative rings. Everything is animated or derived unless otherwise stated, that is:

- • By “categories” we mean $\infty$ -categories, unless we say “ $1$ -categories”;

- • By “modules” we mean complexes, unless we say “classical modules”;

- • By “rings” we mean animated rings, unless we say “classical rings”;

- • …

But by “sets” we still mean $0$ -groupoids, because we have “animas” for $\infty$ -groupoids.

## 2. $F$ -gauges over a prism

We start by defining the notions of gauges and $F$ -gauges over a prism, which are meant to capture the bunch of structures in the relative prismatic cohomology. Thus in this section we fix an animated prism $(A,I)$ as defined in [BL22a, Definition 2.4], and everything we are going to talk about will be $(p,I)$ -complete whenever it is over $A$ , unless otherwise stated. For example, $\mathsf{D}(A)$ will denote the $(p,I)$ -complete derived category of $A$ . Readers not familiar with animated prisms can assume that $(A,I)$ is a bounded classical prism. Let $\bar{A}=A/I$ .

### 2.1. Reminders on filtered objects

In this subsection we recall the definition of filtered objects and some basic constructions on them, roughly following [HA, §1.2.2] and [Rak20, §3.1, §3.2]. Let $\mathcal{C}$ be a stable $\infty$ -category.

#### Definition 2.1 (Filtered objects).

A filtered object $\fil^{\bullet}M$ of $\mathcal{C}$ is a functor $\mathbb{Z}^{\mathrm{op}}\to\mathcal{C}$ , where $\mathbb{Z}=(\mathbb{Z},\leq)$ is the poset viewed as a category. We denote its value on $n\in\mathbb{Z}$ by $\fil^{n}M$ . The $n$ th graded piece of $\fil^{\bullet}M$ is defined as $\fil^{n}M/\fil^{n+1}M$ and is denoted $\gr^{n}M$ . If $\fil^{\bullet}M$ has all its graded pieces vanishing, namely it takes all arrows in $\mathbb{Z}^{\mathrm{op}}$ to isomorphisms, then we call it a constant filtered object.

The category of filtered objects of $\mathcal{C}$ is defined as the functor category $\mathsf{Fun}(\mathbb{Z}^{\mathrm{op}},\mathcal{C})$ and is denoted $\mathsf{Fil}(\mathcal{C})$ . All the graded pieces assemble to a functor $\gr\colon\mathsf{Fil}(\mathcal{C})\to\mathcal{C}{Z}$ , called taking associated graded objects. Taking constant objects is also a functor $\const\colon\mathcal{C}\to\mathsf{Fil}(\mathcal{C})$ .

#### Remark 2.2 (Increasing filtrations).

What Definition 2.1 defines are the so-called decreasing filtrations, in that if we do the same construction for an abelian category and require all the transition maps to be injective, then $\fil^{n}M$ gets smaller when $n$ gets larger. One can similarly define increasing filtrations as functors $\mathbb{Z}\to\mathcal{C}$ , where the same theory applies with indices reversed. We will sometimes use increasing filtrations below, and these will be denoted by $\fil_{\bullet}M$ .

#### Definition 2.3 (Underlying objects).

Suppose $\mathcal{C}$ admits countable colimits. Then $\const\colon\mathcal{C}\to\mathsf{Fil}(\mathcal{C})$ has an obvious left adjoint, given by

$$ \fil^{\bullet}M\mapsto\colim_{n\to-\infty}\fil^{n}M. $$

We call it the underlying object of $\fil^{\bullet}M$ and denote it by $M$ .

#### Definition 2.4 (Day convolution).

Suppose $\mathcal{C}$ admits countable colimits, and let $\otimes$ be a symmetric monoidal structure on it compatible with countable colimits. Then there is a natural symmetric monoidal structure on $\mathsf{Fil}(\mathcal{C})$ called Day convolution, defined as

$$ \fil^{r}(M\otimes N)=\colim_{m+n\geq r}(\fil^{m}M\otimes\fil^{n}N), $$

where the colimit is taken over the full subcategory of $\mathbb{Z}^{\mathrm{op}}\times\mathbb{Z}^{\mathrm{op}}$ spanned by $\{(m,n)\mid m+n\geq r\}$ . For a rigorous $\infty$ -categorical definition, see [HA, §2.2.6].

By our compatibility assumption, it is easy to see that taking underlying objects is symmetric monoidal, so our notation above is compatible. It is also worth noting that taking associated graded objects is symmetric monoidal with respect to the tensor product

$$ (X\otimes Y)_{r}=\bigoplus_{m+n=r}X_{m}\otimes Y_{n} $$

for graded objects.

#### Definition 2.5 (Completion).

Suppose $\mathcal{C}$ admits countable limits. We say that a filtered object $\fil^{\bullet}M$ of $\mathcal{C}$ is complete if

$$ \lim_{n\to+\infty}\fil^{n}M=0. $$

We denote the full subcategory of complete filtered objects of $\mathcal{C}$ by $\widehat{\mathsf{Fil}}(\mathcal{C})$ , and write $\widehat{\mathsf{DF}}(-)$ for $\widehat{\mathsf{Fil}}(\mathsf{D}(-))$ as above. The inclusion functor $\widehat{\mathsf{Fil}}(\mathcal{C})\to\mathsf{Fil}(\mathcal{C})$ has an obvious left adjoint, given by

$$ \fil^{\bullet}M\mapsto\frac{\fil^{\bullet}M}{\lim_{n\to+\infty}\fil^{n}M}, $$

called completion. Note that a filtered object is constant if and only if its completion is zero, and the completion functor is a localization with kernel the constant objects.

#### Remark 2.6 (Monoidality of completion).

Suppose $(\mathcal{C},\otimes)$ satisfies the assumptions of both Definition 2.4 and Definition 2.5. Obviously, constant objects form a tensor ideal under Day convolution; therefore, by [HA, Proposition 2.2.1.9] there is a natural symmetric monoidal structure on $\widehat{\mathsf{Fil}}(\mathcal{C})$ , where the completion functor is symmetric monoidal, and the inclusion functor is lax symmetric monoidal.

#### Definition 2.7 (Trivial filtration).

For $M\in\mathcal{C}$ , we call the filtered object

$$ \begin{array}[]{cc}\fil^{n}M=\begin{cases}M,&m\leq 0;\\
0,&m>0;\end{cases}&\end{array} $$

$M$ with trivial filtration, and by abuse of notation we often denote it by $M$ . This is natural in $M$ , giving rise to a functor $\triv\colon\mathcal{C}\to\mathsf{Fil}(\mathcal{C})$ , which is easily seen to be the left adjoint of taking $\fil^{0}$ . When $\mathcal{C}$ satisfies the assumption of Definition 2.4, it is also easy to see that $\triv$ is symmetric monoidal.

#### Definition 2.8 (Translation).

For a filtered object $\fil^{\bullet}M$ , its translation by $n$ is defined as $\fil^{\bullet+n}M$ . Sometimes we also denote this translation functor by $-(n)$ .

#### Definition 2.9 (Filtered $\mathbb{E}_{\infty}$ -algebras).

Suppose $(\mathcal{C},\otimes)$ satisfies the assumption of Definition 2.4. Then a filtered $\mathbb{E}_{\infty}$ -algebra in $\mathcal{C}$ is defined as an $\mathbb{E}_{\infty}$ -algebra in $\mathsf{Fil}(\mathcal{C})$ with respect to Day convolution. By the above, one can take underlying $\mathbb{E}_{\infty}$ -algebras, associated graded $\mathbb{E}_{\infty}$ -algebras, and completions of filtered $\mathbb{E}_{\infty}$ -algebras, and make trivially filtered $\mathbb{E}_{\infty}$ -algebras starting with $\mathbb{E}_{\infty}$ -algebras in $\mathcal{C}$ .

For a filtered $\mathbb{E}_{\infty}$ -algebra $R$ , we often call its modules in $\mathsf{Fil}(\mathcal{C})$ filtered $R$ -modules, and denote the category of them by $\mathsf{DF}(R)$ . This is compatible with the notation in [BMS19, §5.1], as when $R$ is an $\mathbb{E}_{\infty}$ -algebra in $\mathcal{C}$ that is trivially filtered, $\mathsf{DF}(R)$ is just $\mathsf{Fil}(\mathsf{D}(R))$ , where $\mathsf{D}(R)$ denotes the category of $R$ -modules in $\mathcal{C}$ .

#### Definition 2.10 (Filtered rings).

Using [Rak20, Definition 4.2.22, Construction 4.3.4], we define the category of derived filtered rings to be $\mathsf{DAlg}(\mathsf{DF}(\mathbb{Z}))$ , and that of animated filtered rings to be the full subcategory spanned by those derived filtered rings $R$ with $\fil^{n}R$ connective for all $n$ . By [Rak20, Remark 4.2.24], one can alternatively define the category of animated filtered rings to be the animation, namely $\mathsf{P}_{\Sigma}$ , of the $1$ -category of classical filtered rings of the form $\lsym(M)$ , where $M$ runs through finite direct sums of translations of the trivially filtered $\mathbb{Z}$ . Passing through the Rees algebra construction, one can also view an animated filtered ring as an animated graded algebra over $\mathbb{Z}[t]$ (cf. Definition 5.11 below).

#### Remark 2.11.

By our convention, “filtered rings” will mean animated filtered rings. However, this filtered animation is never really used in this section and only rarely used in §5. Readers can safely replace filtered rings with filtered $\mathbb{E}_{\infty}$ -rings in this section if they are willing to.

### 2.2. Generalities on filtered modules

In this subsection we discuss general properties of filtered $A$ -modules that do not depend on the $\delta$ -ring structure on $A$ .

We view both $A$ and $A[1/I]$ as filtered rings with the $I$ -adic filtrations, i.e.

$$ \begin{array}[]{cc}\fil^{m}A=\begin{cases}I^{m},&m\geq 0;\\
A,&m<0;\end{cases}&\fil^{m}A[1/I]=I^{m}.\end{array} $$

Accordingly, $\mathsf{DF}(A)$ and $\mathsf{DF}(A[1/I])$ refer to the filtered derived categories with respect to the $I$ -adic filtrations. Note that we are not breaking our convention that everything is $(p,I)$ -complete; $A[1/I]$ is just a filtered $(p,I)$ -complete $A$ -algebra with underlying object $0$ . We view $\bar{A}$ as with the trivial filtration, i.e.

$$ \fil^{m}\bar{A}=\begin{cases}\bar{A},&m\leq 0;\\
0,&m>0;\end{cases} $$

then the reduction map $A\to\bar{A}$ is naturally a filtered map.

#### Proposition 2.12.

Taking $\fil^{0}$ gives an equivalence $\mathsf{DF}(A[1/I])\cong\mathsf{D}(A)$ , whose inverse is $M\mapsto I^{\bullet}M$ .

#### Proof.

$M\mapsto I^{\bullet}M$ is obviously right inverse to $\fil^{0}(-)$ . Conversely, for $\fil^{\bullet}N\in\mathsf{DF}(A[1/I])$ , from the filtered multiplication map $I^{\bullet}\otimes\fil^{\bullet}N\to\fil^{\bullet}N$ one gets maps $I^{m}\otimes\fil^{n}N\to\fil^{m+n}N$ for all $m,n\in\mathbb{Z}$ . By their compatibility one can easily see that they are all isomorphisms, so $\fil^{\bullet}N=I^{\bullet}\fil^{0}N$ . ∎

Now we introduce two specializations of filtered $A$ -modules, both of which take values in filtered $\bar{A}$ -modules.

#### Definition 2.13 (Hodge–Tate specialization).

For $\fil^{\bullet}N\in\mathsf{DF}(A)$ , the associated graded object $\gr^{\bullet}N$ is a graded module over $\gr^{\bullet}A=\bigoplus_{m\in\mathbb{N}}I^{m}/I^{m+1}$ . Twist the $m$ th grade by $(I/I^{2})^{\otimes(-m)}$ ; the module $\gr^{\bullet}N\{-\bullet\}$ we get is a graded module over $\gr^{\bullet}A\{-\bullet\}=\bar{A}[u]$ where $u$ is in the $1$ st grade. Note that such a graded module corresponds to an increasingly filtered $\bar{A}$ -module, since multiplying by $u$ gives us the maps. This increasingly filtered $\bar{A}$ -module is called the Hodge–Tate specialization of $N$ , denoted by $\fil_{\bullet}N^{\mathrm{HT}}\in\mathsf{DF}(\bar{A})$ .

#### Definition 2.14 (De Rham specialization).

The de Rham specialization of $\fil^{\bullet}N\in\mathsf{DF}(A)$ is its base change along the filtered map $A\to\bar{A}$ , denoted by $\fil^{\bullet}\bar{N}\in\mathsf{DF}(\bar{A})$ .

#### Remark 2.15.

Since taking associated graded objects commutes with filtered base change, and the associated graded of the map $A\to\bar{A}$ is the map $\bigoplus_{m\in\mathbb{N}}I^{m}/I^{m+1}\to\bar{A}$ that kills all the $m>0$ summands, we can naturally identify the graded pieces of the Hodge–Tate specialization with those of the de Rham specialization up to twists by $I/I^{2}$ . More specifically, for $N\in\mathsf{DF}(A)$ , we have

$$ \gr_{\bullet}N^{\mathrm{HT}}\{\bullet\}\cong\gr^{\bullet}\bar{N}. $$

In Example 2.33 below, this corresponds to the fact that the Hodge–Tate filtration on $\overline{{{\mathbbl{\Delta}}}_{R/A}}$ has graded pieces $\Omega_{R/\bar{A}}^{\bullet}\{-\bullet\}$ while the de Rham filtration on $\overline{{{\mathbbl{\Delta}}}_{R/A}^{(1)}}$ has graded pieces $\Omega_{R/\bar{A}}^{\bullet}$ .

#### Remark 2.16 (The underlying object of the Hodge–Tate specialization).

If we view a graded $\bar{A}[u]$ -module $X_{\bullet}$ as an increasing filtration, then by definition its underlying object is the colimit of $X_{n}$ along multiplying $u$ , which is the same as the $0$ th grade of $X_{\bullet}[u^{-1}]$ . Accordingly, the underlying object $N^{\mathrm{HT}}$ of $\fil_{\bullet}N^{\mathrm{HT}}$ is the same as the $0$ th grade of the base change of $\gr^{\bullet}N$ from $\gr^{\bullet}A=\bigoplus_{m\in\mathbb{N}}I^{m}/I^{m+1}$ to $\gr^{\bullet}A[1/I]=\bigoplus_{m\in\mathbb{Z}}I^{m}/I^{m+1}$ , which means that

$$ N^{\mathrm{HT}}=\gr^{0}(N[1/I])=\fil^{0}(N[1/I])\otimes_{A}\bar{A}, $$

where $\fil^{\bullet}N[1/I]$ denotes the filtered base change of $\fil^{\bullet}N$ from $A$ to $A[1/I]$ , and the last equality comes from Proposition 2.12.

Finally we give some dualizability criteria.

#### Proposition 2.17.

Let $\mathcal{C}$ be a presentably symmetric monoidal category. Then:

- • If $1_{\mathcal{C}}$ is compact, then dualizable objects in $\mathcal{C}$ are compact.

- • If $\mathcal{C}$ is compactly generated by its dualizable objects, then compact objects in $\mathcal{C}$ are dualizable.

#### Proof.

If $1$ is compact and $X\in\mathcal{C}$ is dualizable with dual $X^{\vee}$ , then since

$$ \Hom(X,-)=\Hom(1,\inhom(X,-))=\Hom(1,X^{\vee}\otimes-) $$

commutes with filtered colimits, $X$ is compact.

If $\mathcal{C}$ is stable, then finite colimits of dualizable objects are dualizable: for finite direct sums it is obvious, and for cofibers one easily verify that $\cofib(X\to Y)^{\vee}=\fib(Y^{\vee}\to X^{\vee})$ . In general, retracts of dualizable objects are dualizable. Thus, if $\mathcal{C}$ is compactly generated by its dualizable objects, then compact objects, as retracts of finite colimits of generators, are dualizable. ∎

#### Corollary 2.18.

Let $R$ be a filtered ring. Then in $\mathsf{DF}(R)$ , dualizable objects coincide with compact objects. If moreover the filtration of $R$ is trivial, then they are exactly the complete filtered objects with only finitely many nonzero graded pieces that are all dualizable in $\mathsf{D}(R)$ .

#### Proof.

Note that:

- • $1_{\mathsf{DF}(R)}=R$ and $\Hom(R,-)=\fil^{0}(-)$ commutes with colimits, so $1_{\mathsf{DF}(R)}$ is compact.

- • The translations $R(n)$ are all dualizable with $R(n)^{\vee}=R(-n)$ , and form a family of compact generators of $\mathsf{DF}(R)$ , since the functor $\mathsf{DF}(R)\to\mathsf{Sp}{Z}$ , $\fil^{\bullet}N\mapsto(\fil^{n}N)_{n\in\mathbb{Z}}$ is clearly conservative.

If the filtration of $R$ is trivial, then it is in particular complete, so every $R(n)$ is complete, with only one nonzero graded piece $\gr^{-n}R(n)=R$ . Therefore, the compact objects in $\mathsf{DF}(R)$ , as retracts of finite colimits of objects of the form $R(n)[d]$ , are also complete, with only finitely many nonzero graded pieces that are all compact in $\mathsf{D}(R)$ . Conversely, let $\fil^{\bullet}M\in\mathsf{DF}(R)$ be complete with only finitely many nonzero graded pieces that are all compact in $\mathsf{D}(R)$ . Then for $m\gg 0$ we have $\fil^{m}M=0$ and $\fil^{-m}M=M$ . Also the terms $\fil^{m}M$ are all compact in $\mathsf{D}(R)$ , being a finite extension of compact objects. Now it is easy to write $\fil^{\bullet}M$ as a finite extension of compact objects in $\mathsf{D}(R)$ with trivial filtration, which are clearly compact in $\mathsf{DF}(R)$ . ∎

#### Lemma 2.19.

Let $\mathcal{C}$ and $\mathcal{D}$ be presentably symmetric monoidal categories and $F\colon\mathcal{C}\to\mathcal{D}$ be a conservative symmetric monoidal functor that preserves internal Homs. Then $c\in\mathcal{C}$ is dualizable if and only if $Fc\in\mathcal{D}$ is dualizable.

#### Proof.

If $c\in\mathcal{C}$ is dualizable, clearly so is $Fc\in\mathcal{D}$ since $F$ is symmetric monoidal. Conversely if $Fc\in\mathcal{D}$ is dualizable, let $c^{\vee}=\inhom_{\mathcal{C}}(c,1_{\mathcal{C}})$ , then since $F$ is symmetric monoidal and preserves internal Homs, $F(c^{\vee})=(Fc)^{\vee}$ . To prove that $c\in\mathcal{C}$ is dualizable, it suffices to show that the natural transformation $c^{\vee}\otimes_{\mathcal{C}}-\to\inhom_{\mathcal{C}}(c,-)$ is an isomorphism. This can be checked after applying $F$ by conservativity, whence it becomes obvious. ∎

#### Remark 2.20.

Lemma 2.19 applies when $A\in\mathsf{CAlg}(\mathcal{C})$ is dualizable in $\mathcal{C}$ , $\mathcal{D}=\mathsf{Mod}_{\mathcal{C}}(A)$ is the module category and the base change functor $F=-\otimes_{\mathcal{C}}A$ is conservative, since

$$ \inhom_{\mathcal{D}}(X\otimes_{\mathcal{C}}A,Y\otimes_{\mathcal{C}}A)=\inhom_{\mathcal{C}}(X,Y\otimes_{\mathcal{C}}A)=\inhom_{\mathcal{C}}(X,Y)\otimes_{\mathcal{C}}A $$

by dualizability.

#### Corollary 2.21.

An object in $\mathsf{DF}(\bar{A})$ is dualizable if and only if it is complete and has only finitely many nonzero graded pieces that are all dualizable in $\mathsf{D}(\bar{A})$ .

#### Proof.

By Lemma 2.19, $M\in\mathsf{DF}(\bar{A})$ is dualizable if and only if $M/p\in\mathsf{DF}(\bar{A}/p)$ is. Now the corollary follows from Corollary 2.18. ∎

#### Proposition 2.22.

The functor $N\mapsto(\fil_{\bullet}N^{\mathrm{HT}},\fil^{\bullet}\bar{N})$ from $\mathsf{DF}(A)$ to $\mathsf{DF}(\bar{A})\times\mathsf{DF}(\bar{A})$ is conservative.

#### Proof.

Assume $\fil_{\bullet}N^{\mathrm{HT}}=\fil^{\bullet}\bar{N}=0$ ; we want to prove that $N=0$ . This is easy: $\fil_{\bullet}N^{\mathrm{HT}}=0$ just means $\gr^{\bullet}N=0$ by definition, so the filtration is constant; then $\fil^{\bullet}\bar{N}$ is also constant, and that it is zero implies that $N$ is zero by $I$ -completeness. ∎

#### Remark 2.23.

The conservativity above has a geometric interpretation: view filtered $A$ -modules as graded modules over the Rees algebra $\mathcal{R}=\bigoplus_{m\in\mathbb{Z}}I^{m}t^{-m}$ where $t$ is in the $(-1)$ st grade. For simplicity assume $I=(d)$ is principal, so $\mathcal{R}=A[t,u]/(tu-d)$ . Then the two specializations correspond to taking quotients by $t$ and $u$ , so they are jointly conservative since $tu=d$ and everything is $d$ -complete.

#### Proposition 2.24.

An object $N\in\mathsf{DF}(A)$ is dualizable if and only if its two specializations $\fil_{\bullet}N^{\mathrm{HT}}$ and $\fil^{\bullet}\bar{N}$ are both dualizable in $\mathsf{DF}(\bar{A})$ , equivalently they are both complete and has only finitely many nonzero graded pieces that are all dualizable in $\mathsf{D}(\bar{A})$ .

#### Proof.

It suffices to prove that the functor $N\mapsto(\fil_{\bullet}N^{\mathrm{HT}},\fil^{\bullet}\bar{N})$ satisfies the assumptions of Lemma 2.19. Note that the algebras $\bar{A}$ and $\gr^{\bullet}A$ in $\mathsf{DF}(A)$ are both dualizable, being cofibers of maps $I\to A$ and $A(1)\to A$ . Hence the proposition follows from Remark 2.20 and Proposition 2.22. ∎

### 2.3. $F$ -gauges over a prism

#### Definition 2.25 (Gauges and $F$ -gauges).

A gauge over $(A,I)$ is a pair $(M,\fil^{\bullet}M^{(1)})$ where $M\in\mathsf{D}(A)$ and $\fil^{\bullet}M^{(1)}\in\mathsf{DF}(A)$ with underlying object $M^{(1)}=\varphi_{A}^{*}M$ . An $F$ -gauge over $(A,I)$ is a triple $(M,\fil^{\bullet}M^{(1)},F)$ where $(M,\fil^{\bullet}M^{(1)})$ is a gauge over $(A,I)$ and $F\colon\fil^{\bullet}M^{(1)}[1/I]\to I^{\bullet}M$ is an isomorphism in $\mathsf{DF}(A[1/I])$ . As above, $-[1/I]$ denotes the base change functor from $\mathsf{DF}(A)$ to $\mathsf{DF}(A[1/I])$ and $I^{\bullet}M$ denotes the obvious filtered module of $A[1/I]$ with underlying object $M[1/I]$ .

Denote the categories of gauges and $F$ -gauges over $(A,I)$ by $\mathsf{Gauge}(A,I)$ and ${F\text{-}\mathsf{Gauge}}(A,I)$ , respectively. They are both presentably symmetric monoidal stable $\infty$ -categories, since they are finite limits of such categories by definition. Clearly, the forgetful functor ${F\text{-}\mathsf{Gauge}}(A,I)\to\mathsf{Gauge}(A,I)$ is symmetric monoidal and preserves all colimits.

#### Remark 2.26.

We often view $F$ as a morphism $F\colon\fil^{\bullet}M^{(1)}\to I^{\bullet}M$ in $\mathsf{DF}(A)$ that exhibits $I^{\bullet}M\in\mathsf{DF}(A[1/I])$ as the base change of $\fil^{\bullet}M^{(1)}\in\mathsf{DF}(A)$ to $A[1/I]$ . Thus $\fil^{\bullet}M^{(1)}$ and $F$ actually determine $M$ , as the $\fil^{0}$ of this base change.

#### Remark 2.27 (Changing prisms).

Let $(A,I)\to(B,J)$ be a morphism of prisms. Then $(M,\fil^{\bullet}M^{(1)})\mapsto(M\otimes_{A}B,(\fil^{\bullet}M^{(1)})\otimes_{A^{(1)}}B^{(1)})$ gives base change functors $\mathsf{Gauge}(A,I)\to\mathsf{Gauge}(B,J)$ and ${F\text{-}\mathsf{Gauge}}(A,I)\to{F\text{-}\mathsf{Gauge}}(B,J)$ . We denote them by $-\otimes_{A}B$ and call their right adjoints forgetful functors. Note that these forgetful functors commute with the forgetful functor $\mathsf{D}(B)\to\mathsf{D}(A)$ in the first component but not in the second, since for $N\in\mathsf{D}(B)$ , $\varphi_{B}^{*}N$ and $\varphi_{A}^{*}N$ are in general different.

#### Remark 2.28 (Descent).

Since each datum of a gauge or an $F$ -gauge satisfies $(p,I)$ -completely flat descent, so do gauges and $F$ -gauges. In other words, $\mathsf{Gauge}$ and ${F\text{-}\mathsf{Gauge}}$ are sheaves of $\infty$ -categories on the absolute prismatic site.

#### Example 2.29 (Breuil–Kisin twists).

For $n\in\mathbb{Z}$ , consider the Breuil–Kisin twist $A\{n\}$ defined in [BL22, Definition 2.5.2, Notation 2.5.4]. It is an invertible $A$ -module with canonical isomorphism $A\{n\}^{(1)}\cong I^{-n}A\{n\}$ . We view it as an $F$ -gauge over $(A,I)$ by defining

$$ \fil^{m}A\{n\}^{(1)}=\begin{cases}I^{m+n}A\{n\}^{(1)},&m\geq-n;\\
A\{n\}^{(1)},&m<-n;\end{cases} $$

and taking $F$ to be the canonical isomorphism. Note that $\fil^{m}A\{n\}^{(1)}$ is chosen to correspond to $I^{m}A\{n\}$ under the canonical isomorphism for $m\geq-n$ .

Obviously, $A=A\{0\}$ is the tensor unit of ${F\text{-}\mathsf{Gauge}}(A,I)$ , and $A\{n\}\otimes A\{n^{\prime}\}=A\{n+n^{\prime}\}$ for all $n,n^{\prime}\in\mathbb{Z}$ . By [BL22, Remark 2.5.5], the Breuil–Kisin twists commute with base changes, i.e. $A\{n\}\otimes_{A}B=B\{n\}$ for every prism $(B,J)$ over $(A,I)$ .

For a gauge or an $F$ -gauge $M$ , let $M\{n\}$ denote the tensor product $M\otimes A\{n\}$ in the respective category. Then it is easy to see that

$$ \fil^{m}(M\{n\}^{(1)})=(\fil^{m+n}M^{(1)})\{n\}, $$

where the $\{n\}$ outside the brackets means the Breuil–Kisin twist relative to the animated prism $(A^{(1)},IA^{(1)})$ .

We discuss several specializations of $F$ -gauges.

#### Definition 2.30 (Hodge–Tate specialization).

For $M\in\mathsf{Gauge}(A,I)$ , its Hodge–Tate specialization is defined as the Hodge–Tate specialization of $M^{(1)}\in\mathsf{DF}(A)$ as in Definition 2.13. For $M\in{F\text{-}\mathsf{Gauge}}(A,I)$ , by Proposition 2.12 and Remark 2.16, the underlying object of its Hodge–Tate specialization is $\bar{M}=M\otimes_{A}\bar{A}$ , so in this case we denote it by $\fil_{\bullet}\bar{M}$ .

#### Definition 2.31 (De Rham specialization).

For $M\in\mathsf{Gauge}(A,I)$ , its de Rham specialization is defined as the base change of $\fil^{\bullet}M^{(1)}\in\mathsf{DF}(A)$ to $\bar{A}$ , denoted by $\fil^{\bullet}\overline{M^{(1)}}$ . It is also a functor $\mathsf{Gauge}(A,I)\to\mathsf{DF}(\bar{A})$ .

#### Definition 2.32 (Étale specialization).

Here we suspend the convention that everything is $(p,I)$ -complete. Suppose the prism $(A,I)$ is perfect with $R=A/p$ , so $A=W(R)$ and $A[1/I]_{p}^{\wedge}=W(R[1/I])$ . For $M\in{F\text{-}\mathsf{Gauge}}(A,I)$ , since $M^{(1)}$ is just $M$ with the $A$ -module structure twisted by Frobenius, we can view the isomorphism $F\colon M^{(1)}[1/I]_{p}^{\wedge}\to M[1/I]_{p}^{\wedge}$ as a Frobenius-semilinear automorphism of $M[1/I]_{p}^{\wedge}$ . Now view $M[1/I]_{p}^{\wedge}$ as a sheaf on $\spa(R[1/I],R)_{\mathrm{pro\acute{e}t}}\cong\spd(\bar{A}[1/p],\bar{A})_{\mathrm{pro\acute{e}t}}$ , and form the equalizer of $\id$ and $F$ . This defines a functor $M\mapsto(M[1/I]_{p}^{\wedge})^{F=1}:{F\text{-}\mathsf{Gauge}}(A,I)\to\mathsf{D}_{\mathrm{pro\acute{e}t}}(\spd(\bar{A}[1/p],\bar{A}),\mathbb{Z}_{p})$ , which we call the étale specialization.

#### Example 2.33 (Prismatic cohomology).

Let $X$ be a smooth formal scheme over $\spf(\bar{A})$ . Then [BS22, Theorem 1.8, Theorem 1.16] gives the prismatic cohomology $\mathrm{R}\Gamma_{{\mathbbl{\Delta}}}(X/A)$ an $F$ -gauge structure, whose Hodge–Tate specialization is the conjugate-filtered Hodge–Tate cohomology, whose de Rham specialization is the Hodge-filtered de Rham cohomology, and when $(A,I)$ is perfect whose étale specialization is the étale pushforward of $\mathbb{Z}_{p}$ along the diamond generic fiber of $X\to\spf(\bar{A})$ . This can be generalized to general stacks over $\spf(\bar{A})$ using [BL22, §5.1, §5.2].

#### Remark 2.34 (Relative gauges and $F$ -gauges).

It is possible to define for every formal scheme $X$ over $\spf(\bar{A})$ the categories $\mathsf{Gauge}(X/A)$ and ${F\text{-}\mathsf{Gauge}}(X/A)$ that serve as coefficients for the prismatic cohomology of $X$ over $(A,I)$ : First for $X=\spf(R)$ with $R$ a large quasisyntomic $\bar{A}$ -algebra as in [BS22, Definition 15.1], define

$$ \mathsf{Gauge}(X/A)=\{(M,\fil^{\bullet}M^{(1)})\mid M\in\mathsf{D}({{\mathbbl{\Delta}}}_{R/A}),\,\fil^{\bullet}M^{(1)}\in\mathsf{DF}(\fil^{\bullet}{{\mathbbl{\Delta}}}_{R/A}^{(1)})\}, $$

$$ {F\text{-}\mathsf{Gauge}}(X/A)=\{(M,\fil^{\bullet}M^{(1)},F)\mid(M,\fil^{\bullet}M^{(1)})\in\mathsf{Gauge}(X/A), $$

$$ F\colon\fil^{\bullet}M^{(1)}\otimes_{{{\mathbbl{\Delta}}}_{R/A}^{(1)},\varphi}{{\mathbbl{\Delta}}}_{R/A}[1/I]\cong M[1/I]\}; $$

next for smooth affine $X$ use quasisyntomic descent from the large algebras; then for general affine $X$ use left Kan extension from the smooth ones; finally for general $X$ use descent again.

${F\text{-}\mathsf{Gauge}}(X/A)$ should have specialization to relative prismatic crystals (i.e. quasicoherent $\mathcal{O}_{{\mathbbl{\Delta}}}$ -modules on the site $(X/A)_{{\mathbbl{\Delta}}}$ ), Hodge–Tate specialization to Higgs modules, de Rham specialization to $\mathcal{D}$ -modules, and when $(A,I)$ is perfect, étale specialization to étale sheaves on the generic fiber. Also, the Poincaré duality should hold for proper smooth $X$ with dualizable coefficients in these categories. However we will not explore these in this paper.

The following proposition computes global sections of gauges and $F$ -gauges, with which we can reinterpret the relative syntomic cohomology $\mathbb{Z}_{p}(n)(X/A)$ in [AKN22] as $\Hom_{{F\text{-}\mathsf{Gauge}}(A,I)}(A,\mathrm{R}\Gamma_{{\mathbbl{\Delta}}}(X/A)\{n\})$ , cf. Example 2.29 and Example 2.33.

#### Proposition 2.35.

If $M$ is a gauge, then

$$ \Hom_{\mathsf{Gauge}(A,I)}(A,M)=M\times_{M^{(1)}}\fil^{0}M^{(1)}, $$

where the map $M\to M^{(1)}=M\otimes_{A,\varphi}A$ is $m\mapsto m\otimes 1$ . If $M$ is an $F$ -gauge, then

$$ \Hom_{{F\text{-}\mathsf{Gauge}}(A,I)}(A,M)=\eq(\fil^{0}M^{(1)}\rightrightarrows M^{(1)}), $$

where the two maps are the natural map and the composition

$$ \fil^{0}M^{(1)}\to\fil^{0}(M^{(1)}[1/I])=M\to M^{(1)}. $$

#### Proof.

The first sentence is clear from the definition of $\mathsf{Gauge}(A,I)$ , and the second sentence is clear from Remark 2.26. ∎

We finally offer a dualizability criterion using Proposition 2.24.

#### Proposition 2.36 (Dualizability of gauges).

Let $M$ be a gauge or an $F$ -gauge. Then $M$ is dualizable if and only if it satisfies the following conditions:

- (1) $M$ is dualizable in $\mathsf{D}(A)$ .

- (2) The Hodge–Tate specialization of $M$ is dualizable, i.e. is complete with only finitely many graded pieces that are perfect complexes.

- (3) The de Rham specialization of $M$ is dualizable, i.e. is complete with only finitely many graded pieces that are perfect complexes.

The perfectnesses of the graded pieces in (2) and (3) are equivalent, and in the $F$ -gauge case, (2) implies (1).

#### Proof.

Recall that the symmetric monoidal category of gauges is defined as the pullback

$$ {\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathsf{Gauge}(A,I)} {\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathsf{DF}(A)} {\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathsf{D}(A)} {\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathsf{D}(A)} $$

where the right vertical arrow is taking underlying objects and the lower horizontal arrow is base change along $\varphi$ . Therefore, $M\in\mathsf{Gauge}(A,I)$ is dualizable if and only if its two images in $\fil^{\bullet}M^{(1)}\in\mathsf{DF}(A)$ and $M\in\mathsf{D}(A)$ are dualizable. Now the proposition follows from Proposition 2.24. The two perfectnesses are equivalent because of Remark 2.15.

Recall that by Proposition 2.12, the symmetric monoidal category of $F$ -gauges is defined as the equalizer

$$ {F\text{-}\mathsf{Gauge}}(A,I)\to\mathsf{Gauge}(A,I)\rightrightarrows\mathsf{D}(A) $$

where the two arrows send a gauge $(M,\fil^{\bullet}M^{(1)})\in\mathsf{Gauge}(A,I)$ to $M\in\mathsf{D}(A)$ and $\fil^{\bullet}M^{(1)}[1/I]\in\mathsf{DF}(A[1/I])\cong\mathsf{D}(A)$ , respectively. Therefore, an $F$ -gauge $M$ is dualizable if and only if it is dualizable as a gauge. Since $\bar{M}\in\mathsf{D}(\bar{A})$ is the underlying object of the Hodge–Tate specialization, the dualizability of the Hodge–Tate specialization implies that of $\bar{M}$ , which in turn implies that of $M$ by Lemma 2.19. ∎

#### Corollary 2.37.

Let $X$ be a proper smooth formal algebraic space over $\spf(\bar{A})$ . Then $\mathrm{R}\Gamma_{{\mathbbl{\Delta}}}(X/A)\in{F\text{-}\mathsf{Gauge}}(A,I)$ is dualizable.

#### Proof.

By Proposition 2.36 we only need to show that the Hodge–Tate specialization and the de Rham specialization of $\mathrm{R}\Gamma_{{\mathbbl{\Delta}}}(X/A)$ are both dualizable. This is clear: both are complete with the graded pieces zero outside $[0,\dim(X)]$ ; the nonzero graded pieces are $\mathrm{R}\Gamma(X,\Omega^{\star}_{X/\bar{A}}[-\star])$ , which is dualizable by [Stacks, 0A1P]. ∎

## 3. Weighted homotopy invariance of cohomologies

One remarkable property that the $\ell$ -adic étale cohomology enjoys is the $\mathbb{A}^{1}$ -invariance, namely $\mathrm{R}\Gamma_{\mathrm{\acute{e}t}}(\mathbb{A}^{1}_{X},\mathbb{Z}_{\ell})=\mathrm{R}\Gamma_{\mathrm{\acute{e}t}}(X,\mathbb{Z}_{\ell})$ for $\ell$ invertible on $X$ . Not only does this fact help us compute the étale cohomology for many schemes, it has also been a crucial input to the norm residue isomorphism theorem of Suslin and Voevodsky; see for example [SV00].

However, various cohomologies studied in $p$ -adic Hodge theory, including Hodge, de Rham, prismatic, and syntomic, usually do not satisfy the $\mathbb{A}^{1}$ -invariance. Fortunately, as [Cla21] suggests, they actually enjoy a weaker property, the weighted $\mathbb{A}^{1}$ -invariance, namely $\mathcal{F}(X\times\mathbb{A}^{1}/\mathbb{G}_{m})=\mathcal{F}(X\times\mathrm{B}\mathbb{G}_{m})$ for $\mathcal{F}$ being some of the above cohomologies. In this section, we will formulate this invariance property in general, and prove it for some cohomologies, in order for later sections to exploit.

### 3.1. Big étale sheaves

We first study the notion of big étale sheaves.

#### Definition 3.1 (Big étale sheaves).

Let $\mathcal{C}$ be a presentable $\infty$ -category. A big étale sheaf with values in $\mathcal{C}$ is an accessible functor $\mathcal{F}\colon\mathsf{Ring}\to\mathcal{C}$ that satisfies étale descent, i.e. a $\mathcal{C}$ -object of the big étale topos. A stack in this paper is a big étale sheaf of animas. For a stack $S$ , a big étale sheaf over $S$ with values in $\mathcal{C}$ is an accessible functor $\mathcal{F}\colon\mathsf{Ring}_{/S}\to\mathcal{C}$ that satisfies étale descent, i.e. a $\mathcal{C}$ -object of the slice topos over $S$ . A big étale sheaf of animas over $S$ is the same as a stack with a map to $S$ , and thus is called a stack over $S$ .

#### Remark 3.2 (Small étale sheaves).

Let $A$ be a ring and let $X$ be a sheaf of animas on the small étale site $A_{\mathrm{\acute{e}t}}$ , i.e. the étale site of étale $A$ -algebras. Then one can view it as a stack over $A$ by pulling back along the topos map $(\mathsf{Ring}_{/A})_{\mathrm{\acute{e}t}}\to A_{\mathrm{\acute{e}t}}$ . Such a stack is called an étale stack over $A$ . We call a map of stacks étale if it is étale after every pullback to a representable.

#### Example 3.3.

All geometric objects that appear in this paper are stacks, including:

- • Rings, i.e. affine schemes. For a ring $A$ , the functor $R\mapsto\Hom(A,R)$ is a stack, denoted $\spec(A)$ . We often identify $A$ and $\spec(A)$ .

- • Deligne–Mumford stacks. They are just stacks that are affine schemes étale locally. Namely, a Deligne–Mumford stack is a stack $X$ that is covered by a family of étale maps from affine schemes, cf. [SAG, §1.6.4].

- • Algebraic spaces. They are just those Deligne–Mumford stacks that take classical rings to sets, cf. [SAG, Definition 1.6.8.1].

- • Affine formal schemes. For a ring $A$ and a finitely generated ideal $I\subseteq\pi_{0}A$ , the functor

$$ R\mapsto\{f\in\Hom(A,R)\mid\text{$\pi_{0}(f)(I)$ is nilpotent}\} $$

is a stack, denoted $\spf(A,I)$ , or $\spf(A)$ if not confusing. We often identify $A$ and $\spf(A)$ whenever $A$ is complete, so $\mathsf{D}(A)$ will mean the category of derived $I$ -complete complexes, and in particular this applies to $\mathsf{D}(\mathbb{Z}_{p})$ .

- • Formal Deligne–Mumford stacks. They are just stacks that are affine formal schemes étale locally, in the same way as above.

- • Formal algebraic spaces. They are just formal Deligne–Mumford stacks that take classical rings to sets.

- • Quotient stacks. Let $X$ be a stack and $G$ be a group scheme smooth over $\mathbb{Z}$ acting on $X$ . Then

$$ X/G=(R\mapsto\{(E,f)\mid\text{$E\to\spec(R)$ is a $G$-torsor, $f\colon E\to X$ is $G$-equivariant}\}) $$

is a stack that receives an effective epimorphism from $X$ , since smooth maps have sections étale locally. Alternatively, $X/G=\colim_{n\in\Delta^{\mathrm{op}}}(X\times G^{n})$ , where the simplicial object is defined by the group action.

#### Remark 3.4 (Taking values in stacks).

Let $\mathcal{C}$ be a presentable category and let $S$ be a stack. Let $\mathcal{F}$ be a big étale sheaf over $S$ and let $X$ be a stack over $S$ . Viewing $X$ as a big étale sheaf over $S$ with values in $\mathsf{Ani}$ , since $\mathcal{C}$ is naturally powered over $\mathsf{Ani}$ , the anima $\Hom_{S}(X,\mathcal{F})$ is naturally enhanced to an object $\mathcal{F}(X)\in\mathcal{C}$ , which we call the value of $\mathcal{F}$ on $X$ . Equivalently,

$$ \mathcal{F}(X)=\lim_{\spec(R)\to X}\mathcal{F}(R). $$

Note that $\mathcal{F}(X)$ takes colimits in $X$ to limits, since it is $\Hom$ out of it.

The following notion is central in this section.

#### Definition 3.5 (Weighted homotopy invariance).

We say that a big étale sheaf $\mathcal{F}$ over a stack $S$ satisfies strong weighted homotopy invariance if, for every $\mathbb{N}$ -graded ring $R=\bigoplus_{n\in\mathbb{N}}R_{n}$ over $S$ , viewed as acted by $\mathbb{G}_{m}$ naturally by grading,

$$ \mathcal{F}(\spec(R)/\mathbb{G}_{m})=\mathcal{F}(\spec(R_{0})/\mathbb{G}_{m}). $$

In this case, we have in particular $\mathcal{F}(V/\mathbb{G}_{m})=\mathcal{F}(X/\mathbb{G}_{m})$ for any stack $X$ and vector bundle $V$ over it, where $\mathbb{G}_{m}$ acts on $X$ trivially and acts on $V$ by scaling. This follows from take the limit of the definition over all $\spec(R_{0})\to X$ . Therefore, we say that $\mathcal{F}$ satifies smooth weighted homotopy invariance if, for every vector bundle $V\to X$ with $X$ smooth over $S$ , we have $\mathcal{F}(V/\mathbb{G}_{m})=\mathcal{F}(X/\mathbb{G}_{m})$ .

#### Remark 3.6 (Quasicoherent sheaves on stacks).

Let $\mathsf{Pr}_{\mathrm{st}}^{\mathrm{L}}$ denote the category of presentable stable categories with morphisms the left adjoints. Then $R\mapsto\mathsf{D}(R)$ satisfies étale descent, and is nearly a big étale sheaf except that $\mathsf{Pr}_{\mathrm{st}}^{\mathrm{L}}$ is itself not presentable. Yet $\mathsf{Pr}_{\mathrm{st}}^{\mathrm{L}}$ admits arbitrary small limits, so Remark 3.4 gives rise to a presentable stable category $\mathsf{D}(X)$ for any stack $X$ , called the derived category of $X$ , and its object is called a quasicoherent sheaf on $X$ . By construction, for a stack map $f\colon X\to S$ , we have the adjoint pair $(f^{*},f_{*})\colon\mathsf{D}(S)\rightleftarrows\mathsf{D}(X)$ . We sometimes write $\mathrm{R}\Gamma_{X/S}$ instead of $f_{*}$ .

#### Remark 3.7 (Small étale $\mathbb{Z}_{p}$ -sheaves on stacks).

Similarly, $R\mapsto\mathsf{D}_{\mathrm{\acute{e}t}}(\spec(R),\mathbb{Z}_{p})$ satisfies étale descent, so Remark 3.4 gives rise to a presentable stable category $\mathsf{D}_{\mathrm{\acute{e}t}}(X,\mathbb{Z}_{p})$ for any stack $X$ , whose object is called an étale $\mathbb{Z}_{p}$ -sheaf on $X$ . Here we also have an adjoint pair $(f^{*},f_{*})\colon\mathsf{D}_{\mathrm{\acute{e}t}}(S,\mathbb{Z}_{p})\rightleftarrows\mathsf{D}_{\mathrm{\acute{e}t}}(X,\mathbb{Z}_{p})$ for every stack map $X\to S$ . Alternatively, $\mathsf{D}_{\mathrm{\acute{e}t}}(-,\mathbb{Z}_{p})$ is the big étale sheafification of the constant functor $\mathsf{Ring}\to\mathsf{Pr}_{\mathrm{st}}^{\mathrm{L}}$ with value $\mathsf{D}(\mathbb{Z}_{p})$ .

#### Example 3.8 (Étale cohomology).

Let $S$ be a stack and let $\mathcal{F}$ be an étale $\mathbb{Z}_{p}$ -sheaf on $S$ . Then the étale cohomology $X\mapsto\mathrm{R}\Gamma_{\mathrm{\acute{e}t}}(X,f^{*}\mathcal{F})$ is a big étale sheaf over $S$ with values in $\mathsf{D}(\mathbb{Z}_{p})$ , where $f\colon X\to S$ is the structure map. By abuse of notation, we denote this big étale sheaf still by $\mathcal{F}$ . Some important special cases of this construction are:

- (1) $S=\spec(\mathbb{Z}[1/p])$ and $\mathcal{F}=\mathbb{Z}_{p}(n)$ is the Tate twist, where $n\in\mathbb{Z}$ .

- (2) $S=\spec(\mathbb{Z})$ and $\mathcal{F}=j_{!}\mathbb{Z}_{p}(n)$ where $j\colon\spec(\mathbb{Z}[1/p])\to\spec(\mathbb{Z})$ .

#### Example 3.9 (Étale cohomology of the adic generic fiber).

Let $S$ be a stack over $\spec(\mathbb{Z}[t])$ and let $\mathcal{F}$ be an étale $\mathbb{Z}_{p}$ -sheaf on $S$ . Then the étale cohomology of the adic generic fiber $R\mapsto\mathrm{R}\Gamma_{\mathrm{\acute{e}t}}(\hat{R}_{t}[1/t],f^{*}\mathcal{F})$ is a big étale sheaf over $S$ with values in $\mathsf{D}(\mathbb{Z}_{p})$ , where $\hat{R}_{t}$ is the $t$ -completion of $R$ and $f\colon\spec(\hat{R}_{t}[1/t])\to S$ is the obvious map. In fact, by [BM21, Corollary 6.17], it is even an $\mathrm{arc}_{t}$ sheaf. The most important special case is $S=\spec(\mathbb{Z})$ with structure map $t\mapsto p$ .

#### Example 3.10 (Hodge cohomology).

Let $S$ be a stack. The Hodge cohomology $X\mapsto\mathrm{R}\Gamma_{X/S}(\mathrm{L}\Omega_{X/S}^{\star})[-\star]$ is a big étale sheaf over $S$ with values in $\mathsf{Gr}(S)$ . We denote it by $\mathrm{L}\Omega_{-/S}^{\star}[-\star]$ . When $S=\spec(\mathbb{Z})$ we often omit the “ $/S$ ”.

#### Example 3.11 (De Rham cohomology).

Let $S$ be a stack. The de Rham cohomology $X\mapsto\fil^{\bullet}\mathrm{dR}_{X/S}$ is a big étale sheaf over $S$ with values in $\mathsf{DF}(S)$ . Note that its associated graded object is the Hodge cohomology.

#### Example 3.12 (Relative prismatic cohomology).

Let $(A,I)$ be a prism and let $\bar{A}=A/I$ . The relative prismatic cohomology $R\mapsto{{\mathbbl{\Delta}}}_{R/A}$ is a big étale sheaf over $\bar{A}$ with values in ${F\text{-}\mathsf{Gauge}}(A,I)$ . Its Hodge–Tate specialization $\fil_{\bullet}\overline{{{\mathbbl{\Delta}}}}_{-/A}$ (Definition 2.30) is called the relative Hodge–Tate cohomology, and its de Rham specialization (Definition 2.31) is the de Rham cohomology over $\spf(\bar{A})$ .

#### Example 3.13 (Absolute prismatic cohomology).

Let $\mathrm{WCart}$ and $\mathrm{WCart}^{\mathrm{HT}}$ be the Cartier–Witt stack and its Hodge–Tate divisor, as in [BL22, §3.3,§3.4]. The prismatic cohomology sheaf $\mathcal{H}_{{\mathbbl{\Delta}}}$ defined in [BL22, Construction 4.4.1] is a big étale sheaf with values in $\mathsf{D}(\mathrm{WCart})$ , and the (twisted and Nygaard filtered) absolute prismatic cohomology is the sheaf ${{\mathbbl{\Delta}}}_{-}\{n\}=\mathrm{R}\Gamma(\mathrm{WCart},\mathcal{H}_{{\mathbbl{\Delta}}}\{n\})\in\mathsf{DF}(\mathbb{Z}_{p})$ defined in [BL22, Construction 4.4.10] with the Nygaard filtration $\fil^{\bullet}{{\mathbbl{\Delta}}}_{-}\{n\}$ as in [BL22, Construction 5.5.3], for $n\in\mathbb{Z}$ . The (conjugate filtered) Hodge–Tate cohomology sheaf $\fil_{\bullet}\mathcal{H}_{\overline{{{\mathbbl{\Delta}}}}}$ defined in [BL22, Construction 4.5.1] is a big étale sheaf with values in $\mathsf{DF}(\mathrm{WCart}^{\mathrm{HT}})$ , and similarly the (twisted and conjugate filtered) absolute Hodge–Tate cohomology is the sheaf $\fil_{\bullet}\overline{{{\mathbbl{\Delta}}}}_{-}\{n\}=\mathrm{R}\Gamma(\mathrm{WCart}^{\mathrm{HT}},\fil_{\bullet}\mathcal{H}_{\overline{{{\mathbbl{\Delta}}}}}\{n\})\in\mathsf{DF}(\mathbb{Z}_{p})$ , for $n\in\mathbb{Z}$ .

#### Example 3.14 (Diffracted Hodge cohomology).

The diffracted Hodge cohomology $\fil_{\bullet}\Omega^{\not{D}}_{-}$ , defined in [BL22, §4.9], is a big étale sheaf with values in $\mathsf{DF}(\mathrm{B}\mathbb{G}_{m}^{\sharp})$ . Rationally it is the Hodge cohomology with the filtration naïvely defined by the grading, under the identifications $\mathbb{G}^{\sharp}_{m,\mathbb{Q}}=\mathbb{G}_{m,\mathbb{Q}}$ and $\mathsf{D}(\mathrm{B}\mathbb{G}_{m,\mathbb{Q}})=\mathsf{Gr}(\mathbb{Q})$ , while after $p$ -completion it is the Hodge–Tate cohomology sheaf, under the identification $\mathrm{B}\mathbb{G}^{\sharp}_{m,\mathbb{Z}_{p}}=\mathrm{WCart}^{\mathrm{HT}}$ (see [BL22, Theorem 3.4.13]). Its associated graded object is the Hodge cohomology, where the $\mathbb{G}_{m}^{\sharp}$ -action on the $n$ th grade comes from the $\mathbb{G}_{m}$ -action of weight $-n$ .

#### Example 3.15 (Syntomic cohomology).

The syntomic cohomology $\mathbb{Z}_{p}(\star)$ , defined in [BL22, §8.4], is a big étale sheaf with values in $\mathsf{Gr}(\mathbb{Z}_{p})$ . By [BL22, Construction 7.4.1], for $n\in\mathbb{Z}$ and $X$ over $\spf(\mathbb{Z}_{p})$ , $\mathbb{Z}_{p}(n)(X)$ is the equalizer of the maps $\varphi\{n\}$ and $\iota$ from $\fil^{n}{{\mathbbl{\Delta}}}_{X}\{n\}$ to ${{\mathbbl{\Delta}}}_{X}\{n\}$ , while by [BL22, Remark 8.4.4], for a stack $X$ with $p$ -completion $\hat{X}$ , there is a fiber sequence

$$ j_{!}\mathbb{Z}_{p}(n)(X)\to\mathbb{Z}_{p}(n)(X)\to\mathbb{Z}_{p}(n)(\hat{X}) $$

where the first term is as in Example 3.8.

#### Remark 3.16.

As [BL22] has constructed, all the examples above except 3.8(2) have symmetric algebra structures in their respective categories, i.e. they actually have values in $\mathsf{CAlg}(\mathbb{Z}_{p})$ , $\mathsf{CAlg}\mathsf{DF}(\mathbb{Z}_{p})$ , and so on. We have omitted this clumsy “ $\mathsf{CAlg}$ ” notation in above.

#### Remark 3.17.

Almost every cohomology theory that we encounter is left Kan extended from its restriction to smooth $\mathbb{Z}$ -algebras, at least when formulated properly. See [BL22, Proposition 4.5.8, Proposition 4.5.10, Proposition 4.9.6, Remark 5.5.10, Proposition 8.4.10]. Therefore, our generality of allowing arbitrary animated rings to be “test objects” of stacks may be redundant; in most cases smooth $\mathbb{Z}$ -algebras suffice. However, in order not to introduce more complication, we refrain from restricting test objects.

### 3.2. Comparing cohomology

This subsection aims to abstract the arguments of [BL22, Proposition 9.2.9] and [BL22, §9.4]. We first generalize the notion of quasisyntomic rings in [BMS19, §4.2] to animated rings. Before that let us recall the notion of $\tor$ amplitude. Note that unlike [BMS19, §4.1], we use the homological indexing here.

#### Definition 3.18 ( $\tor$ amplitude).

Let $A$ be a ring and let $M\in\mathsf{D}(A)$ . For $a,b\in\mathbb{Z}$ , we say that the ( $p$ -complete) $\tor$ amplitude of $M$ is in $[a,b]$ if, for every classical $A$ -module $N$ (with $pN=0$ ), $M\otimes_{A}N$ has nonzero homotopy groups only in degree $[a,b]$ . Similarly we have the notion of ( $p$ -complete) $\tor$ amplitude in $\geq a$ or $\leq b$ . If an $A$ -module $M$ has ( $p$ -complete) $\tor$ amplitude concentrated at $0$ , we say that it is ( $p$ -completely) flat.

Obviously, ( $p$ -complete) $\tor$ amplitude is preserved by arbitrary base change.

#### Proposition 3.19.

Let $n\in\mathbb{N}$ and let $A$ be a ring whose homotopy groups of degrees $>n$ are zero. Let $a,b\in\mathbb{Z}$ and let $M\in\mathsf{D}(A)$ have $\tor$ amplitude in $[a,b]$ (resp. $\geq a$ , $\leq b$ ). Then $M$ has nonzero homotopy groups only in degree $[a,b+n]$ (resp. $\geq a$ , $\leq b+n$ ).

#### Proof.

This is simply because $A$ itself is an iterated extension of $(\pi_{i}A)[i]$ for $i=0,1,\ldots,n$ , and each $\pi_{i}A$ is a classical $A$ -module. ∎

The following lemmas discuss commutation of cosimplicial totalizations and filtered colimits, under some coconnectivity conditions. Let $I$ be a filtered index category and $\Delta$ be the opposite category of ordered nonempty finite sets, which is also called the category of standard simplices.

#### Lemma 3.20.

Let $M$ be a diagram of spectra indexed by $\Delta\times I$ . Suppose $\tau_{>0}M$ is ind-zero as a diagram $I\to\mathsf{Fun}(\Delta,\mathsf{Sp})$ , i.e. for every $i\in I$ , there is a map $i\to j$ in $I$ such that the map $\tau_{>0}M_{i}\to\tau_{>0}M_{j}$ is zero in $\mathsf{Fun}(\Delta,\mathsf{Sp})$ . Then

$$ \colim_{I}\lim_{\Delta}M=\lim_{\Delta}\colim_{I}M $$

and is coconnective.

#### Proof.

There is an obvious map from the left hand side to the right hand side. The fiber sequence $\tau_{>0}M\to M\to\tau_{\leq 0}M$ of diagrams induces fiber sequences for both sides. The assumption implies that

$$ \colim_{I}\lim_{\Delta}\tau_{>0}M=\lim_{\Delta}\colim_{I}\tau_{>0}M=0. $$

Therefore, one can assume that $M=\tau_{\leq 0}M$ is coconnective. For $n\in\mathbb{N}$ , let $M_{\leq n}$ be the restriction of $M$ to $\Delta_{\leq n}\times I$ , where $\Delta_{\leq n}$ is the full subcategory of $\Delta$ generated by the simplices of dimension $\leq n$ . Then for every $n\in\mathbb{N}$ :

- • For every $i\in I$ we have

$$ \fib(\lim_{\Delta}M_{i}\to\lim_{\Delta_{\leq n}}M_{\leq n,i})\in\mathsf{Sp}_{\leq-n}; $$

since filtered colimits respect coconnectivity, we can take $\colim_{I}$ and get

$$ \fib(\colim_{I}\lim_{\Delta}M\to\colim_{I}\lim_{\Delta_{\leq n}}M_{\leq n})\in\mathsf{Sp}_{<-n}. $$

- • Also by the fact that filtered colimits respect coconnectivity,

$$ \fib(\lim_{\Delta}\colim_{I}M\to\lim_{\Delta_{\leq n}}\colim_{I}M_{\leq n})\in\mathsf{Sp}_{<-n}. $$

- • Since $\Delta_{\leq n}$ is finite and in a stable $\infty$ -category finite limits are just shifts of finite colimits,

$$ \colim_{I}\lim_{\Delta_{\leq n}}M_{\leq n}=\lim_{\Delta_{\leq n}}\colim_{I}M_{\leq n}. $$

Combining, we get

$$ \fib(\colim_{I}\lim_{\Delta}M\to\lim_{\Delta}\colim_{I}M)\in\mathsf{Sp}_{\leq-n}, $$

but the fiber is independent of $n$ , so it is zero, and the lemma follows. ∎

#### Lemma 3.21.

Let $A$ be a homotopically bounded ring, i.e. $\pi_{n}A=0$ for $n\gg 0$ . Let $M$ be a diagram of objects in $\mathsf{D}(A)$ with $\tor$ amplitude $\leq 0$ , indexed by $\Delta\times I$ . Then

$$ \colim_{I}\lim_{\Delta}M=\lim_{\Delta}\colim_{I}M. $$

#### Proof.

Combine Proposition 3.19 and (some shift of) Lemma 3.20. ∎

The terms below are taken from [HRW22, §4.1]. Their apparent incompatibility originates from [BMS19, Definition 4.10].

#### Definition 3.22.

Let $A\to R$ be a ring map. We say that it is ( $p$ -)quasi-lci if $\mathrm{L}_{R/A}\in\mathsf{D}(R)$ has ( $p$ -complete) $\tor$ amplitude $\leq 1$ . If it is moreover ( $p$ -completely) flat, we say that it is ( $p$ -)quasisyntomic. A ( $p$ -)quasisyntomic ring means a ring that is ( $p$ -)quasi-lci over $\mathbb{Z}$ .

If $A\to R$ is a ( $p$ -)quasi-lci ring map, since $\mathrm{L}_{R/A}$ is connective, $\mathrm{L}_{R/A}$ actually has ( $p$ -complete) $\tor$ amplitude in $[0,1]$ . Therefore, its wedge product $\mathrm{L}\Omega^{n}_{R/A}$ has ( $p$ -complete) $\tor$ amplitude in $[0,n]$ , for all $n\in\mathbb{N}$ .

Now we begin to compare the cohomology of different stacks. In what follows, let $(X_{i})_{i\in I}$ be a finite diagram of stacks, and let $X$ be a stack receiving compatible maps from them. Rigorously speaking, the data should be a diagram $(X_{i})_{i\in I\star\Delta^{0}}$ , where $X=X_{\Delta^{0}}$ . Then for any big étale sheaf $\mathcal{F}$ with values in any presentable category $\mathcal{C}$ , we have a natural map

$$ \mathcal{F}(X)\to\lim_{i\in I}\mathcal{F}(X_{i}). $$
