### 3.3. Cohomologies of graded rings

In this subsection, we finally establish the strong weighted homotopy invariance of the syntomic cohomology.

First we discuss the Hodge cohomology. The first part of the following definition is taken from [Cla21, Lecture 13]; beware that it is expected to be somewhat reasonable only when $Z$ is an Artin stack.

#### Definition 3.27 (Cotangent complex).

For a stack $Z$ over a ring $A$ , let

$$ \mathrm{L}_{Z/A}=\lim_{g\colon\spec(R)\to Z}g_{*}\mathrm{L}_{R/A}\in\mathsf{D}(Z), $$

where $g_{*}$ denotes the quasicoherent pushforward as in Remark 3.6. We often write $\mathrm{L}_{Z}$ for $\mathrm{L}_{Z/\mathbb{Z}}$ . For a map of stacks $X\to Y$ , let

$$ \mathrm{L}_{X/Y}=\lim_{f\colon\spec(R)\to Y}(f_{X})_{*}\mathrm{L}_{(X\times_{Y}\spec(R))/R}\in\mathsf{D}(X), $$

where $f_{X}$ is the base change of $f$ along $X\to Y$ .

#### Remark 3.28.

Note that the assignment $R\mapsto(\mathsf{D}(R),\mathrm{L}_{R/A})$ is a big étale sheaf over $A$ of pointed categories, and the above definition for $\mathrm{L}_{Z/A}$ is just Remark 3.4 expanded, so $\mathrm{L}_{-/A}$ takes colimits to limits of pushforwards, and so do $\mathrm{L}_{-/Y}$ and $\mathrm{L}_{X\times_{Y}-/-}$ . In particular, to compute $\mathrm{L}_{Z/A}$ , one can write $Z$ as a colimit of affines and take the limit just along these affines, rather than take the whole limit as in the definition. Similarly, one can replace the limit in the definition of $\mathrm{L}_{X/Y}$ by a smaller one, as long as the colimit of the affines is $Y$ .

Let $A$ be a ring and $R=\bigoplus_{n\in\mathbb{Z}}R_{n}$ be a graded $A$ -algebra, considered as acted by $\mathbb{G}_{m}$ naturally by the grading. In the following proposition, we view quasicoherent sheaves over $\spec(R)/\mathbb{G}_{m}$ as graded modules of $R$ , for example by [Mou21, Theorem 4.1] and [SAG, Proposition 2.5.1.2].

#### Proposition 3.29.

Let $Y=\spec(R)/\mathbb{G}_{m}$ and $(Y_{n})$ , $g_{n}\colon Y_{n}\to Y$ be the Čech nerve of the cover $\spec(R)\to\spec(R)/\mathbb{G}_{m}$ . Then the simplicial object $(g_{n})_{*}\mathrm{L}_{Y_{n}/A}$ has its partial totalization tower $(\lim_{\Delta_{\leq n}}(g_{n})_{*}\mathrm{L}_{Y_{n}/A})_{n\in\mathbb{N}}$ pro-constant.

#### Proof.

View stacks affine over $Y$ as graded $R$ -algebras. Then $Y_{n}$ corresponds to $S^{(n)}=R[x_{0}^{\pm 1},\ldots,x_{n}^{\pm 1}]$ with $\deg(x_{i})=1$ , while absolutely $Y_{n}$ is the spectrum of its $0$ th grade part $S^{(n)}_{0}$ . Since $S^{(n)}=S^{(n)}_{0}[x_{0}^{\pm 1}]$ , it is easy to see that for an $S^{(n)}_{0}$ -module $M$ , the pushforward along $g_{n}$ of $M$ is the graded module $M[x_{0}^{\pm 1}]$ . Hence there is a fiber sequence of graded modules

$$ (g_{n})_{*}\mathrm{L}_{Y_{n}/A}=\mathrm{L}_{S^{(n)}_{0}/A}\otimes_{S^{(n)}_{0}}S^{(n)}\to\mathrm{L}_{S^{(n)}/A}\to\mathrm{L}_{S^{(n)}/S^{(n)}_{0}}=S^{(n)}. $$

Now consider both $(\mathrm{L}_{S^{(n)}/A})$ and $(S^{(n)})$ as cosimplicial objects; then they are functorially made from the Čech nerve of $R\to S^{(0)}=R[x_{0}^{\pm 1}]$ ; but this has a left inverse as a map of ungraded rings, so both $(\mathrm{L}_{S^{(n)}/A})$ and $S^{(n)}$ split as cosimplicial ungraded modules, and in particular their pro-objects of partial totalizations are pro-constant ungradedly; now this forces them to also be pro-constant gradedly, and hence so is the pro-object of partial totalizations of the fiber $((g_{n})_{*}\mathrm{L}_{Y_{n}/A})$ . ∎

#### Proposition 3.30.

Consider the natural graded map $\mathrm{L}_{R/A}\to R$ defined as the left Kan extension of the map $\Omega_{R/A}\to R$ , $\mathrm{d}r\mapsto\deg(r)r$ . Then there is a natural isomorphism

$$ \mathrm{L}_{(\spec(R)/\mathbb{G}_{m})/A}\cong\fib(\mathrm{L}_{R/A}\to R) $$

of graded $R$ -modules.

#### Proof.

Descend the fiber sequence in the proof of Proposition 3.29 and we have

$$ \mathrm{L}_{(\spec(R)/\mathbb{G}_{m})/A}=\fib(\mathrm{L}_{R/A}\to\mathrm{L}_{R/(\spec(R)/\mathbb{G}_{m})}) $$

as graded $R$ -modules. Now view stacks affine over $\spec(R)/\mathbb{G}_{m}$ as graded rings over $R$ . Then by definition, the stack $\spec(R)$ over $\spec(R)/\mathbb{G}_{m}$ corresponds to the ring $R[t^{\pm 1}]$ with $\deg(t)=1$ . Note that here $R=\mathrm{R}\Gamma(\spec(R),\mathcal{O}_{\spec(R)})$ is identified with the $0$ th grade part of $R[t^{\pm 1}]$ , which is $\bigoplus_{n\in\mathbb{Z}}R_{n}t^{n}$ , while on the other hand $\mathrm{L}_{R/(\spec(R)/\mathbb{G}_{m})}=\mathrm{R}\Gamma(\spec(R),\mathrm{L}_{R/(\spec(R)/\mathbb{G}_{m})})$ is identified with that of $\mathrm{L}_{R[t^{\pm 1}]/R}=R[t^{\pm 1}]\mathrm{d}t$ , which is $\bigoplus_{n\in\mathbb{Z}}R_{n}t^{n-1}\mathrm{d}t$ . Therefore, the map $\mathrm{L}_{R/A}\to\mathrm{L}_{R/(\spec(R)/\mathbb{G}_{m})}$ sends $r\in R_{n}$ to $\mathrm{d}(rt^{n})=nrt^{n-1}\mathrm{d}t$ , which gives the identification of $\mathrm{L}_{(\spec(R)/\mathbb{G}_{m})/A}$ in the proposition. ∎

The following corollary is [BL22, Proposition B.9], which was left as an exercise by the authors there.

#### Corollary 3.31.

If $R$ is $\mathbb{N}$ -graded, then $\mathrm{L}_{(\spec(R)/\mathbb{G}_{m})/A}$ is also $\mathbb{N}$ -graded, with $0$ th grade part $R_{0}[-1]\oplus\mathrm{L}_{R_{0}/A}$ , which is the same as $\mathrm{L}_{(\spec(R_{0})/\mathbb{G}_{m})/A}$ . Therefore, for every integer $n$ , the natural map

$$ \mathrm{R}\Gamma(\spec(R_{0})/\mathbb{G}_{m},\mathrm{L}\Omega_{(\spec(R_{0})/\mathbb{G}_{m})/A}^{n})\to\mathrm{R}\Gamma(\spec(R)/\mathbb{G}_{m},\mathrm{L}\Omega_{(\spec(R)/\mathbb{G}_{m})/A}^{n}) $$

is an isomorphism. Namely, the Hodge cohomology satisfies strong weighted homotopy invariance.

#### Proof.

Clearly, if $R$ is $\mathbb{N}$ -graded, then so is $\mathrm{L}_{R/A}$ , with $0$ th graded part $\mathrm{L}_{R_{0}/A}$ , and thus so is $\mathrm{L}_{(\spec(R)/\mathbb{G}_{m})/A}=\fib(\mathrm{L}_{R/A}\to R)$ , with $0$ th graded part $\fib(0\colon\mathrm{L}_{R_{0}/A}\to R_{0})=R_{0}[-1]\oplus\mathrm{L}_{R_{0}/A}$ . Note that this only depends on $R_{0}$ , so if we replace $R$ by another $\mathbb{N}$ -graded $A$ -algebra with the same $R_{0}$ , the cotangent complex will be the same. This applies in particular to $R_{0}$ , as a graded ring purely in the $0$ th grade. Now by Proposition 3.29, one can commute the wedge power with the Čech descent and conclude that

$$ \mathrm{L}\Omega_{(\spec(R)/\mathbb{G}_{m})/A}^{n}=\mathrm{L}\Lambda^{n}\mathrm{L}_{(\spec(R)/\mathbb{G}_{m})/A}, $$

where the wedge power is over $\spec(R)/\mathbb{G}_{m}$ . So the desired isomorphism follows from the fact that the wedge power of an $\mathbb{N}$ -graded $R$ -module $M$ is still $\mathbb{N}$ -graded, whose $0$ th graded part is just the wedge power of the $R_{0}$ -module $M_{0}$ . ∎

#### Example 3.32.

Take $A=R=\mathbb{Z}$ . We get

$$ \mathrm{L}_{\mathrm{B}\mathbb{G}_{m}/\mathbb{Z}}=\fib(0\to\mathbb{Z})=\mathbb{Z}[-1]. $$

#### Example 3.33.

Take $A=\mathbb{Z}$ and $R=\mathbb{Z}[t]$ with $\deg(t)=1$ . We get

$$ \mathrm{L}_{(\mathbb{A}^{1}/\mathbb{G}_{m})/\mathbb{Z}}=\fib(\mathbb{Z}[t]\mathrm{d}t\to\mathbb{Z}[t])=\mathbb{Z}[-1] $$

as a graded $\mathbb{Z}[t]$ -module purely in $0$ th grade, since the map here is $\mathrm{d}t\mapsto t$ .

Next we discuss the étale cohomology.

#### Lemma 3.34.

Let $S$ be a $\mathbb{Z}[1/p]$ -scheme, $\pi\colon L\to S$ be a line bundle, and $i_{0}\colon S\to L$ be the zero section. Let $\mathcal{M}\in\mathsf{D}_{\mathrm{\acute{e}t}}(S,\mathbb{Z}_{p})$ . Then $\pi$ or equivalently $i_{0}$ induces an isomorphism

$$ \mathrm{R}\Gamma_{\mathrm{\acute{e}t}}(S,\mathcal{M})\cong\mathrm{R}\Gamma_{\mathrm{\acute{e}t}}(L,\pi^{*}\mathcal{M}). $$

#### Proof.

Let $P=\mathbb{P}(L\oplus\mathcal{O}_{S})$ be the compactification of $L$ and $\pi_{P}\colon P\to S$ be the projection. Let $j_{\infty}\colon L\to P$ and $i_{\infty}\colon S\to P$ be the inclusions of $L$ and $\infty$ , respectively. Then there is a natural fiber sequence

$$ {i_{\infty}}_{!}i_{\infty}^{!}\pi_{P}^{*}\mathcal{M}\to\pi_{P}^{*}\mathcal{M}\to{j_{\infty}}_{*}\pi^{*}\mathcal{M}. $$

By the étale Poincaré duality, $\pi_{P}^{*}\mathcal{M}=\pi_{P}^{!}\mathcal{M}(-1)[-2]$ , so $i_{\infty}^{!}\pi_{P}^{*}\mathcal{M}=\mathcal{M}(-1)[-2]$ . Now take $\mathrm{R}\Gamma_{\mathrm{\acute{e}t}}(P,-)$ of the above sequence, and the lemma follows from the classical computation of the étale cohomology of the projective line. ∎

Let $R=\bigoplus_{i\in\mathbb{N}}R_{i}$ be a graded $\mathbb{Z}[1/p]$ -algebra, considered as acted by $\mathbb{G}_{m}$ naturally by the grading. Let $\pi\colon\spec(R)\to\spec(R_{0})$ and $i\colon\spec(R_{0})\to\spec(R)$ denote the obvious maps.

#### Proposition 3.35.

Let $\mathcal{M}\in\mathsf{D}_{\mathrm{\acute{e}t}}(\spec(R_{0}),\mathbb{Z}_{p})$ . Then $\pi$ or equivalently $i$ induces an isomorphism

$$ \mathrm{R}\Gamma_{\mathrm{\acute{e}t}}(\spec(R_{0}),\mathcal{M})\cong\mathrm{R}\Gamma_{\mathrm{\acute{e}t}}(\spec(R),\pi^{*}\mathcal{M}). $$

#### Proof.

Since the étale cohomology is insensitive to thickenings, without loss of generality we can assume that $R$ is classical. Let $U=\spec(R)\setminus\spec(R_{0})$ and let $\pi_{U}\colon U\to\spec(R_{0})$ and $j_{U}\colon U\to\spec(R)$ denote the obvious maps. By the exact triangle

$$ {j_{U}}_{!}\pi_{U}^{*}\mathcal{M}\to\pi^{*}\mathcal{M}\to i_{*}\mathcal{M}, $$

it suffices to prove $\mathrm{R}\Gamma_{\mathrm{\acute{e}t}}(\spec(R),{j_{U}}_{!}\pi_{U}^{*}\mathcal{M})=0$ . Let $X$ be the blowup of $\spec(R_{0})$ in $\spec(R)$ , and let $D$ denote the exceptional divisor. Then $U$ is also $X\setminus D$ , and it suffices to prove $\mathrm{R}\Gamma_{\mathrm{\acute{e}t}}(X,{j_{U}}_{!}\pi_{U}^{*}\mathcal{M})=0$ , where $j_{U}$ now denotes the open immersion $U\to X$ . Let $\mathcal{O}(-1)$ denote the invertible sheaf on $\proj(R)$ as usual. Then by the construction of blowup, $X$ is the total space of $\mathcal{O}(-1)$ and $D$ is $\proj(R)$ itself, so the proposition follows from Lemma 3.34. ∎

#### Corollary 3.36.

For every $n\in\mathbb{Z}$ ,

$$ \mathrm{R}\Gamma_{\mathrm{\acute{e}t}}(\spec(R_{0})/\mathbb{G}_{m},\mathbb{Z}_{p}(n))\cong\mathrm{R}\Gamma_{\mathrm{\acute{e}t}}(\spec(R)/\mathbb{G}_{m},\mathbb{Z}_{p}(n)). $$

Namely, the étale cohomology satisfies strong weighted homotopy invariance.

#### Proof.

This follows immediately from Proposition 3.35 by descent. ∎

Finally we discuss the étale cohomology of the adic generic fiber, generalizing [KP21, Remark 5.3.7]. Therefore let $\mathcal{F}(R)=\mathrm{R}\Gamma_{\mathrm{\acute{e}t}}(\spec(\hat{R}[1/p]),\mathbb{Z}_{p}(n))$ as in Example 3.9, where $n\in\mathbb{Z}$ is fixed. Recall from [BS22, §9] that, for $R$ over a perfectoid,

$$ \mathrm{R}\Gamma_{\mathrm{\acute{e}t}}(\spec(\hat{R}[1/p]),\mathbb{Z}_{p})=({{\mathbbl{\Delta}}}_{R}[1/I]_{p}^{\wedge})^{\varphi=1}=({{\mathbbl{\Delta}}}_{R,\mathrm{perf}}[1/I]_{p}^{\wedge})^{\varphi=1}. $$

In what follows we will use this to control $\mathcal{F}$ . Before this, let us extend the functor ${{\mathbbl{\Delta}}}_{-,\mathrm{perf}}$ to arbitrary rings.

#### Definition 3.37 (Perfect prismatic cohomology).

Recall from [BS22, Lemma 8.8] that perfectoid rings form a basis of the topology $\mathrm{arc}_{p}$ on $\mathsf{Ring}$ . For $m\in\mathbb{Z}$ , let ${{\mathbbl{\Delta}}}^{[m]}_{-,\mathrm{perf}}$ denote the $\mathrm{arc}_{p}$ sheaves on $\mathsf{Ring}$ whose values on a perfectoid ring $R$ is $I^{m}{{\mathbbl{\Delta}}}_{R}$ . Obviously, they are always coconnective and depend on the $\pi_{0}$ of a ring. By [BS22, Proposition 8.10, Corollary 8.11], ${{\mathbbl{\Delta}}}_{-,\mathrm{perf}}={{\mathbbl{\Delta}}}^{[0]}_{-,\mathrm{perf}}$ is well-defined and coincides with the notion there on rings over perfectoids. Let ${{\mathbbl{\Delta}}}_{-,\mathrm{perf}}[1/I]=\colim_{m}{{\mathbbl{\Delta}}}^{[m]}_{-,\mathrm{perf}}$ as a functor. By Lemma 3.20, it is automatically an $\mathrm{arc}_{p}$ sheaf, and we also have

$$ \mathrm{R}\Gamma_{\mathrm{\acute{e}t}}(\spec(\hat{R}[1/p]),\mathbb{Z}_{p})=({{\mathbbl{\Delta}}}_{R,\mathrm{perf}}[1/I]_{p}^{\wedge})^{\varphi=1} $$

for any ring $R$ .

Now let $R=\bigoplus_{i\in\mathbb{N}}R_{i}$ be a graded ring, considered as acted by $\mathbb{G}_{m}$ naturally by the grading.

#### Proposition 3.38.

The perfect prismatic cohomology satisfies strong weighted homotopy invariance. Namely,

$$ {{\mathbbl{\Delta}}}_{\spec(R)/\mathbb{G}_{m},\mathrm{perf}}={{\mathbbl{\Delta}}}_{\spec(R_{0})/\mathbb{G}_{m},\mathrm{perf}}. $$

#### Proof.

Since $\spec(R)/\mathbb{G}_{m}$ and $\spec(R_{0})/\mathbb{G}_{m}$ are stacks over $R_{0}$ , both sides are $\mathrm{arc}_{p}$ sheaves with respect to $R_{0}$ , so we can assume that $R_{0}$ is perfectoid. Consider the Čech nerves of $\spec(R)\to\spec(R)/\mathbb{G}_{m}$ and $\spec(R_{0})\to\spec(R_{0})/\mathbb{G}_{m}$ , from which we know that ${{\mathbbl{\Delta}}}_{\spec(R)/\mathbb{G}_{m},\mathrm{perf}}=\lim_{i\in\Delta}{{\mathbbl{\Delta}}}_{\spec(R)\times\mathbb{G}_{m}^{i},\mathrm{perf}}$ and similarly for ${{\mathbbl{\Delta}}}_{\spec(R_{0})/\mathbb{G}_{m},\mathrm{perf}}$ . Therefore:

- • We can assume that $R$ is classical.

- • By Lemma 3.20, we can pass to limit and assume that $R$ is finitely presented over $R_{0}$ . Say $R=\pi_{0}(R_{0}[x_{1},\ldots,x_{a}]/(f_{1},\ldots,f_{b}))$ , where $x_{1},\ldots,x_{a}$ and $f_{1},\ldots,f_{b}$ are homogeneous in positive grade.

- • We can replace $R$ by the non-classical $R_{0}[x_{1},\ldots,x_{a}]/(f_{1},\ldots,f_{b})$ .

Now we are in the case that $R_{0}$ and $R$ are homotopically bounded $p$ -quasisyntomic rings: $R_{0}$ is perfectoid and hence $p$ -quasisyntomic, and $R$ is a derived complete intersection over $R_{0}$ . Therefore by Lemma 3.24, we have ${{\mathbbl{\Delta}}}_{\spec(R)/\mathbb{G}_{m}}={{\mathbbl{\Delta}}}_{\spec(R_{0})/\mathbb{G}_{m}}$ . Reducing modulo $p$ , since the Frobenius is functorially nullhomotopic in positive homotopical degrees (see the proof of [BS22, Lemma 8.4], or use [BS17, Remark 11.8], since ${{\mathbbl{\Delta}}}_{-}$ actually has derived rings as values), by Lemma 3.20 we have ${{\mathbbl{\Delta}}}_{\spec(R)/\mathbb{G}_{m},\mathrm{perf}}/p={{\mathbbl{\Delta}}}_{\spec(R_{0})/\mathbb{G}_{m},\mathrm{perf}}/p$ . Finally by $p$ -completeness of both sides we get the desired equality. ∎

#### Remark 3.39.

By similar limiting and replacement argument, then using Remark 3.25 to descend from something over a perfectoid, one can prove in steps that:

- • The functors ${{\mathbbl{\Delta}}}_{-,\mathrm{perf}}$ commutes with filtered colimits of rings.

- • For any ring $S$ we have ${{\mathbbl{\Delta}}}_{S,\mathrm{perf}}=\colim_{\varphi}{{\mathbbl{\Delta}}}_{S}$ , where the colimit is taken in the category of ${{\mathbbl{\Delta}}}_{S}$ -modules that are complete along ${{\mathbbl{\Delta}}}_{S}\to\overline{{{\mathbbl{\Delta}}}}_{S}/p$ .

- • Equation (5) holds for rings not necessarily over a perfectoid.

#### Corollary 3.40.

The étale cohomology of the adic generic fiber satisfies strong weighted homotopy invariance. Namely,

$$ \mathcal{F}(\spec(R)/\mathbb{G}_{m})=\mathcal{F}(\spec(R_{0})/\mathbb{G}_{m}). $$

#### Proof.

By [BM21, Corollary 6.17], both sides are $\mathrm{arc}_{p}$ sheaves with respect to $R_{0}$ . Therefore we can assume that $R_{0}$ is over $\mathbb{Z}_{p}^{\mathrm{cyc}}$ . Since $\mathbb{Z}_{p}(n)\cong\mathbb{Z}_{p}$ on $\spec(\mathbb{Q}_{p}^{\mathrm{cyc}})$ , we can assume $n=0$ . Again use Čech nerves to compute both sides. Since $\mathrm{R}\Gamma_{\mathrm{\acute{e}t}}(\spec(\hat{S}[1/p]),\mathbb{Z}_{p})=({{\mathbbl{\Delta}}}_{S,\mathrm{perf}}[1/I]_{p}^{\wedge})^{\varphi=1}$ and ${{\mathbbl{\Delta}}}_{S,\mathrm{perf}}$ is coconnective for any ring $S$ , the desired equality follows from Proposition 3.38 and Lemma 3.20. ∎

#### Theorem 3.41.

The syntomic cohomology satisfies strong weighted homotopy invariance. Namely, for all $n\in\mathbb{Z}$ ,

$$ \mathrm{R}\Gamma_{\mathrm{syn}}(\spec(R)/\mathbb{G}_{m},\mathbb{Z}_{p}(n))=\mathrm{R}\Gamma_{\mathrm{syn}}(\spec(R_{0})/\mathbb{G}_{m},\mathbb{Z}_{p}(n)). $$

#### Proof.

Combine Lemma 3.23, Corollary 3.31, Corollary 3.36, and Corollary 3.40. ∎

#### Remark 3.42.

The failure of strong weighted homotopy invariance of the absolute prismatic cohomology ${{\mathbbl{\Delta}}}_{-}$ results from the failure of Lemma 3.24 for general stacks. Probably, this is because we are using the wrong category of values, and may be remedied by viewing ${{\mathbbl{\Delta}}}_{-}$ as taking values in the category of “absolute $F$ -gauges”, along with a careful study of the strong weighted homotopy invariance of the (non-Hodge-completed) derived de Rham cohomology.

## 4. Thom classes

We now produce the theory of Thom classes for cohomologies that satisfy a coconnectivity condition. In this and the next sections we will often encounter relative cohomology, so for a big étale sheaf $\mathcal{F}$ with values in a pointed category $\mathcal{C}$ :

- • For stacks $X$ and $Y$ with a map $Y\to X$ understood, we let $\mathcal{F}(X,Y)$ denote $\fib(\mathcal{F}(X)\to\mathcal{F}(Y))$ .

- • For a pointed stack $*\to X$ , we let $\tilde{\mathcal{F}}(X)$ denote $\mathcal{F}(X,*)$ .

Throughout this section we are in the following situation:

#### Situation 4.1.

Let $\mathcal{F}=\bigoplus_{n\in\mathbb{Z}}\mathcal{F}^{n}$ be a big étale sheaf with values in $\mathsf{Gr}\mathsf{CAlg}(\mathsf{Sp})$ . Fix a point $c_{1}\in\Omega^{\infty}\mathcal{F}^{1}(\mathrm{B}\mathbb{G}_{m})$ , call it the first Chern class, and suppose that:

- (1) $\mathcal{F}$ satisfies the projective bundle formula. More precisely, for any $r\in\mathbb{N}$ and any rank $r$ vector bundle $V\to X$ , $(c_{1}(\mathcal{O}(1))^{i})_{i=0}^{r-1}$ induces an isomorphism

$$ \bigoplus_{i=0}^{r-1}\mathcal{F}^{\star-i}(X)\cong\mathcal{F}^{\star}(\mathbb{P}(V)). $$

- (2) $\mathcal{F}$ satisfies the strong weighted homotopy invariance of Definition 3.5.

- (3) $\mathcal{F}^{\leq 0}(\spec(\mathbb{Z}))$ is coconnective.

Note that with the projective bundle formula and the strong weighted homotopy invariance in hand, the proof of [BL22, Theorem 9.3.1] actually shows that:

- • $\mathcal{F}$ has Chern classes, i.e. for $r\in\mathbb{N}$ and a stack $X$ with $\mathcal{F}^{\leq 0}(X)$ coconnective,

$$ \pi_{*}\mathcal{F}(X\times\mathrm{B}\mathrm{GL}_{r})=(\pi_{*}\mathcal{F}(X))[c_{1},\ldots,c_{r}] $$

as doubly graded rings, where $c_{i}\in\pi_{0}\mathcal{F}^{i}(\mathrm{B}\mathrm{GL}_{r})$ . These Chern classes are additive, i.e. for $r,s\in\mathbb{N}$ , the direct sum map $\mathrm{B}\mathrm{GL}_{r}\times\mathrm{B}\mathrm{GL}_{s}\to\mathrm{B}\mathrm{GL}_{r+s}$ induces the map $c_{i}\mapsto\sum_{j=0}^{i}c^{\prime}_{j}c^{\prime\prime}_{i-j}$ on homotopy groups.

The prototypical examples are $\mathcal{F}^{n}(R)$ being $\mathrm{L}\Omega_{R}^{n}[n]$ , $\mathrm{R}\Gamma_{\mathrm{\acute{e}t}}(R[1/p],\mathbb{Z}_{p}(n))[2n]$ , and $\mathrm{R}\Gamma_{\mathrm{syn}}(R,\mathbb{Z}_{p}(n))[2n]$ , by results of [BL22, §9.1] and the previous section. The main result of this section can be summarized as follows:

#### Theorem 4.2.

To every stack $X$ and every rank $r$ vector bundle $V\to X$ , one can assign the Thom class

$$ \mathrm{Th}_{V}^{\mathcal{F}}\in\Omega^{\infty}\mathcal{F}^{r}(V,V\setminus 0), $$

where $0$ denotes the zero section of $V$ . The assignment is uniquely determined (up to contractible ambiguity) by the following requirements:

For $f\colon Y\to X$ a morphism of stacks, we have $\mathrm{Th}_{f^{*}V}^{\mathcal{F}}=f^{*}\mathrm{Th}_{V}^{\mathcal{F}}$ . Rigorously speaking, let $\mathsf{VB}_{r}$ denote the category

$$ \{V\to X\mid\text{$X$ is a stack, $V$ is a rank $r$ vector bundle over $X$}\} $$

with morphisms the pullback squares. Then $\mathrm{Th}^{\mathcal{F}}$ is a natural transformation $*\to\Omega^{\infty}\mathcal{F}^{r}(V,V\setminus 0)$ in the functor category $\mathsf{Fun}(\mathsf{VB}_{r}^{\mathrm{op}},\mathsf{Ani})$ .

After restricting along the zero section $0\colon X\to V$ and taking $\pi_{0}$ , $\mathrm{Th}_{V}^{\mathcal{F}}$ becomes the Chern class $c_{r}(V)$ .

Moreover, the Thom classes are natural in $\mathcal{F}$ and have the following properties:

Promote $V$ to the vector bundle $V/\mathbb{G}_{m}\to X/\mathbb{G}_{m}=X\times\mathrm{B}\mathbb{G}_{m}$ by scalar multiplication. Then $\mathrm{Th}^{\mathcal{F}}_{V/\mathbb{G}_{m}}$ induces an isomorphism

$$ \mathcal{F}^{\star}(X\times\mathrm{B}\mathbb{G}_{m})\cong\mathcal{F}^{\star+r}(V/\mathbb{G}_{m},\mathbb{P}(V)). $$

If $V=V^{\prime}\oplus V^{\prime\prime}$ , then $\mathrm{Th}_{V}^{\mathcal{F}}=\mathrm{Th}_{V^{\prime}}^{\mathcal{F}}\boxtimes\mathrm{Th}_{V^{\prime\prime}}^{\mathcal{F}}$ , i.e. the product of the pullback of $\mathrm{Th}_{V^{\prime}}$ in $\Omega^{\infty}\mathcal{F}^{r^{\prime}}(V,V\setminus V^{\prime\prime})$ and the pullback of $\mathrm{Th}_{V^{\prime\prime}}$ in $\Omega^{\infty}\mathcal{F}^{r^{\prime\prime}}(V,V\setminus V^{\prime})$ , where $r^{\prime}=\rk(V^{\prime})$ , $r^{\prime\prime}=\rk(V^{\prime\prime})$ .

Note that the category $\mathsf{VB}_{r}$ has a final object, i.e. the universal rank $r$ vector bundle which we denote by $\mathrm{E}_{r}\to\mathrm{B}\mathrm{GL}_{r}$ . So by the Yoneda Lemma, in order to prove Theorem 4.2, we only need to treat the universal case, i.e. $X=\mathrm{B}\mathrm{GL}_{r}$ and $V=\mathrm{E}_{r}$ . Therefore let us study the cohomology of $\mathrm{E}_{r}$ and $\mathrm{E}_{r}\setminus 0$ . Recall that by definition $\mathrm{E}_{r}=\mathbb{G}_{a}^{r}/\mathrm{GL}_{r}$ , where $\mathrm{GL}_{r}$ acts on $\mathbb{G}_{a}^{r}$ tautologically.

#### Proposition 4.3.

As stacks over $\mathrm{B}\mathrm{GL}_{r}$ we have $\mathrm{E}_{r}\setminus 0\cong\mathrm{B}\mathrm{Aff}_{r-1}$ where

$$ \mathrm{Aff}_{r-1}=\mathbb{G}_{a}^{r-1}\rtimes\mathrm{GL}_{r-1}=\begin{bmatrix}1&\mathbb{G}_{a}^{r-1}\\
0&\mathrm{GL}_{r-1}\end{bmatrix}\subseteq\mathrm{GL}_{r}. $$

#### Proof.

This is simply because $\mathrm{E}_{r}\setminus 0=(\mathbb{G}_{a}^{r}\setminus 0)/\mathrm{GL}_{r}$ , while $\mathrm{GL}_{r}$ acts transitively on $\mathbb{G}_{a}^{r}\setminus 0$ with point stabilizer $\mathrm{Aff}_{r-1}$ . ∎

#### Proposition 4.4.

Let $X$ be a stack and $G\subseteq\mathrm{GL}_{r,X}$ be a subgroup smooth over $X$ that contains the central $\mathbb{G}_{m,X}\to\mathrm{GL}_{r,X}$ . Then the projection $\mathbb{G}_{a,X}^{r}/G\to\mathrm{B}G$ induces an isomorphism $\mathcal{F}(\mathrm{B}G)\cong\mathcal{F}(\mathbb{G}_{a,X}^{r}/G)$ . In particular, taking $G=\mathrm{GL}_{r,X}$ we have that the projection $X\times\mathrm{E}_{r}\to X\times\mathrm{B}\mathrm{GL}_{r}$ induces an isomorphism $\mathcal{F}(X\times\mathrm{B}\mathrm{GL}_{r})\cong\mathcal{F}(X\times\mathrm{E}_{r})$ .

#### Proof.

The proposition basically follows from the proof of [BL22, Corollary 9.2.10], but the statement there does not contain the case here, so we redo the proof.

Let everything be over $X$ . Let $H=G/\mathbb{G}_{m}$ . Then $H$ is also smooth, and

$$ {\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathrm{B}\mathbb{G}_{m}} {\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathrm{B}G} {\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces*} {\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathrm{B}H} $$

is a fiber square. View $\mathrm{B}G$ as over $\mathrm{B}H$ . If we can prove that for every stack $Y$ over $X$ and every $X$ -map $Y\to\mathrm{B}H$ , the base change of $\mathbb{G}_{a}^{r}/G\to*/G$ to $Y$ induces an isomorphism after taking $\mathcal{F}$ , then the proposition will follow by descent. Now the base change is nothing but $\mathbb{G}_{a,Y}^{r}/\mathbb{G}_{m,Y}\to Y/\mathbb{G}_{m,Y}$ , where $\mathbb{G}_{m,Y}$ acts on $\mathbb{G}_{a,Y}^{r}$ by scalar multiplication, so we are done by weighted homotopy invariance. ∎

#### Proposition 4.5.

For any stack $X$ , the natural map $\mathrm{GL}_{r-1}\to\mathrm{Aff}_{r-1}$ induces an isomorphism

$$ \mathcal{F}(X\times\mathrm{B}\mathrm{Aff}_{r-1})\cong\mathcal{F}(X\times\mathrm{B}\mathrm{GL}_{r-1}). $$

#### Proof.

Let everything be over $X$ to simplify notations. By $\mathrm{Aff}_{r-1}=\mathbb{G}_{a}^{r-1}\rtimes\mathrm{GL}_{r-1}$ we have $\mathrm{B}\mathrm{Aff}_{r-1}=\mathrm{B}\mathbb{G}_{a}^{r-1}/\mathrm{GL}_{r-1}$ , where $\mathrm{GL}_{r-1}$ tautologically acts on $\mathbb{G}_{a}^{r-1}$ . Under this identification, $\mathrm{B}\mathrm{GL}_{r-1}\to\mathrm{B}\mathrm{Aff}_{r-1}$ corresponds to the map $*/\mathrm{GL}_{r-1}\to\mathrm{B}\mathbb{G}_{a}^{r-1}/\mathrm{GL}_{r-1}$ defined as the canonical covering $*\to\mathrm{B}\mathbb{G}_{a}^{r-1}$ quotient by $\mathrm{GL}_{r-1}$ . By descent, we only need to prove that the Čech nerves of $*/\mathrm{GL}_{r-1}\to\mathrm{B}\mathbb{G}_{a}^{r-1}/\mathrm{GL}_{r-1}$ and $*/\mathrm{GL}_{r-1}\to*/\mathrm{GL}_{r-1}$ have the same cohomology on each term, i.e. for each $k\in\mathbb{N}$ the map $(\mathbb{G}_{a}^{r-1})^{k}/\mathrm{GL}_{r-1}\to*/\mathrm{GL}_{r-1}$ induces an isomorphism after applying $\mathcal{F}$ , but this follows immediately from Proposition 4.4. ∎

#### Proposition 4.6.

For any stack $X$ with $\mathcal{F}^{\leq 0}(X)$ coconnective, the natural restriction map $\pi_{*}\mathcal{F}(X\times\mathrm{E}_{r})\to\pi_{*}\mathcal{F}(X\times(\mathrm{E}_{r}\setminus 0))$ is the map

$$ (\pi_{*}\mathcal{F}(X))[c_{1},\ldots,c_{r}]\to(\pi_{*}\mathcal{F}(X))[c_{1},\ldots,c_{r-1}] $$

that leaves $c_{1},\ldots,c_{r-1}$ unchanged and maps $c_{r}$ to $0$ . In particular, it is surjective, and thus

$$ \displaystyle\pi_{*}\mathcal{F}(X\times\mathrm{E}_{r},X\times(\mathrm{E}_{r}\setminus 0)) \displaystyle=\ker(\pi_{*}\mathcal{F}(X\times\mathrm{E}_{r})\to\pi_{*}\mathcal{F}(X\times(\mathrm{E}_{r}\setminus 0))) \displaystyle=c_{r}(\pi_{*}\mathcal{F}(X)[c_{1},\ldots,c_{r}]). $$

#### Proof.

By Proposition 4.3, Proposition 4.4 and Proposition 4.5, the map $X\times(\mathrm{E}_{r}\setminus 0)\to X\times\mathrm{E}_{r}$ is cohomologically the same as the map $X\times\mathrm{B}\mathrm{GL}_{r-1}\to X\times\mathrm{B}\mathrm{GL}_{r}$ induced by adding a trivial line bundle. So the proposition follows from the additivity formula of Chern classes. ∎

#### Proof of Theorem 4.2.

By Proposition 4.6,

$$ \pi_{*}\mathcal{F}(\mathrm{E}_{r},\mathrm{E}_{r}\setminus 0)=c_{r}(\pi_{*}\mathcal{F}(\spec(\mathbb{Z}))[c_{1},\ldots,c_{r}]). $$

Since $c_{i}\in\pi_{0}\mathcal{F}^{i}$ , among the right hand side only $\pi_{*}\mathcal{F}^{\leq 0}(\spec(\mathbb{Z}))$ may contribute to $\pi_{*}\mathcal{F}^{r}(\mathrm{E}_{r},\mathrm{E}_{r}\setminus 0)$ . By assumption (3) of Situation 4.1, this implies that $\mathcal{F}^{r}(\mathrm{E}_{r},\mathrm{E}_{r}\setminus 0)$ is coconnective, so $\Omega^{\infty}\mathcal{F}^{r}(\mathrm{E}_{r},\mathrm{E}_{r}\setminus 0)$ is a $0$ -truncated anima, in which $c_{r}$ is naturally a point. Therefore by normalization, the Thom class of the universal bundle $\mathrm{E}_{r}\to\mathrm{B}\mathrm{GL}_{r}$ can be and must be defined as $c_{r}\in\Omega^{\infty}\mathcal{F}^{r}(\mathrm{E}_{r},\mathrm{E}_{r}\setminus 0)$ , which is unique up to contractible choice. Now the Thom class of a general rank $r$ vector bundle is uniquely determined by the universal case.

To prove the additivity, one reduces to the universal case, where it follows from the additivity of the Chern class. To prove the Thom isomorphism, note by weighted homotopy invariance that $V/\mathbb{G}_{m}\to\mathrm{B}\mathbb{G}_{m}\times X$ induces an isomorphism $\mathcal{F}(\mathrm{B}\mathbb{G}_{m}\times X)\cong\mathcal{F}(V/\mathbb{G}_{m})$ , while $(V/\mathbb{G}_{m})\setminus(0/\mathbb{G}_{m})=\mathbb{P}(V)$ is the projective bundle. Now by additivity and the projective bundle formula, the Thom isomorphism reduces to the case $r=1$ , where it follows immediately by the projective bundle formula. ∎

#### Remark 4.7.

It seems magical that, starting with Chern classes in the homotopy groups, we are able to get the desired Thom class up to contractible ambiguity. This is in fact because the assumption (3) of Situation 4.1 essentially guarantees that the “candidate space” $\Omega^{\infty}\mathcal{F}^{r}(\mathrm{E}_{r},\mathrm{E}_{r}\setminus 0)$ of the Thom class is discrete, so once we have specified the connected component that the class lives in, we have specified the class up to contractible ambiguity.

#### Remark 4.8.

Alternatively, one can impose the normalization only for line bundles but add the additivity of Thom classes to get the uniqueness statement, because by additivity of Chern classes, the natural map

$$ \pi_{*}\mathcal{F}(\mathrm{E}_{r},\mathrm{E}_{r}\setminus 0)\to\pi_{*}\mathcal{F}(\mathrm{E}_{1}^{r},\mathrm{E}_{1}^{r}\setminus 0) $$

is injective, sending $c_{r}$ to the box product of the $r$ different $c_{1}$ ’s on the right.

#### Remark 4.9 (Naturality).

By uniqueness, the Thom class $\mathrm{Th}^{\mathcal{F}}$ is natural in $\mathcal{F}$ , with respect to maps that preserve $c_{1}$ . In particular, it is natural along the map

$$ \mathbb{Z}_{p}(n)\to\fil^{n}{{\mathbbl{\Delta}}}_{-}\{n\}\to\fil^{n}\widehat{\mathrm{dR}_{-}}\to\widehat{\mathrm{L}\Omega^{n}_{-}}[-n] $$

from the syntomic cohomology to the $p$ -completed Hodge cohomology, by [BL22, Theorem 7.6.2].

#### Remark 4.10 (Identifying $c_{1}^{\mathrm{Hod}}$ and $\mathrm{Th}_{1}^{\mathrm{Hod}}$ ).

Take $\mathcal{F}^{n}(R)=\mathrm{L}\Omega^{n}_{R}[n]$ . By Example 3.32, $\mathcal{F}^{1}(\mathrm{B}\mathbb{G}_{m})=\mathbb{Z}$ , in which $1$ corresponds to the Hodge first Chern class originally defined by the map $\mathrm{dlog}\colon\mathbb{G}_{m}\to\mathrm{L}\Omega^{1}$ , thanks to the proof of Proposition 3.30. Therefore the Thom class is also $1\in\mathbb{Z}$ , under the identification of Example 3.33.

#### Remark 4.11.

Our way of stating Situation 4.1 and Theorem 4.2 is convenient for later uses in the paper, but far from optimal:

- • We can use general base stacks in place of $\spec(\mathbb{Z})$ .

- • Formulated properly, the values of $\mathcal{F}$ need not be graded. See [AI23, §3].

- • We only need the smooth weighted homotopy invariance rather than the strong one, except for the Thom isomorphism.

- • With $\mathbb{P}^{1}$ -homotopy techniques as in [AI23], one should be able to get rid of all the coconnectivity assumptions in this section. This can be for example applied to the Hodge cohomology over an animated ring.

## 5. Cycle classes

In this section we construct cycle classes, by reducing to Thom classes with deformation to the normal cone, following [Cla21, Lecture 15]. In §5.1, we define the weighted deformation to the normal cone for a general closed immersion, and prove that for any regular immersion, the cohomology of this deformation space coincides with that of its special fiber, for several cohomology theories. These results are then used in §5.2 to generate cycle classes from Thom classes.

### 5.1. Deformation to the normal cone

Classically, deformation to the normal cone is a construction that deforms a regular immersion into the zero section of its normal cone. Here, with derived algebraic geometry in hand, we are able to perform this construction for all closed immersions of derived stacks, and it will behave well especially for derived regular immersions.

Before going into the construction, we first study closed immersions of derived stacks in general.

#### Definition 5.1 (Animated pairs).

A pair is a map $A\to B$ of animated rings with $\pi_{0}A\to\pi_{0}B$ surjective. Let $\mathsf{Pair}$ denote the category of pairs, i.e. the full category of $\mathsf{Fun}(\Delta^{1},\mathsf{Ring})$ spanned by the pairs. We say that a pair $A\to B$ is classical if both $A$ and $B$ are classical. This coincides with the classical notion of a pair: a ring $A$ with an ideal $I=\ker(A\to B)$ of it.

#### Remark 5.2 (Colimits in $\mathsf{Pair}$ ).

Let $(A_{i}\to B_{i})_{i\in I}$ be a diagram in $\mathsf{Pair}$ . Then its colimit in $\mathsf{Fun}(\Delta^{1},\mathsf{Ring})$ is $\colim A_{i}\to\colim B_{i}$ . Since $\pi_{0}\colon\mathsf{Ring}\to\mathsf{Ring}^{\heartsuit}$ preserves colimits and colimits in $\mathsf{Ring}^{\heartsuit}$ preserve surjections, we see that $(\colim A_{i}\to\colim B_{i})\in\mathsf{Pair}$ , so it is also the colimit of $(A_{i}\to B_{i})_{i\in I}$ in $\mathsf{Pair}$ .

Alternatively, one can take the colimit of $(A_{i}\to B_{i})_{i\in I}$ in two steps: first take $A=\colim A_{i}$ and take base changes $B_{i}^{\prime}=B_{i}\otimes_{A_{i}}A$ , then take $B=\colim B_{i}^{\prime}$ in the category of $A$ -algebras, and the resulting $A\to B$ will be the desired colimit.

#### Remark 5.3 (Projective generators of $\mathsf{Pair}$ ).

Consider two objects $\mathbb{Z}[x]\to\mathbb{Z}$ and $\mathbb{Z}[y]\to\mathbb{Z}[y]$ in $\mathsf{Pair}$ , where the maps are $x\mapsto 0$ and $\id$ , respectively. It is easy to see that $\mathbb{Z}[x]\to\mathbb{Z}$ corepresents the functor $(A\to B)\mapsto\fib(A\to B)$ , while $\mathbb{Z}[y]\to\mathbb{Z}[y]$ corepresents the functor $(A\to B)\mapsto A$ . Since both functors commute with sifted colimits, both objects are projective, and hence so are their finite products $\mathbb{Z}[x_{1},\ldots,x_{r},y_{1},\ldots,y_{s}]\to\mathbb{Z}[y_{1},\ldots,y_{s}]$ for all $r,s\in\mathbb{N}$ . Also, since the functor $\mathsf{Pair}\to\mathsf{Ani}\times\mathsf{Ani}$ , $(A\to B)\mapsto(A,\fib(A\to B))$ is conservative, the two objects generate $\mathsf{Pair}$ . Let

$$ \mathsf{Pair}_{\mathrm{c}}=\{\mathbb{Z}[x_{1},\ldots,x_{r},y_{1},\ldots,y_{s}]\to\mathbb{Z}[y_{1},\ldots,y_{s}]\mid r,s\in\mathbb{N}\} $$

be the full subcategory of $\mathsf{Pair}$ spanned by these finite products. Then by [HTT, Proposition 5.5.8.22], $\mathsf{Pair}=\mathsf{P}_{\Sigma}(\mathsf{Pair}_{\mathrm{c}})$ , namely the animation of $\mathsf{Pair}_{\mathrm{c}}$ .

#### Remark 5.4 ( $n$ -truncated objects in $\mathsf{Pair}$ ).

By Remark 5.3 and [HTT, Remark 5.5.8.26], for $n\in\mathbb{N}$ , an object $(A\to B)\in\mathsf{Pair}$ is $n$ -truncated if and only if both $A$ and $\fib(A\to B)$ are $n$ -truncated as animas. Therefore, a $0$ -truncated object in $\mathsf{Pair}$ is not always classical. See also [Mao21, Remark 3.9].

#### Definition 5.5 (Closed immersions).

Let $Y\to X$ be a map of stacks. We say that it is a closed immersion if it is corepresentable by pairs, or in other words, for any ring $A$ and any map $\spec(A)\to X$ , the pullback $Y\times_{X}\spec(A)$ is some $\spec(B)$ with $\pi_{0}A\twoheadrightarrow\pi_{0}B$ . In this case we also say that $Y$ is a closed substack of $X$ .

#### Definition 5.6 (Regular immersions).

We say that a pair $A\to B$ is regular of codimension $r$ if Zariski locally it is a base change of the pair $\mathbb{Z}[x_{1},\ldots,x_{r}]\to\mathbb{Z}$ , $x_{1},\ldots,x_{r}\mapsto 0$ . We say that a closed immersion $Y\to X$ of stacks is a regular immersion of codimension $r$ if it is corepresentable by regular pairs of codimension $r$ ; we say that it is a regular immersion if it is a disjoint union of regular immersions of codimension $r$ for different $r\in\mathbb{N}$ .

#### Definition 5.7 (The classifying stack of pairs).

Consider the functor $\mathsf{Pair}\to\mathsf{Ring}$ , $(A\to B)\mapsto A$ . It is a cocartesian fibration with small fibers, whose cocartesian edges are

$$ \{(A\to B)\to(A^{\prime}\to B^{\prime})\mid B^{\prime}=B\otimes_{A}A^{\prime}\}. $$

Therefore, by the Grothendieck construction in [HTT, §3.2], it corresponds to a functor $\mathsf{Ring}\to\mathsf{Cat}$ , taking $A$ to the category of all pairs $A\to B$ .

Let $\mathrm{Pair}\colon\mathsf{Ring}\to\mathsf{Ani}$ be the functor taking $A$ to the anima of pairs $A\to B$ , corresponding under the Grothendieck construction to the subcategory of $\mathsf{Pair}$ that contains only the cocartesian edges. Then it is obviously a stack, which we call the classifying stack of pairs or the classifying stack of closed immersions. Denote the universal closed immersion by $\mathrm{Closed}\to\mathrm{Pair}$ . Then by definition,

$$ \mathrm{Closed}(A)=\{\text{a pair $A\to B$ along with a section $B\to A$}\}, $$

i.e. a closed immersion $\spec(B)\to\spec(A)$ with a point of $\spec(B)$ . Denote the universal open complement by $\mathrm{Open}\to\mathrm{Pair}$ . Then similarly

$$ \mathrm{Open}(A)=\{\text{a pair $A\to B$ along with a section $\spec(A)\to\spec(A)\setminus\spec(B)$}\}, $$

which implies that $\mathrm{Open}=*$ , since the section forces $B=0$ .

For $r\in\mathbb{N}$ , we can also define the classifying stacks of regular immersions of codimension $r$ in exactly the same way, which we denote by $\mathrm{Pair}_{r}$ , and similarly $\mathrm{Closed}_{r}$ and $\mathrm{Open}_{r}$ for the universal closed and open substacks. By definition, $\mathrm{Pair}_{r}$ is the image of the étale sheaf map $\mathbb{A}^{r}\to\mathrm{Pair}$ classifying the standard immersion $*\to\mathbb{A}^{r}$ . Note that $\mathrm{Open}_{r}$ is always $*$ , except for $r=0$ where it is empty.

The tensor product of $A$ -algebras gives $\mathrm{Pair}(A)$ an $\mathbb{E}_{\infty}$ -monoid structure, making $\mathrm{Pair}$ an $\mathbb{E}_{\infty}$ -monoid stack. Note that the point $*=\mathrm{Open}\to\mathrm{Pair}$ is a zero element of this monoid; in other words, $\mathrm{Pair}$ is an $\mathbb{E}_{\infty}$ -monoid in the category of pointed stacks, with respect to the smash product.

#### Remark 5.8.

By base change of the cotangent complex, for $Y\to X$ a regular immersion (of codimension $r$ ), it is easy to see that $\mathrm{L}_{Y/X}[-1]$ is locally free (of rank $r$ ) on $Y$ .

Now we construct the derived Rees algebra. The following proposition is [Complex, Proposition 13.3].

#### Proposition 5.9 (cf. [Mao21, Corollary 3.54]).

Let $(A\to B)\in\mathsf{Pair}$ . Consider the initial animated filtered $A$ -algebra $I^{\bullet}$ equipped with a map of animated $A$ -algebras $B\to I^{0}/I^{1}$ . Then we have $I^{n}=A$ for $n\leq 0$ , and $I^{0}/I^{1}=B$ ; in particular $I=I^{1}$ is the fiber of $A\to B$ . Moreover, we have $I/I^{2}=\mathrm{L}_{B/A}[-1]$ and $I^{n}/I^{n+1}=\lsym_{B}^{n}(I/I^{2})$ for $n\geq 0$ . The formation of $I^{\bullet}$ preserves all colimits as a functor $\mathsf{Pair}\to\mathsf{Fil}\mathsf{Ring}$ , commutes with base change in $A$ , and if $A\to B$ is classical and is a local complete intersection, then $I^{\bullet}$ is classical and agrees with the usual filtered $A$ -algebra of powers of $I$ .

#### Remark 5.10.

Proposition 5.9 can be generalized to general morphisms in $\mathsf{Ring}$ , not necessarily surjective on $\pi_{0}$ , but one needs to use derived rings as in [Rak20, Example 4.3.1, Construction 4.3.4], in place of animated rings. It is similar to but different from [Rak20, §5.3].

In the following definitions, the notation $I^{n}$ is as in Proposition 5.9.

#### Definition 5.11 (Rees algebra and deformation to the normal cone).

For a pair $A\to B$ , its Rees algebra is the graded $A[t]$ -algebra

$$ \mathcal{R}_{B/A}=\bigoplus_{n\in\mathbb{Z}}I^{-n}t^{n}, $$

where $t$ is called the Rees parameter. There is an obvious graded map $\mathcal{R}_{B/A}\to B[t]$ , which we denote by $\mathcal{R}(A\to B)\in\mathsf{Pair}$ . By Proposition 5.9, $\mathcal{R}$ commutes with all colimits, when viewed as a functor from pairs to graded pairs over the graded ring $\mathbb{Z}[t]$ . The (weighted) deformation to the normal cone of $A\to B$ is the closed immersion of Artin stacks obtained by quotienting $\mathcal{R}(A\to B)$ by the $\mathbb{G}_{m}$ -action defined by the grading, i.e. the map

$$ \spec(B)\times\mathbb{A}^{1}/\mathbb{G}_{m}=\spec(B[t])/\mathbb{G}_{m}\to\spec(\mathcal{R}_{B/A})/\mathbb{G}_{m}, $$

viewed as a map of stacks over $\mathbb{A}^{1}/\mathbb{G}_{m}$ . Its open fiber (the fiber over $\mathbb{G}_{m}/\mathbb{G}_{m}\to\mathbb{A}^{1}/\mathbb{G}_{m}$ ) is $\spec(B)\to\spec(A)$ , while its closed fiber (the fiber over $0/\mathbb{G}_{m}\to\mathbb{A}^{1}/\mathbb{G}_{m}$ ) is $\spec(B)/\mathbb{G}_{m}\to\spec(\lsym_{B}^{\star}(I/I^{2}))/\mathbb{G}_{m}$ , which is the quotient by the $\mathbb{G}_{m}$ -multiplication on the normal cone of $\spec(B)\to\spec(A)$ .

This construction clearly satisfies étale descent and commutes with base change of $A$ , and hence can be globalized and classified. More precisely, $(A\to B)\mapsto\spec(\mathcal{R}_{B/A})/\mathbb{G}_{m}$ defines a stack over $\mathrm{Pair}\times\mathbb{A}^{1}/\mathbb{G}_{m}$ , denoted by $\mathrm{DNC}$ , whose fiber over $\mathrm{Closed}\times\mathbb{A}^{1}/\mathbb{G}_{m}$ is $\mathrm{Closed}\times\mathbb{A}^{1}/\mathbb{G}_{m}$ itself. Its restriction to $\mathrm{Pair}\times\mathbb{G}_{m}/\mathbb{G}_{m}$ is $\id_{\mathrm{Pair}}$ , while its restriction to $\mathrm{Pair}\times 0/\mathbb{G}_{m}$ is the quotient by $\mathbb{G}_{m}$ of the normal cone $\underline{\spec}_{\mathrm{Pair}}(\lsym^{\star}(\mathcal{I}_{\mathrm{Closed}}/\mathcal{I}_{\mathrm{Closed}}^{2}))$ of $\mathrm{Closed}\to\mathrm{Pair}$ . For a closed immersion $Y\to X$ of stacks, its deformation to the normal cone can be constructed as the base change of $\mathrm{Closed}\times\mathbb{A}^{1}/\mathbb{G}_{m}\to\mathrm{DNC}$ along the classifying map $X\to\mathrm{Pair}$ .

#### Definition 5.12 (Animated blowup).

The blowup of a pair $A\to B$ is the $A$ -scheme $\mathrm{Bl}_{B}(A)=\proj\left(\bigoplus_{n\in\mathbb{N}}I^{n}\right)$ . The natural “inclusion” map $\bigoplus_{n\in\mathbb{N}}I^{n+1}\to\bigoplus_{n\in\mathbb{N}}I^{n}$ defines a section of the line bundle $\mathcal{O}(-1)$ , whose zero locus is by definition $\proj\left(\bigoplus_{n\in\mathbb{N}}I^{n}/I^{n+1}\right)$ , which we call the exceptional divisor. Note that it is the projectivized normal cone $\proj(\lsym_{B}^{\star}(I/I^{2}))$ of $\spec(B)$ in $\spec(A)$ . Similarly, this construction can also be globalized and classified. For a closed immersion $Y\to X$ of stacks, we denote its blowup by $\mathrm{Bl}_{Y}(X)$ .

#### Remark 5.13.

The two concepts are closely related. Namely, one can check that:

- • $\mathrm{Bl}_{B}(A)=(\spec(\mathcal{R}_{B/A})\setminus(\spec(B[t])\cup\spec(A)))/\mathbb{G}_{m}$ .

- • $\spec(\mathcal{R}_{B/A})=\mathrm{Bl}_{B}(A[t])\setminus\mathrm{Bl}_{B}(A)$ , where the map $A[t]\to A$ sends $t$ to $0$ .

Next we study the cohomology of the deformation to the normal cone. Fix an $r\in\mathbb{N}$ , let $Y\to X$ be a regular immersion of stacks of codimension $r$ , and let $\mathfrak{Y}\to\mathfrak{X}$ be its deformation to the normal cone, with closed fiber $\mathfrak{Y}_{0}\to\mathfrak{X}_{0}$ .

We begin with the Hodge cohomology. Recall that stacks affine over $\mathrm{B}\mathbb{G}_{m}$ correspond to graded rings, whose quasicoherent sheaves correspond to graded modules, and taking global section corresponds to taking the $0$ th grade.

#### Proposition 5.14.

Let $A\to B$ be a regular pair of codimension $r$ . For any $n\in\mathbb{Z}$ , the local cohomology $\mathrm{R}\Gamma_{\spec(B[t])}(\mathrm{L}\Omega^{n}_{\mathcal{R}_{B/A}/\mathbb{Z}[t]})$ and $\mathrm{R}\Gamma_{\spec(B)}(\mathrm{L}\Omega^{n}_{\lsym_{B}^{\star}(I/I^{2})/\mathbb{Z}})$ are both nonnegatively graded, and the base change map along $A[t]\to A$ , $t\mapsto 0$ identifies the $0$ th grade parts of them.

#### Proof.

Localizing, we can assume that $A\to B$ is a base change of $\mathbb{Z}[x_{1},\ldots,x_{r}]\to\mathbb{Z}$ . Consider the direct sums

$$ \bigoplus_{n\in\mathbb{Z}}\mathrm{R}\Gamma_{\spec(B[t])}(\mathrm{L}\Omega^{n}_{\mathcal{R}_{B/A}/\mathbb{Z}[t]}[-n])\in\mathsf{D}(\mathbb{Z}[t]) $$

and

$$ \bigoplus_{n\in\mathbb{Z}}\mathrm{R}\Gamma_{\spec(B)}(\mathrm{L}\Omega^{n}_{\lsym_{B}^{\star}(I/I^{2})/\mathbb{Z}}[-n])\in\mathsf{D}(\mathbb{Z}) $$

instead of individual complexes. Then they commute with sifted colimits in $A$ as $\mathbb{Z}[x_{1},\ldots,x_{r}]$ -algebras, and take coproducts of pairs to tensor products, so one reduces to the case $r$ is either $1$ or $0$ and $A\to B$ is either $\mathbb{Z}[x]\to\mathbb{Z}$ or $\mathbb{Z}[y]\to\mathbb{Z}[y]$ , respectively. Now $\mathrm{L}\Omega^{n}$ is nonzero only when $n=0$ or $n=1$ .

In the $\mathbb{Z}[x]\to\mathbb{Z}$ case, $\mathcal{R}_{B/A}=\mathbb{Z}[xt^{-1},t]$ with the surjection to $B[t]=\mathbb{Z}[t]$ killing $xt^{-1}$ , so one computes

$$ \mathrm{R}\Gamma_{\spec(B[t])}(\mathcal{R}_{B/A})=\mathrm{R}\Gamma_{xt^{-1}}(\mathbb{Z}[xt^{-1},t])=\bigoplus_{k=1}^{\infty}\mathbb{Z}[t]t^{k}x^{-k}[-1], $$

$$ \mathrm{R}\Gamma_{\spec(B)}(\lsym_{B}^{\star}(I/I^{2}))=\mathrm{R}\Gamma_{xt^{-1}}(\mathbb{Z}[xt^{-1}])=\bigoplus_{k=1}^{\infty}\mathbb{Z}t^{k}x^{-k}[-1], $$

$$ \mathrm{R}\Gamma_{\spec(B[t])}(\mathrm{L}_{\mathcal{R}_{B/A}/\mathbb{Z}[t]})=\mathrm{R}\Gamma_{xt^{-1}}(\mathbb{Z}[xt^{-1},t]\mathrm{d}(xt^{-1}))=\bigoplus_{k=1}^{\infty}\mathbb{Z}[t]t^{k}x^{-k}\mathrm{d}(xt^{-1})[-1], $$

$$ \mathrm{R}\Gamma_{\spec(B)}(\mathrm{L}_{\lsym_{B}^{\star}(I/I^{2})/\mathbb{Z}})=\mathrm{R}\Gamma_{xt^{-1}}(\mathbb{Z}[xt^{-1}]\mathrm{d}(xt^{-1}))=\bigoplus_{k=1}^{\infty}\mathbb{Z}t^{k}x^{-k}\mathrm{d}(xt^{-1})[-1]. $$

In the $\mathbb{Z}[y]\to\mathbb{Z}[y]$ case, $A=B$ , $I=0$ and $\mathcal{R}_{B/A}=B[t]=\mathbb{Z}[y,t]$ , so the local cohomology does nothing, and one computes

$$ \mathrm{R}\Gamma_{\spec(B[t])}(\mathcal{R}_{B/A})=\mathbb{Z}[y,t], $$

$$ \mathrm{R}\Gamma_{\spec(B)}(\lsym_{B}^{\star}(I/I^{2}))=\mathbb{Z}[y], $$

$$ \mathrm{R}\Gamma_{\spec(B[t])}(\mathrm{L}_{\mathcal{R}_{B/A}/\mathbb{Z}[t]})=\mathbb{Z}[y,t]\mathrm{d}y, $$

$$ \mathrm{R}\Gamma_{\spec(B)}(\mathrm{L}_{\lsym_{B}^{\star}(I/I^{2})/\mathbb{Z}})=\mathbb{Z}[y]\mathrm{d}y. $$

In all these cases one easily verifies the proposition. ∎

#### Corollary 5.15.

For every $n\in\mathbb{N}$ , the inclusion $\mathfrak{X}_{0}\to\mathfrak{X}$ induces an isomorphism

$$ \mathrm{R}\Gamma_{\mathfrak{Y}}(\mathfrak{X},\mathrm{L}\Omega^{n}_{\mathfrak{X}})\cong\mathrm{R}\Gamma_{\mathfrak{Y}_{0}}(\mathfrak{X}_{0},\mathrm{L}\Omega^{n}_{\mathfrak{X}_{0}}). $$

#### Proof.

Both sides are sheaves with respect to $X$ , so one can assume that $X=\spec(A)$ is affine, and hence so is $Y=\spec(B)$ . Let $f\colon\mathfrak{X}\to\mathbb{A}^{1}/\mathbb{G}_{m}$ and $f_{0}\colon\mathfrak{X}_{0}\to\mathrm{B}\mathbb{G}_{m}$ be the structure maps. Then we have the fiber sequences

$$ f^{*}\mathrm{L}_{\mathbb{A}^{1}/\mathbb{G}_{m}}\to\mathrm{L}_{\mathfrak{X}}\to\mathrm{L}_{\mathfrak{X}/(\mathbb{A}^{1}/\mathbb{G}_{m})} $$

and

$$ f_{0}^{*}\mathrm{L}_{\mathrm{B}\mathbb{G}_{m}}\to\mathrm{L}_{\mathfrak{X}_{0}}\to\mathrm{L}_{\mathfrak{X}_{0}/\mathrm{B}\mathbb{G}_{m}}, $$

which imply that $\mathrm{L}\Omega_{\mathfrak{X}}^{n}$ is filtered by $\mathrm{L}\Omega_{\mathfrak{X}/(\mathbb{A}^{1}/\mathbb{G}_{m})}^{i}\otimes f^{*}\mathrm{L}\Omega_{\mathbb{A}^{1}/\mathbb{G}_{m}}^{j}$ with $i+j=n$ , and similarly for $\mathfrak{X}_{0}$ . Now by Example 3.33, $\mathrm{R}\Gamma_{\mathfrak{Y}}(\mathrm{L}\Omega_{\mathfrak{X}/(\mathbb{A}^{1}/\mathbb{G}_{m})}^{i}\otimes f^{*}\mathrm{L}\Omega_{\mathbb{A}^{1}/\mathbb{G}_{m}}^{j})$ is computed by taking the $0$ th grade part of

$$ \mathrm{R}\Gamma_{\spec(B[t])}(\mathrm{L}\Omega^{n}_{\mathcal{R}_{B/A}/\mathbb{Z}[t]})\otimes_{\mathbb{Z}[t]}\mathrm{L}\Lambda_{\mathbb{Z}[t]}^{j}(\mathbb{Z}[-1]), $$

while by Example 3.32, $\mathrm{R}\Gamma_{\mathfrak{Y}_{0}}(\mathrm{L}\Omega_{\mathfrak{X}_{0}/\mathrm{B}\mathbb{G}_{m}}^{i}\otimes f_{0}^{*}\mathrm{L}\Omega_{\mathrm{B}\mathbb{G}_{m}}^{j})$ is computed by taking the $0$ th grade part of

$$ \mathrm{R}\Gamma_{\spec(B)}(\mathrm{L}\Omega^{n}_{\lsym_{B}^{\star}(I/I^{2})})\otimes{Z}\mathrm{L}\Lambda{Z}^{j}(\mathbb{Z}[-1]), $$

and by Proposition 5.14 it is not hard to see that the two are isomorphic via the natural map. ∎

We then study the étale cohomology.

#### Proposition 5.16.

Suppose $X$ and $Y$ are over $\mathbb{Z}[1/p]$ . Let $\tilde{\mathfrak{Y}}\to\tilde{\mathfrak{X}}$ be the deformation to the normal cone without quotient by $\mathbb{G}_{m}$ , and $\tilde{\mathfrak{Y}}_{0}\to\tilde{\mathfrak{X}}_{0}$ be the fiber over $0\to\mathbb{A}^{1}$ . Then for every étale $\mathbb{Z}_{p}$ -sheaf $\mathcal{M}$ on $X$ , the inclusion $\tilde{\mathfrak{X}}_{0}\to\tilde{\mathfrak{X}}$ induces an isomorphism on local cohomology

$$ \mathrm{R}\Gamma_{\mathrm{\acute{e}t},\tilde{\mathfrak{Y}}}(\tilde{\mathfrak{X}},\tilde{f}^{*}\mathcal{M})\cong\mathrm{R}\Gamma_{\mathrm{\acute{e}t},\tilde{\mathfrak{Y}}_{0}}(\tilde{\mathfrak{X}}_{0},\tilde{f}_{0}^{*}\mathcal{M}). $$

Here $\tilde{f}\colon\tilde{\mathfrak{X}}\to X$ and $\tilde{f}_{0}\colon\tilde{\mathfrak{X}}_{0}\to\tilde{\mathfrak{X}}\to X$ are the natural maps.

#### Proof.

The proposition is clearly étale local on $X$ , so we can assume that $X=\spec(A)$ is affine, and hence so is $Y=\spec(B)$ . Then $\tilde{\mathfrak{X}}=\spec(\mathcal{R}_{B/A})$ , $\tilde{\mathfrak{Y}}=\spec(B[t])$ , $\tilde{\mathfrak{X}}_{0}=\spec(\lsym_{B}^{\star}(I/I^{2}))$ , $\tilde{\mathfrak{Y}}_{0}=\spec(B)$ , as in Definition 5.11. By excision, we can assume that the pair $A\to B$ is Henselian, i.e. the classical pair $\pi_{0}A\to\pi_{0}B$ is Henselian.

Now by Remark 5.13 and excision, the left hand side is

$$ \mathrm{R}\Gamma_{\mathrm{\acute{e}t}}(\mathrm{Bl}_{Y}(\mathbb{A}^{1}_{X}),\mathrm{Bl}_{Y}(\mathbb{A}^{1}_{X})\setminus\spec(\mathbb{A}^{1}_{Y}),g^{*}\mathcal{M}), $$

where $g\colon\mathrm{Bl}_{Y}(\mathbb{A}^{1}_{X})\to X$ is the projection. To compute it, we consider the compactification $j\colon\mathrm{Bl}_{Y}(\mathbb{A}^{1}_{X})\to\mathrm{Bl}_{Y}(\mathbb{P}^{1}_{X})$ , which also compactifies $\mathbb{A}^{1}_{Y}$ to $\mathbb{P}^{1}_{Y}$ . Let $\pi$ denote the projections $\mathrm{Bl}_{Y}(\mathbb{P}^{1}_{X})\to X$ , and $i$ denote the complement of $j$ . Since the inclusion $Y\to\mathbb{A}^{1}_{X}$ has image in $0\to\mathbb{A}^{1}_{X}$ , the blowup changes nothing near $\infty\to\mathbb{P}^{1}_{X}$ . Therefore by the étale Poincaré duality and by excision again, we have $i^{!}\pi^{*}\mathcal{M}=\mathcal{M}(-1)[-2]$ . Hence

$$ \displaystyle\mathrm{R}\Gamma_{\mathrm{\acute{e}t}}(\mathrm{Bl}_{Y}(\mathbb{A}^{1}_{X}),g^{*}\mathcal{M}) \displaystyle=\mathrm{R}\Gamma_{\mathrm{\acute{e}t}}(\mathrm{Bl}_{Y}(\mathbb{P}^{1}_{X}),j_{*}g^{*}\mathcal{M}) \displaystyle=\mathrm{R}\Gamma_{\mathrm{\acute{e}t}}(\mathrm{Bl}_{Y}(\mathbb{P}^{1}_{X}),\cofib(i_{!}i^{!}\pi^{*}\mathcal{M}\to\pi^{*}\mathcal{M})) \displaystyle=\cofib(\mathrm{R}\Gamma_{\mathrm{\acute{e}t}}(X,\mathcal{M}(-1)[-2])\to\mathrm{R}\Gamma_{\mathrm{\acute{e}t}}(\mathrm{Bl}_{Y}(\mathbb{P}^{1}_{X}),\pi^{*}\mathcal{M})). $$

Note that $\mathrm{Bl}_{Y}(\mathbb{P}^{1}_{X})$ is proper over $X$ , whose fiber over $Y$ is $\mathbb{P}^{1}_{Y}\sqcup_{Y}\mathbb{P}(\mathcal{N}_{Y/X}\oplus\mathcal{O}_{Y})$ . Here $\mathcal{N}_{Y/X}$ denotes the normal bundle and $\mathbb{P}$ means projectivization. Therefore by Gabber’s affine proper base change [Stacks, 09ZI],

$$ \mathrm{R}\Gamma_{\mathrm{\acute{e}t}}(\mathrm{Bl}_{Y}(\mathbb{P}^{1}_{X}),\pi^{*}\mathcal{M})=\mathrm{R}\Gamma_{\mathrm{\acute{e}t}}(\mathbb{P}^{1}_{Y}\sqcup_{Y}\mathbb{P}(\mathcal{N}_{Y/X}\oplus\mathcal{O}_{Y}),\bar{\pi}^{*}\mathcal{M}), $$

where $\bar{\pi}$ denotes the corresponding projection. Take the pushout out of $\mathrm{R}\Gamma_{\mathrm{\acute{e}t}}$ , and note that $\mathrm{R}\Gamma_{\mathrm{\acute{e}t}}(X,\mathcal{M}(-1)[-2])=\mathrm{R}\Gamma_{\mathrm{\acute{e}t}}(Y,\mathcal{M}(-1)[-2]|_{Y})$ cancels the $\mathbb{P}^{1}_{Y}\sqcup_{Y}-$ again by the affine proper base change, we conclude that

$$ \mathrm{R}\Gamma_{\mathrm{\acute{e}t}}(\mathrm{Bl}_{Y}(\mathbb{A}^{1}_{X}),g^{*}\mathcal{M})=\mathrm{R}\Gamma_{\mathrm{\acute{e}t}}(\mathbb{P}(\mathcal{N}_{Y/X}\oplus\mathcal{O}_{Y}),\pi_{0}^{*}\mathcal{M}), $$

where $\pi_{0}$ denotes the projection $\mathbb{P}(\mathcal{N}_{Y/X}\oplus\mathcal{O}_{Y})\to X$ . On the other hand, note that $\mathrm{Bl}_{Y}(\mathbb{A}^{1}_{X})\setminus\spec(\mathbb{A}^{1}_{Y})$ is the total space of $\mathcal{O}(-1)$ on $\mathrm{Bl}_{Y}(X)$ , so by Lemma 3.34 and the affine proper base change,

$$ \mathrm{R}\Gamma_{\mathrm{\acute{e}t}}(\mathrm{Bl}_{Y}(\mathbb{A}^{1}_{X})\setminus\spec(\mathbb{A}^{1}_{Y}),\pi^{*}\mathcal{M})=\mathrm{R}\Gamma_{\mathrm{\acute{e}t}}(\mathrm{Bl}_{Y}(X),\beta^{*}\mathcal{M})=\mathrm{R}\Gamma_{\mathrm{\acute{e}t}}(\mathbb{P}(\mathcal{N}_{Y/X}),\beta_{0}^{*}\mathcal{M}), $$

where $\beta\colon\mathrm{Bl}_{Y}(X)\to X$ and $\beta_{0}\colon\mathbb{P}(\mathcal{N}_{Y/X})\to X$ are the projections. Recall that the total space of $\mathcal{O}(-1)$ on $\mathbb{P}(\mathcal{N}_{Y/X})$ is $\mathbb{P}(\mathcal{N}_{Y/X}\oplus\mathcal{O}_{Y})\setminus 0$ , so we finally have

$$ \displaystyle\quad\ \mathrm{R}\Gamma_{\mathrm{\acute{e}t}}(\mathrm{Bl}_{Y}(\mathbb{A}^{1}_{X}),\mathrm{Bl}_{Y}(\mathbb{A}^{1}_{X})\setminus\spec(\mathbb{A}^{1}_{Y}),g^{*}\mathcal{M}) \displaystyle=\fib(\mathrm{R}\Gamma_{\mathrm{\acute{e}t}}(\mathbb{P}(\mathcal{N}_{Y/X}\oplus\mathcal{O}_{Y}),\pi_{0}^{*}\mathcal{M})\to\mathrm{R}\Gamma_{\mathrm{\acute{e}t}}(\mathbb{P}(\mathcal{N}_{Y/X}),\beta_{0}^{*}\mathcal{M})) \displaystyle=\mathrm{R}\Gamma_{\mathrm{\acute{e}t}}(\mathbb{P}(\mathcal{N}_{Y/X}\oplus\mathcal{O}_{Y}),\mathbb{P}(\mathcal{N}_{Y/X}\oplus\mathcal{O}_{Y})\setminus 0,\pi_{0}^{*}\mathcal{M}), $$

but this is exactly the right hand side

$$ \mathrm{R}\Gamma_{\mathrm{\acute{e}t}}(\tilde{\mathfrak{X}}_{0},\tilde{\mathfrak{X}}_{0}\setminus\tilde{\mathfrak{Y}}_{0},\tilde{f}_{0}^{*}\mathcal{M})=\mathrm{R}\Gamma_{\mathrm{\acute{e}t}}(\mathcal{N}_{Y/X},\mathcal{N}_{Y/X}\setminus 0,\tilde{f}_{0}^{*}\mathcal{M}), $$

by excision. ∎

#### Corollary 5.17.

For every $n\in\mathbb{Z}$ , the inclusion $\mathfrak{X}_{0}\to\mathfrak{X}$ induces an isomorphism

$$ \mathrm{R}\Gamma_{\mathrm{\acute{e}t},\mathfrak{Y}}(\mathfrak{X},\mathbb{Z}_{p}(n))\cong\mathrm{R}\Gamma_{\mathrm{\acute{e}t},\mathfrak{Y}_{0}}(\mathfrak{X}_{0},\mathbb{Z}_{p}(n)). $$

#### Proof.

This follows immediately from Proposition 5.16 by descent. ∎

We finally study the étale cohomology of the generic fiber. As before, we use the étale comparison of the prismatic cohomology to control it.

#### Proposition 5.18.

The inclusion $\mathfrak{X}_{0}\to\mathfrak{X}$ induces an isomorphism

$$ {{\mathbbl{\Delta}}}_{\mathfrak{X},\mathfrak{X}\setminus\mathfrak{Y},\mathrm{perf}}\cong{{\mathbbl{\Delta}}}_{\mathfrak{X}_{0},\mathfrak{X}_{0}\setminus\mathfrak{Y}_{0},\mathrm{perf}}. $$

#### Proof.

The proof is similar to that of Proposition 3.38. Both sides are $\mathrm{arc}_{p}$ sheaves over $X$ , so we can assume that $X=\spec(R)$ is the spectrum of a perfectoid ring, and then $Y=\spec(S)$ is the spectrum of an $R$ -algebra. Now $S=R/(x_{1},\ldots,x_{r})$ is a derived complete intersection in $R$ . Then $S$ is homotopically bounded and quasi-lci over $R$ , so by Lemma 3.24 and Corollary 5.15, we have ${{\mathbbl{\Delta}}}_{\mathfrak{X},\mathfrak{X}\setminus\mathfrak{Y}}={{\mathbbl{\Delta}}}_{\mathfrak{X}_{0},\mathfrak{X}_{0}\setminus\mathfrak{Y}_{0}}$ . Finally Lemma 3.20 gives us the desired equality. ∎

#### Corollary 5.19.

Let $\mathcal{F}$ be the big étale sheaf $R\mapsto\mathrm{R}\Gamma_{\mathrm{\acute{e}t}}(\spec(\hat{R}[1/p]),\mathbb{Z}_{p}(n))$ , where $n\in\mathbb{Z}$ is fixed. Then the inclusion $\mathfrak{X}_{0}\to\mathfrak{X}$ induces an isomorphism

$$ \mathcal{F}(\mathfrak{X},\mathfrak{X}\setminus\mathfrak{Y})\cong\mathcal{F}(\mathfrak{X}_{0},\mathfrak{X}_{0}\setminus\mathfrak{Y}_{0}). $$

#### Proof.

The proof is similar to that of Corollary 3.40. Both sides are $\mathrm{arc}_{p}$ sheaves over $X$ , so we can assume that $X=\spec(R)$ for a $\mathbb{Z}_{p}^{\mathrm{cyc}}$ -algebra $R$ . Since $\mathbb{Z}_{p}(n)\cong\mathbb{Z}_{p}$ on $\spec(\mathbb{Q}_{p}^{\mathrm{cyc}})$ , we can assume $n=0$ . Also, both are quotients of qcqs schemes by $\mathbb{G}_{m}$ , so we can use Čech nerves to compute them. Since $\mathcal{F}(U)=({{\mathbbl{\Delta}}}_{U,\mathrm{perf}}[1/I]_{p}^{\wedge})^{\varphi=1}$ for any qcqs scheme $U$ (which follows from the affine case by taking a finite limit), the desired equality follows from Proposition 3.38 and Lemma 3.20. ∎

Finally, we can prove our theorem on the syntomic cohomology of the deformation to the normal cone.

#### Theorem 5.20.

For every integer $n$ , the inclusion $\mathfrak{X}_{0}\to\mathfrak{X}$ induces an isomorphism

$$ \mathrm{R}\Gamma_{\mathrm{syn}}(\mathfrak{X},\mathfrak{X}\setminus\mathfrak{Y},\mathbb{Z}_{p}(n))\cong\mathrm{R}\Gamma_{\mathrm{syn}}(\mathfrak{X}_{0},\mathfrak{X}_{0}\setminus\mathfrak{Y}_{0},\mathbb{Z}_{p}(n)). $$

#### Proof.

Combine Lemma 3.23, Corollary 5.15, Corollary 5.17, and Corollary 5.19. ∎
