We wonder whether the same holds for general closed immersions, not necessarily regular. For the étale cohomology the same proof seems to show the general statement, while for the Hodge cohomology and the étale cohomology of the generic fiber we have no idea.

### 5.2. Constructing cycle classes

We now use what we have computed in the previous subsection to construct cycle classes from Thom classes.

#### Theorem 5.22 (Characteristic classes of regular pairs).

Let $\mathcal{C}$ be a pointed presentable category and let $\mathcal{F}$ be a big étale sheaf with values in $\mathcal{C}$ . Fix $r\in\mathbb{N}$ . Let $\mathrm{E}_{r}$ denotes the universal rank $r$ vector bundle over $\mathrm{B}\mathrm{GL}_{r}$ and $0_{r}$ denotes the zero section. Then since $0_{r}\to\mathrm{E}_{r}$ is a regular immersion of codimension $r$ , it corresponds to a map $\beta_{r}\colon\mathrm{E}_{r}\to\mathrm{Pair}_{r}$ with $\beta_{r}^{-1}(\mathrm{Closed}_{r})=0_{r}$ . Assume that for any regular immersion $Y\to X$ of stacks of codimension $r$ , we have

$$ \mathcal{F}(\mathfrak{X},\mathfrak{X}\setminus\mathfrak{Y})=\mathcal{F}(\mathfrak{X}_{0},\mathfrak{X}_{0}\setminus\mathfrak{Y}_{0}), $$

where $\mathfrak{Y}\to\mathfrak{X}$ is the deformation to the normal cone of $Y\to X$ and $\mathfrak{Y}_{0}\to\mathfrak{X}_{0}$ is its closed fiber. Then $\beta_{r}$ induces an isomorphism

$$ \beta_{r}^{*}\colon\mathcal{F}(\mathrm{Pair}_{r},\mathrm{Open}_{r})\cong\mathcal{F}(\mathrm{E}_{r},\mathrm{E}_{r}\setminus 0_{r}). $$

In other words, all the $\mathcal{F}$ -characteristic classes of pairs that vanish on the open loci come from those of zero sections in rank $r$ vector bundles.

#### Proof.

Let $\mathrm{DNC}_{r}\to\mathrm{Pair}_{r}\times\mathbb{A}^{1}/\mathbb{G}_{m}$ denote the deformation to the normal cone of $\mathrm{Pair}_{r}$ , and $\mathrm{Open}_{\mathrm{DNC}_{r}}$ denote the complement of $\mathrm{Closed}_{r}\times\mathbb{A}^{1}/\mathbb{G}_{m}$ in $\mathrm{DNC}_{r}$ . Let $\mathrm{DNC}_{r,0}$ and $\mathrm{Open}_{\mathrm{DNC}_{r,0}}$ denote the fiber of $\mathrm{DNC}_{r}$ and $\mathrm{Open}_{\mathrm{DNC}_{r}}$ , respectively. By construction, $\mathrm{DNC}_{r,0}$ is the weighted normal bundle of $\mathrm{Closed}_{r}\to\mathrm{Pair}_{r}$ , so there is a natural classifying map $\mathrm{DNC}_{r,0}\to\mathrm{E}_{r}$ . Consider the diagram

$$ {\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathrm{DNC}_{r,0}} {\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathrm{E}_{r}} {\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathrm{Pair}_{r}} {\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathrm{DNC}_{r}} {\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathrm{Pair}_{r}} $$

where the lower left map is the natural open immersion identifying $\mathrm{Pair}_{r}$ with the fiber over $\mathbb{G}_{m}/\mathbb{G}_{m}$ of $\mathrm{DNC}_{r}$ . Then it exhibits $\mathrm{Pair}_{r}$ as a retract of $\mathrm{DNC}_{r}$ . Now take $\mathcal{F}$ relative to the open parts. Since the central vertical map becomes an isomorphism after this operation, the diagram exhibits $\mathcal{F}(\mathrm{Pair}_{r},\mathrm{Open}_{r})$ as a retract of $\mathcal{F}(\mathrm{E}_{r},\mathrm{E}_{r}\setminus 0_{r})$ , i.e. $\beta_{r}^{*}$ has a left inverse.

Note that the above diagram gives an endomorphism of $\mathcal{F}(\mathrm{E}_{r},\mathrm{E}_{r}\setminus 0_{r})$ by splicing $\beta_{r}\colon\mathrm{E}_{r}\to\mathrm{Pair}_{r}$ to its lower left corner. We will finish the proof by showing that it is the identity, since then the left inverse of $\beta_{r}^{*}$ will also be the right inverse. To this end, we can base change the above diagram from $\mathrm{Pair}_{r}$ to $\mathrm{E}_{r}$ and get the diagram

$$ {\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathrm{DNC}_{r,0}\times_{\mathrm{Pair}_{r}}\mathrm{E}_{r}} {\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathrm{E}_{r}} {\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathrm{E}_{r}} {\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathrm{DNC}_{r}\times_{\mathrm{Pair}_{r}}\mathrm{E}_{r}} $$

where the upper right map is not the projection but the classifying map of the weighted normal bundle. Now by Lemma 5.23 below, there is a map indicated by the dashed arrow that makes the diagram commutes and exhibits $\mathrm{E}_{r}$ as a retract of $\mathrm{DNC}_{r}\times_{\mathrm{Pair}_{r}}\mathrm{E}_{r}$ , therefore completing the proof. ∎

#### Lemma 5.23.

The deformation to the normal cone of the zero section of a vector bundle $V$ on a stack $X$ is the zero section of the vector bundle $V(-1)$ on $X\times\mathbb{A}^{1}/\mathbb{G}_{m}$ , where $(-1)$ denotes the twist by the inverse of the universal bundle on $\mathrm{B}\mathbb{G}_{m}$ . Therefore, it restricts to $V$ itself on the open fiber, and restricts to the weighted normal bundle on the closed fiber.

#### Proof.

Recall that the deformation to the normal cone of $\mathbb{Z}[x]\to\mathbb{Z}$ is $\mathbb{Z}[xt^{-1},t]\to\mathbb{Z}[t]$ . By its compatibility of base change and products, we know that the deformation to the normal cone of $B[x_{1},\ldots,x_{r}]\to B$ is $B[x_{1}t^{-1},\ldots,x_{r}t^{-1},t]\to B[t]$ , which is the zero section of the $(-1)$ -twisted trivial bundle on $\spec(B)\times\mathbb{A}^{1}/\mathbb{G}_{m}$ as described. Note that this identification is compatible with change of coordinates, so we can globalize it and conclude. ∎

#### Remark 5.24.

The proof of Theorem 5.22 actually proves a stronger statement: Let $\mathcal{F}$ be a big étale sheaf over $\mathrm{Pair}_{r}$ that satisfies the same assumption with points taken over $\mathrm{Pair}_{r}$ . Then $\beta_{r}$ induces an isomorphism

$$ \beta_{r}^{*}\colon\mathcal{F}(\mathrm{Pair}_{r},\mathrm{Open}_{r})\cong\mathcal{F}(\mathrm{E}_{r},\mathrm{E}_{r}\setminus 0_{r}), $$

still with points taken over $\mathrm{Pair}_{r}$ .

#### Remark 5.25.

Let $\mathcal{F}$ be as in Theorem 5.22, and $Y\to X$ be a map of stacks. Then $\mathcal{G}(-)=\mathcal{F}(X\times-,Y\times-)$ also satisfies the same assumption as $\mathcal{F}$ does, since deformation to the normal cone commutes with $X\times-$ and $Y\times-$ . Therefore

$$ \mathcal{F}((X,Y)\times(\mathrm{Pair}_{r},\mathrm{Open}_{r}))\cong\mathcal{F}((X,Y)\times(\mathrm{E}_{r},\mathrm{E}_{r}\setminus 0)), $$

where the product is understood as

$$ (X_{0},Y_{0})\times(X_{1},Y_{1})=(X_{0}\times X_{1},(Y_{0}\times X_{1})\sqcup_{Y_{0}\times Y_{1}}(X_{0}\times Y_{1})). $$

In the rest of this subsection, let $\mathcal{F}$ be as in Situation 4.1 and suppose $\mathcal{F}$ satisfies the assumption of Theorem 5.22 for all $r\in\mathbb{N}$ . By the previous subsection, this holds for $\mathcal{F}^{n}(R)$ being $\mathrm{L}\Omega^{n}_{R}[n]$ , $\mathrm{R}\Gamma_{\mathrm{\acute{e}t}}(R[1/p],\mathbb{Z}_{p}(n))[2n]$ , and $\mathrm{R}\Gamma_{\mathrm{syn}}(R,\mathbb{Z}_{p}(n))[2n]$ .

#### Definition 5.26 (Cycle classes).

For $r\in\mathbb{N}$ , let $\mathrm{Cl}_{r}^{\mathcal{F}}\in\Omega^{\infty}\mathcal{F}^{r}(\mathrm{Pair}_{r},\mathrm{Open}_{r})$ be the image of the universal Thom class $\mathrm{Th}_{r}^{\mathcal{F}}\in\Omega^{\infty}\mathcal{F}^{r}(\mathrm{E}_{r},\mathrm{E}_{r}\setminus 0_{r})$ under the isomorphism in Theorem 5.22, called the universal cycle class of codimension $r$ . For a regular immersion $Y\to X$ of codimension $r$ , let $\mathrm{Cl}_{Y/X}^{\mathcal{F}}\in\Omega^{\infty}\mathcal{F}^{r}(X,X\setminus Y)$ be the pullback of $\mathrm{Cl}_{r}^{\mathcal{F}}$ along the classifying map $X\to\mathrm{Pair}_{r}$ , called the cycle class of $Y$ in $X$ . By abuse of notation, we also use $\mathrm{Cl}_{Y/X}^{\mathcal{F}}$ to denote its image in $\Omega^{\infty}\mathcal{F}^{r}(X)$ .

#### Remark 5.27 (Relation with blowup).

Suppose the blowup formula holds, i.e.

$$ {\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathcal{F}(D)} {\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathcal{F}(\tilde{X})} {\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathcal{F}(Y)} {\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathcal{F}(X)} $$

is a pullback square for every regular immersion $Y\to X$ of codimension $r$ with blowup $\tilde{X}$ and exceptional divisor $D$ (by [BL22, Theorem 9.4.1] this is the case for syntomic cohomology). Suppose further that we have a decomposition

$$ \mathcal{F}^{\star}(\tilde{X})=\mathcal{F}^{\star}(X)\oplus\bigoplus_{i=1}^{r-1}\mathcal{F}^{\star-i}(Y) $$

functorial on $Y\to X$ , extending the projective bundle formula of $D=\mathbb{P}(\mathcal{N}_{Y/X})$ . Denoting $U=X\setminus Y=\tilde{X}\setminus D$ , one gets from above a similar decomposition

$$ \mathcal{F}^{\star}(\tilde{X},U)=\mathcal{F}^{\star}(X,U)\oplus\bigoplus_{i=1}^{r-1}\mathcal{F}^{\star-i}(Y). $$

In this case, $\mathrm{Cl}_{Y/X}^{\mathcal{F}}$ can also be defined as the image of $-c_{1}(-D)^{r}\in\Omega^{\infty}\mathcal{F}^{r}(\tilde{X},U)$ under the projection to $\Omega^{\infty}\mathcal{F}^{r}(X,U)$ (cf. [Fuj02, Definition 1.1.2]). In fact, by functoriality and Theorem 5.22, it suffices to check the case $0_{r}\to\mathrm{E}_{r}$ , which can be easily done by hand.

#### Remark 5.28 (Uniqueness).

By construction, it is easy to see that the cycle class is uniquely determined by the following requirements:

For $f\colon X^{\prime}\to X$ a morphism of stacks with $Y^{\prime}=Y\times_{X}X^{\prime}$ , we have $\mathrm{Cl}_{Y^{\prime}/X^{\prime}}^{\mathcal{F}}=f^{*}\mathrm{Cl}_{Y/X}^{\mathcal{F}}$ .

For the zero section of a vector bundle, it is the Thom class in Theorem 4.2.

Therefore, the cycle class is natural in $\mathcal{F}$ with respect to maps that preserve $c_{1}$ , cf. Remark 4.9.

#### Remark 5.29 (Multiplicativity).

By Theorem 5.22 and the additivity of Thom classes, one easily deduces that $\mathrm{Cl}_{r^{\prime}}^{\mathcal{F}}\boxtimes\mathrm{Cl}_{r^{\prime\prime}}^{\mathcal{F}}=m^{*}\mathrm{Cl}_{r}^{\mathcal{F}}$ , where $r=r^{\prime}+r^{\prime\prime}$ and $m\colon\mathrm{Pair}_{r^{\prime}}\times\mathrm{Pair}_{r^{\prime\prime}}\to\mathrm{Pair}_{r}$ represents the intersection. By Remark 4.8 and Theorem 5.22, the cycle classes are uniquely determined by multiplicativity and the normalization in codimension $1$ , which states that $\mathrm{Cl}_{D/X}=c_{1}(\mathcal{O}(D))$ for a Cartier divisor $D\to X$ .

The multiplicativity in the above remark has no homotopy coherence a priori, but the coconnectivity condition on $\mathcal{F}$ actually forces the coherence. This will not be used in the sequel.

#### Lemma 5.30.

Let $\mathcal{C}^{\otimes}$ be a symmetric monoidal category and let $A,B\in\mathsf{CAlg}(\mathcal{C})$ . Suppose for every $n\in\mathbb{N}$ that $\Hom_{\mathcal{C}}(A^{\otimes n},B)$ is $0$ -truncated. Then

$$ \Hom_{\mathsf{CAlg}(\mathcal{C})}(A,B)=\Hom_{\mathsf{CAlg}(\mathrm{h}\mathcal{C})}(A,B) $$

and is $0$ -truncated, where $\mathrm{h}\mathcal{C}$ means the homotopy $1$ -category of $\mathcal{C}$ .

#### Proof.

Recall from [HA, Definition 2.1.3.1] that $\mathsf{CAlg}(\mathcal{C})=\mathsf{Fun}_{\mathsf{Fin}_{*}}(\mathsf{Fin}_{*},\mathcal{C}^{\otimes})$ , and $A,B\in\mathsf{CAlg}(\mathcal{C})$ are actually functors $A^{\otimes},B^{\otimes}\colon\mathsf{Fin}_{*}\to\mathcal{C}^{\otimes}$ that takes $\left<1\right>$ to $A,B\in\mathcal{C}$ . As $\Hom$ in the functor category, $\Hom_{\mathsf{CAlg}(\mathcal{C})}(A,B)$ is built up as a limit of $\Hom_{\mathcal{C}^{\otimes}}^{f}(A^{\otimes}_{\left<n\right>},B^{\otimes}_{\left<m\right>})$ for $n,m\in\mathbb{N}$ and $f\colon\left<n\right>\to\left<m\right>$ in $\mathsf{Fin}_{*}$ . Since by definition $\mathcal{C}^{\otimes}\to\mathsf{Fin}_{*}$ is a cocartesian fibration, we have

$$ \Hom_{\mathcal{C}^{\otimes}}^{f}(A^{\otimes}_{\left<n\right>},B^{\otimes}_{\left<m\right>})=\Hom_{\mathcal{C}^{\otimes}_{\left<m\right>}}(\otimes_{f}(A^{\otimes}_{\left<n\right>}),B^{\otimes}_{\left<m\right>}) $$

in the notation of [HA, Remark 2.1.2.16]; then by [HA, Remark 2.1.2.19] one easily computes that

$$ \Hom_{\mathcal{C}^{\otimes}_{\left<m\right>}}(\otimes_{f}(A^{\otimes}_{\left<n\right>}),B^{\otimes}_{\left<m\right>})=\prod_{i=1}^{m}\Hom_{\mathcal{C}}(A^{\otimes f^{-1}(i)},B), $$

which is $0$ -truncated by assumption. Therefore, as a limit of $0$ -truncated animas, $\Hom_{\mathsf{CAlg}(\mathcal{C})}(A,B)$ is also $0$ -truncated. Finally we conclude by noting that $\Hom_{\mathsf{CAlg}(\mathrm{h}\mathcal{C})}(A,B)$ is computed by exactly the same limit. ∎

Let $\mathrm{Pair}_{\mathrm{reg}}\subseteq\mathrm{Pair}$ denote the stack of regular pairs without a fixed dimension; then it inherits the $\mathbb{E}_{\infty}$ -monoid structure of $\mathrm{Pair}$ with respect to the smash product, as described at the end of Definition 5.7. Let $\Sigma^{\infty}$ denote the left adjoint of the functor $\Omega^{\infty}$ from the category of $\mathsf{Sp}$ -valued big étale sheaves to the category of pointed stacks, by abuse of notation. Then since $\mathrm{Pair}_{\mathrm{reg}}=(\mathrm{Pair}_{0})_{+}\vee\bigvee_{r\in\mathbb{Z}_{+}}\mathrm{Pair}_{r}$ is graded, $\Sigma^{\infty}\mathrm{Pair}_{\mathrm{reg}}$ is naturally a graded $\mathbb{E}_{\infty}$ -ring.

#### Proposition 5.31.

The multiplicativity in Remark 5.29 uniquely determines a map $\Sigma^{\infty}\mathrm{Pair}_{\mathrm{reg}}\to\mathcal{F}$ of big étale sheaves with values graded $\mathbb{E}_{\infty}$ -rings.

#### Proof.

By Lemma 5.30, it suffices to check for every $n\in\mathbb{N}$ that

$$ \Hom_{\mathsf{Fun}(\mathsf{Ring},\mathsf{Gr}\mathsf{Sp})}((\Sigma^{\infty}\mathrm{Pair}_{\mathrm{reg}})^{\otimes n},\mathcal{F})\in\mathsf{Ani}_{\leq 0}. $$

Passing to each grade and using the fact that $\Sigma^{\infty}$ takes the smash product to the tensor product, we need to check that for $r_{1},\ldots,r_{n}\in\mathbb{Z}_{+}$ and $r=\sum_{i=1}^{n}r_{i}$ ,

$$ \tilde{\mathcal{F}}^{r}\left(\bigwedge_{i=1}^{n}\mathrm{Pair}_{r_{i}}\right)\in\mathsf{Sp}_{\leq 0}. $$

Now by Remark 5.25,

$$ \tilde{\mathcal{F}}\left(\bigwedge_{i=1}^{n}\mathrm{Pair}_{r_{i}}\right)=\mathcal{F}\left(\prod_{i=1}^{n}(\mathrm{E}_{r_{i}},\mathrm{E}_{r_{i}}\setminus 0)\right), $$

so the desired coconnectivity follows by applying Proposition 4.6 $n$ times. ∎

Cycle classes can be upgraded to Gysin maps as follows:

#### Definition 5.32 (Gysin maps).

Fix $r\in\mathbb{N}$ . Let $Y\to X$ be a regular immersion of codimension $r$ , $\mathfrak{Y}\to\mathfrak{X}$ be its deformation to the normal cone and $\mathfrak{Y}_{0}\to\mathfrak{X}_{0}$ be the closed fiber. Then the Gysin map of $Y\to X$ is constructed as the composition

$$ \mathcal{F}^{\star}(Y)\to\mathcal{F}^{\star}(\mathfrak{Y}_{0})\to\mathcal{F}^{\star+r}(\mathfrak{X}_{0},\mathfrak{X}_{0}\setminus\mathfrak{Y}_{0})=\mathcal{F}^{\star+r}(\mathfrak{X},\mathfrak{X}\setminus\mathfrak{Y})\to\mathcal{F}^{\star+r}(X,X\setminus Y), $$

where the first arrow comes from the projection $\mathfrak{Y}_{0}=Y\times 0/\mathbb{G}_{m}\to Y$ , the second arrow is the Thom map, and the final arrow is restriction to the open fiber. By Theorem 5.22, $\mathrm{Cl}^{\mathcal{F}}_{Y/X}$ is the image of $1\in\Omega^{\infty}\mathcal{F}^{0}(Y)$ under the Gysin map. By the definition of the Thom map, after composing with the restriction $\mathcal{F}(X,X\setminus Y)\to\mathcal{F}(Y)$ , the Gysin map becomes multiplying $c_{r}(\mathcal{N}_{Y/X})$ .

We now identify the Gysin map for the Hodge cohomology. For a regular pair $R\to S$ , the functor $i_{*}\colon\mathsf{D}(S)\to\mathsf{D}(R)$ commutes with colimits, preserves compact objects, and hence has a right adjoint $i^{!}\colon\mathsf{D}(R)\to\mathsf{D}(S)$ that preserves colimits.

#### Lemma 5.33.

$i^{!}\colon\mathsf{D}(R)\to\mathsf{D}(S)$ satisfies the projection formula $i^{!}-=i^{!}R\otimes_{S}i^{*}-$ , and is compatible with base change of pairs.

#### Proof.

For $M\in\mathsf{D}(R)$ , the natural map

$$ M=\inhom_{R}(R,M)\to\inhom_{R}(i_{*}i^{!}R,M)=i_{*}\inhom_{S}(i^{!}R,i^{!}M) $$

gives by adjunction the desired map

$$ i^{!}R\otimes_{S}i^{*}M\to i^{!}M. $$

Now it is an isomorphism when $M=R$ , and both sides commute with colimits in $M$ , so it is an isomorphism for all $M\in\mathsf{D}(R)$ . For the compatibility with base change, one can check after $i_{*}$ , which follows from the fact that $i_{*}i^{!}-=\inhom_{R}(S,-)=S^{\vee}\otimes_{R}-$ , since by assumption $S$ is dualizable in $\mathsf{D}(R)$ . ∎

Now consider a regular immersion $i\colon Y\to X$ of stacks of codimension $r$ . Recall by Remark 3.6 that we still have the functor $i_{*}\colon\mathsf{D}(Y)\to\mathsf{D}(X)$ . Since colimits of quasicoherent sheaves can be computed locally, $i_{*}$ still commutes with colimits, is compatible with base change, and thus has a right adjoint $i^{!}$ that also has these properties and satisfies the projection formula.

#### Lemma 5.34.

There is a natural identification of $i^{!}\mathcal{O}_{X}=\det(\mathcal{N}_{Y/X})[-r]$ compatible with base change and product of pairs, where $\mathcal{N}_{Y/X}$ denotes the normal bundle.

#### Proof.

Computing locally, we see that $i^{!}\mathcal{O}_{X}$ is an invertible object in $\mathsf{D}(Y)$ . To identify it, we first consider the case where $\pi\colon X\to Y$ is a rank $r$ vector bundle and $i\colon Y\to X$ is the immersion of the zero section. Let $\mathcal{O}=\mathcal{O}_{Y}$ , $\mathcal{N}=\mathcal{N}_{Y/X}$ , and $\mathcal{A}=\lsym_{\mathcal{O}}^{\star}(\mathcal{N}^{\vee})=\pi_{*}\mathcal{O}_{X}$ . Now the Koszul sequence

$$ 0\to\mathcal{A}\otimes\Lambda^{r}\mathcal{N}^{\vee}\to\cdots\to\mathcal{A}\otimes\mathcal{N}^{\vee}\to\mathcal{A}\to\mathcal{O}\to 0 $$

gives a natural identification $\inhom_{\mathcal{A}}(\mathcal{O},\mathcal{A})=\det(\mathcal{N})[-r]$ as an $\mathcal{A}$ -module, so

$$ i^{!}\mathcal{O}_{X}=\pi_{*}i_{*}i^{!}\mathcal{O}_{X}=\pi_{*}\inhom_{\mathcal{A}}(\mathcal{O},\mathcal{A})=\det(\mathcal{N})[-r] $$

as an $\mathcal{O}$ -module.

For a general $i\colon Y\to X$ , we consider its deformation to the normal cone $\mathfrak{i}\colon\mathfrak{Y}\to\mathfrak{X}$ , whose closed fiber $\mathfrak{i}_{0}\colon\mathfrak{Y}_{0}\to\mathfrak{X}_{0}$ is naturally the vector bundle $\mathcal{N}_{Y/X}/\mathbb{G}_{m}$ on $\mathfrak{Y}_{0}=Y\times\mathrm{B}\mathbb{G}_{m}$ . Therefore by the previous paragraph, $\mathfrak{i}^{!}\mathcal{O}_{\mathfrak{X}}$ is an invertible object in $\mathsf{D}(\mathfrak{Y})$ , whose restriction on $\mathfrak{Y}_{0}=Y\times\mathrm{B}\mathbb{G}_{m}$ is $\det(\mathcal{N}_{Y/X})[-r]$ with $\mathbb{G}_{m}$ acting by weight $r$ . But $\mathfrak{Y}=Y\times\mathbb{A}^{1}/\mathbb{G}_{m}$ , so $\mathsf{D}(\mathfrak{Y})$ can be viewed as the category of graded quasicoherent $\mathcal{O}_{Y}[t]$ -modules. Now $\mathfrak{i}^{!}\mathcal{O}_{\mathfrak{X}}$ is an invertible graded $\mathcal{O}_{Y}[t]$ -modules which gives $\det(\mathcal{N}_{Y/X})[-r]$ on degree $r$ after quotient by $t$ . Hence

$$ \mathfrak{i}^{!}\mathcal{O}_{\mathfrak{X}}=\bigoplus_{n=r}^{\infty}\det(\mathcal{N}_{Y/X})t^{n}[-r], $$

and obviously its restriction to the open part $Y\to\mathfrak{Y}$ is $\det(\mathcal{N}_{Y/X})$ .

The compatibility with base change and product follows from the compatibility of both the deformation to the normal cone and the Koszul sequence. ∎

#### Construction 5.35.

Recall from the shifted fiber sequence of cotangent complexes

$$ \mathrm{L}_{Y/X}[-1]\to i^{*}\mathrm{L}_{X}\to\mathrm{L}_{Y} $$

that the normal bundle $\mathcal{N}_{Y/X}$ can be identified as $\mathrm{L}_{Y/X}[-1]^{\vee}$ . Since $\mathrm{L}_{Y/X}[-1]$ is locally free of rank $r$ , the above sequence gives a natural map

$$ \Lambda^{r}(\mathrm{L}_{Y/X}[-1])\otimes\mathrm{L}\Omega^{n}_{Y}\to i^{*}\mathrm{L}\Omega^{n+r}_{X}; $$

since $\Lambda^{r}(\mathrm{L}_{Y/X}[-1])=(i^{!}\mathcal{O}_{X}[r])^{\vee}$ by Lemma 5.34, we can take it to the right hand side, use the projection formula, and obtain a Gysin map

$$ \mathrm{L}\Omega^{n}_{Y}\to i^{!}\mathcal{O}_{X}\otimes\mathrm{L}\Omega^{n+r}_{X}[r]=i^{!}\mathrm{L}\Omega^{n+r}_{X}[r]. $$

#### Proposition 5.36.

The Gysin map for the Hodge cohomology is the global section of the adjunction $i_{*}\mathrm{L}\Omega^{n}_{Y}\to\mathrm{L}\Omega^{n+r}_{X}[r]$ of the above map. Since $i_{*}\mathrm{L}\Omega^{n}_{Y}$ restricts to $0$ on $X\setminus Y$ , it actually maps to the relative Hodge cohomology of $(X,X\setminus Y)$ .

#### Proof.

Consider the deformation to the normal cone $\mathfrak{Y}\to\mathfrak{X}$ and its closed fiber $\mathfrak{Y}_{0}\to\mathfrak{X}_{0}$ . Since the immersion of the open part exhibits the pair $Y\to X$ as a retract of $\mathfrak{Y}\to\mathfrak{X}$ , it suffices to prove the proposition for $\mathfrak{Y}\to\mathfrak{X}$ . Now by Corollary 5.15 the relative Hodge cohomology of $(\mathfrak{X},\mathfrak{X}\setminus\mathfrak{Y})$ coincides with that of $(\mathfrak{X}_{0},\mathfrak{X}_{0}\setminus\mathfrak{Y}_{0})$ , so it suffices to prove the same for $\mathfrak{Y}_{0}\to\mathfrak{X}_{0}$ .

Therefore, we can assume that $\pi\colon X\to Y$ is a rank $r$ vector bundle and $i\colon Y\to X$ is the immersion of the zero section, and try to prove that the map described above is the Thom map. In this case, the Hodge cohomology of $X$ is naturally a module of the Hodge cohomology of $Y$ by $\pi^{*}$ , and the map described is a module map, so it suffices to prove that the image of $1$ is $\mathrm{Th}_{X/Y}$ . By Remark 4.8, this reduces to checking the functoriality, the additivity, and the normalization for line bundles for this image. Now both the functoriality and the additivity follow from Lemma 5.34. For the normalization for line bundles, we work in the universal case $\mathrm{B}\mathbb{G}_{m}\to\mathbb{A}^{1}/\mathbb{G}_{m}$ by identifying quasicoherent sheaves on $\mathbb{A}^{1}/\mathbb{G}_{m}$ as graded $\mathbb{Z}[t]$ -modules, where it is routine to check that the map $i_{*}\mathcal{O}_{\mathrm{B}\mathbb{G}_{m}}\to\mathrm{L}_{\mathbb{A}^{1}/\mathbb{G}_{m}}[1]$ is $1$ under the identification of Example 3.33, which coincides with $\mathrm{Th}_{1}^{\mathrm{Hod}}$ by Remark 4.10. ∎

Similar method can be used to enhance the Gysin map of the $p$ -completed topological cyclic homology to a motivic filtered map. First we recall the filtration:

#### Proposition 5.37.

There is a natural exhaustive filtration $\fil^{\bullet}\mathrm{TC}(R)_{p}^{\wedge}$ on the $p$ -completed $\mathrm{TC}$ , functorial in $R\in\mathsf{Ring}$ , such that:

- (1) $\gr^{i}\mathrm{TC}(R)_{p}^{\wedge}=\mathbb{Z}_{p}(i)(\hat{R})[2i]$ . In particular, $\fil^{0}\mathrm{TC}(R)_{p}^{\wedge}=\mathrm{TC}(R)_{p}^{\wedge}$ .

- (2) The functor $\fil^{\bullet}\mathrm{TC}_{p}^{\wedge}\colon\mathsf{Ring}\to\mathsf{Fil}(\mathsf{Sp}_{p}^{\wedge})$ commutes with sifted colimits, and hence is left Kan extended from polynomial rings of finite type over $\mathbb{Z}$ .

- (3) $\fil^{\bullet}\mathrm{TC}_{p}^{\wedge}$ is a big étale sheaf, and is even a $p$ -quasisyntomic sheaf when restricted to classical $p$ -bounded $p$ -quasisyntomic rings.

#### Proof.

Note that $\mathrm{TC}(R)_{p}^{\wedge}$ only depends on $\hat{R}$ , since $\mathrm{THH}(R)_{p}^{\wedge}$ is so. Also by [CMM21, Corollary 2.15], the functor $\mathrm{TC}_{p}^{\wedge}\colon\mathsf{Ring}\to\mathsf{Sp}_{p}^{\wedge}$ commutes with sifted colimits, so we can construct the filtration by left Kan extension from classical $p$ -bounded $p$ -quasisyntomic rings, where it follows from [BMS19, §7.4], which automatically implies (3). Now (1) and (2) follow from [BL22, Proposition 7.4.8]. ∎

Recall that $\mathrm{TC}(R)$ is actually an invariant of the category $\mathsf{D}(R)^{\omega}$ of perfect $R$ -complexes, since $\mathrm{THH}$ is so, cf. [BGT13, §10.1]. Hence if $R\to S$ is a regular pair, then there is a wrong-way map $\mathsf{D}(S)^{\omega}\to\mathsf{D}(R)^{\omega}$ , since perfect $S$ -complexes are perfect $R$ -complexes. This induces a pushforward map $\mathrm{TC}(S)\to\mathrm{TC}(R)$ , which can be globalized to a pushforward map $\mathrm{TC}(Y)\to\mathrm{TC}(X)$ associated to every regular immersion $Y\to X$ of stacks. Here the meaning of $\mathrm{TC}(X)$ is as in Remark 3.4. Since the composition $\mathsf{D}(S)^{\omega}\to\mathsf{D}(R)^{\omega}\to\mathsf{D}(\spec(R)\setminus\spec(S))^{\omega}$ is functorially zero, the map $\mathrm{TC}(Y)\to\mathrm{TC}(X)$ factors through $\mathrm{TC}(X,X\setminus Y)$ .

#### Theorem 5.38 (The Gysin map for $\fil^{\bullet}\mathrm{TC}_{p}^{\wedge}$ ).

Fix $r\in\mathbb{N}$ . There is a unique way (up to contractible choice) to enhance the map $\mathrm{TC}(Y)_{p}^{\wedge}\to\mathrm{TC}(X,X\setminus Y)_{p}^{\wedge}$ to a filtered map $\fil^{\bullet}\mathrm{TC}(Y)_{p}^{\wedge}\to\fil^{\bullet+r}\mathrm{TC}(X,X\setminus Y)_{p}^{\wedge}$ functorially for all regular immersions $Y\to X$ of codimension $r$ . Moreover, its associated graded is the Gysin map for the syntomic cohomology of $p$ -formal schemes as in Definition 5.32.

#### Proof.

For notational simplicity, we omit all the $-_{p}^{\wedge}$ , and use $\mathbb{Z}_{p}(i)$ to denote the functor $R\mapsto\mathbb{Z}_{p}(i)(\hat{R})$ . It suffices to prove that for integers $n\geq n^{\prime}$ , the map

$$ \fil^{n}\mathrm{TC}(Y)\to\mathrm{TC}(Y)\to\mathrm{TC}(X,X\setminus Y)\to\mathrm{TC}(X,X\setminus Y)/\fil^{n^{\prime}+r}\mathrm{TC}(X,X\setminus Y) $$

has a unique functorial nullhomotopy. As before, let $\mathfrak{Y}\to\mathfrak{X}$ denote the deformation to the normal cone of $Y\to X$ , and let $\mathfrak{Y}_{0}\to\mathfrak{X}_{0}$ denote its closed fiber. Note that the above map can be written as

$$ \displaystyle\quad\ \!\fil^{n}\mathrm{TC}(Y)\to\fil^{n}\mathrm{TC}(\mathfrak{Y}_{0})\to\mathrm{TC}(\mathfrak{X}_{0},\mathfrak{X}_{0}\setminus\mathfrak{Y}_{0})/\fil^{n^{\prime}+r}\mathrm{TC}(\mathfrak{X}_{0},\mathfrak{X}_{0}\setminus\mathfrak{Y}_{0}) \displaystyle\cong\mathrm{TC}(\mathfrak{X},\mathfrak{X}\setminus\mathfrak{Y})/\fil^{n^{\prime}+r}\mathrm{TC}(\mathfrak{X},\mathfrak{X}\setminus\mathfrak{Y})\to\mathrm{TC}(X,X\setminus Y)/\fil^{n^{\prime}+r}\mathrm{TC}(X,X\setminus Y), $$

where the first arrow comes from the projection $\mathfrak{Y}_{0}\to Y$ , the second arrow is the map (6) for $\mathfrak{Y}_{0}\to\mathfrak{X}_{0}$ , the isomorphism is due to Theorem 5.20 since $\mathrm{TC}/\fil^{n^{\prime}+r}\mathrm{TC}$ is finitely filtered by $\mathbb{Z}_{p}(i)[2i]$ , and the final arrow is restriction to the open fiber. Recall that $\mathfrak{X}_{0}=\mathcal{N}_{Y/X}/\mathbb{G}_{m}$ is the weighted normal bundle over $\mathfrak{Y}_{0}=Y\times\mathrm{B}\mathbb{G}_{m}$ . Therefore the theorem is reduced to the following statement: the map

$$ \fil^{n}\mathrm{TC}(Y)\to\mathrm{TC}(V/\mathbb{G}_{m},(V\setminus 0)/\mathbb{G}_{m})/\fil^{n^{\prime}+r}\mathrm{TC}(V/\mathbb{G}_{m},(V\setminus 0)/\mathbb{G}_{m}) $$

has a unique nullhomotopy that is functorial in the rank $r$ vector bundle $V\to Y$ . Now the right hand side is finitely filtered by

$$ \mathbb{Z}_{p}(i+r)(V/\mathbb{G}_{m},(V\setminus 0)/\mathbb{G}_{m})[2(i+r)]=\mathbb{Z}_{p}(i)(Y\times\mathrm{B}\mathbb{G}_{m})[2i] $$

for $i<n^{\prime}$ by the Thom isomorphism, so it suffices to show that for $i<n^{\prime}$ , any map

$$ \fil^{n}\mathrm{TC}(Y)\to\mathbb{Z}_{p}(i)(Y\times\mathrm{B}\mathbb{G}_{m})[2i] $$

that is functorial in $Y$ is uniquely nullhomotopic. By étale descent we can assume that $Y=\spec(R)$ is affine. Then by descent along the Čech nerve of $Y\to Y\times\mathrm{B}\mathbb{G}_{m}$ , we reduce to show that, for $i<n^{\prime}$ and any ring $A$ smooth over $\mathbb{Z}$ , any map

$$ \fil^{n}\mathrm{TC}(R)\to\mathbb{Z}_{p}(i)(R\otimes A)[2i] $$

that is functorial in $R$ is uniquely nullhomotopic. Since both sides commute with sifted colimits in $R$ , we can assume that $R$ is also smooth over $\mathbb{Z}$ . Now both sides satisfy quasisyntomic descent, and the theorem follows from the fact that quasisyntomic locally, $\fil^{n}\mathrm{TC}$ is $2n$ -connective, but $\mathbb{Z}_{p}(i)[2i]$ lies in homotopical degree $2i<2n^{\prime}\leq 2n$ , cf. [BMS19, §7.4] and [BS22, Theorem 14.1].

To see that the associated graded gives the Gysin map, by the same deformation to the normal cone argument, we only need to show that for a rank $r$ vector bundle $V\to Y$ , it gives the syntomic Thom map

$$ \mathbb{Z}_{p}(\star)(Y)[2\star]\to\mathbb{Z}_{p}(\star+r)(V,V\setminus 0)[2(\star+r)] $$

when applied to the zero section $0\to V$ . This is a map of $\mathbb{Z}_{p}(\star)(Y)[2\star]$ -modules, so it suffices to show that the image of $1\in\mathbb{Z}_{p}(0)(Y)$ is $\mathrm{Th}_{V}^{\mathrm{syn}}\in\mathbb{Z}_{p}(r)(V,V\setminus 0)[2r]$ . By Remark 4.8, this reduces to the functoriality, the additivity, and the normalization for line bundles for this image, which we now check:

This is clear by the functoriality of the Gysin map.

By [CMM21, Theorem 1.7], the $p$ -completed $\mathrm{TC}$ is the étale sheafification of the $p$ -completed connective $K$ -theory. Now $1\in K(Y)$ is just $[\mathcal{O}_{Y}]$ , and the product is just the tensor product, so the additivity follows from the fact that if $V=V^{\prime}\oplus V^{\prime\prime}$ is a direct sum, then $\mathcal{O}_{0}=\mathcal{O}_{V^{\prime}}\otimes_{\mathcal{O}_{V}}\mathcal{O}_{V^{\prime\prime}}$ , where we view $V^{\prime}$ and $V^{\prime\prime}$ as closed substacks of $V$ .

As above, viewing $\mathrm{TC}$ as the étale $K$ -theory, it suffices to show that for a Cartier divisor $D\to X$ , the associated graded class of $[\mathcal{O}_{D}]\in\fil^{1}\mathrm{TC}(X)$ is $c_{1}(\mathcal{O}(D))\in\Omega^{\infty-2}\mathbb{Z}_{p}(1)(X)$ . By étale descent, we can assume that $X=\spec(R)$ is affine. Then by [BL22, Proposition 7.4.8], we can assume that $R$ is smooth over $\mathbb{Z}$ . Now by $p$ -quasisyntomic descent, we can assume that $R$ is over $\mathbb{Z}_{p}^{\mathrm{cyc}}$ and is quasiregular semiperfectoid, where it follows from [ALB20, Theorem 6.7] and [BL22, Corollary 2.6.11, Proposition 7.5.2]. ∎

## 6. Poincaré duality

We finally prove the prismatic Poincaré duality in this section. First we recall its Hodge version in [Cla21, Lecture 16]. Let $S$ be a stack and $X$ be a stack over $S$ . Suppose the structure map $f\colon X\to S$ is representable by algebraic spaces, and is proper smooth of dimension $d\in\mathbb{N}$ . Then the relative diagonal $\Delta\colon X\to X\times_{S}X$ is a regular immersion of codimension $d$ . Note by [Stacks, 0A1P] that the relative Hodge cohomology $f_{*}(\mathrm{L}\Omega_{X/S}^{\star})[-\star]$ is dualizable in $\mathsf{D}(S)$ .

#### Theorem 6.1 (Poincaré duality for Hodge cohomology).

The image of the absolute Hodge cycle class $\mathrm{Cl}^{\mathrm{Hod}}_{\Delta}\in\Omega^{\infty-d}\mathrm{R}\Gamma(X\times_{S}X,\mathrm{L}\Omega_{X\times_{S}X}^{d})$ along

$$ \displaystyle\quad\ \mathrm{R}\Gamma(X\times_{S}X,\mathrm{L}\Omega_{X\times_{S}X}^{\star})\to\mathrm{R}\Gamma(X\times_{S}X,\mathrm{L}\Omega_{(X\times_{S}X)/S}^{\star}) \displaystyle=\mathrm{R}\Gamma(S,(f\times_{S}f)_{*}(\mathrm{L}\Omega_{(X\times_{S}X)/S}^{\star}))=\mathrm{R}\Gamma(S,f_{*}(\mathrm{L}\Omega_{X/S}^{\star})\otimes f_{*}(\mathrm{L}\Omega_{X/S}^{\star})) $$

gives rise to a graded map

$$ \mathcal{O}_{S}\to f_{*}(\mathrm{L}\Omega_{X/S}^{\star})\otimes f_{*}(\mathrm{L}\Omega_{X/S}^{\star})(d)[d], $$

where $(d)$ and $[d]$ denote the shift on the grade and the homological degree, respectively. This map is a perfect copairing, i.e. the dual map

$$ p_{*}(\mathrm{L}\Omega_{X/S}^{\star})^{\vee}\to f_{*}(\mathrm{L}\Omega_{X/S}^{\star})(d)[d] $$

is an isomorphism.

#### Proof.

The proof is the same as in [Cla21, Lecture 16], with our Proposition 5.36 in place of its Lemma 2. For convenience and completeness, we reproduce it here.

Since the cycle class is the image of $1$ under the Gysin map, using Proposition 5.36 with $n=0$ we see that the copairing map in the theorem, in individual grades, can be described as follows: take $d$ th wedge power of the canonical map from the conormal to the cotangent

$$ \mathrm{L}\Omega_{X/S}^{d}=\Lambda^{d}(\mathrm{L}_{X/(X\times_{S}X)}[-1])\to\Delta^{*}\mathrm{L}\Omega_{(X\times_{S}X)/S}^{d}; $$

note that $\Delta^{!}\mathcal{O}_{X\times_{S}X}=(\mathrm{L}\Omega_{X/S}^{d})^{-1}[-d]$ ; tensor this with both sides to get

$$ \mathcal{O}_{X}[-d]\to\Delta^{*}\mathrm{L}\Omega_{X\times_{S}X}^{d}\otimes\Delta^{!}\mathcal{O}_{X\times_{S}X}=\Delta^{!}\mathrm{L}\Omega_{X\times_{S}X}^{d}; $$

then move the $\Delta^{!}$ to the left, apply $(f\times_{S}f)_{*}$ , and finally compose with the canonical map $\mathcal{O}_{S}\to f_{*}\mathcal{O}_{X}$ and the projection to one direct summand in Künneth to get

$$ \mathcal{O}_{S}[-d]\to f_{*}\mathcal{O}_{X}[-d]\to(f\times_{S}f)_{*}\mathrm{L}\Omega_{X\times_{S}X}^{d}\to f_{*}\mathrm{L}\Omega_{X/S}^{i}\otimes f_{*}\mathrm{L}\Omega_{X/S}^{j}, $$

where $i$ and $j$ are fixed with $i+j=d$ . To see that this is perfect, we apply Lemma 6.2 to reduce to perfectness of

$$ \mathrm{L}\Omega_{X/S}^{d}\to\Delta^{*}\mathrm{L}\Omega_{X\times_{S}X}^{d}=\mathrm{L}\Lambda^{d}(\mathrm{L}_{X/S}\oplus\mathrm{L}_{X/S})\to\mathrm{L}\Omega_{X/S}^{i}\otimes\mathrm{L}\Omega_{X/S}^{j}, $$

where the final map is the projection to one direct summand; now this is a claim on quasicoherent sheaves over $X$ , so it can be verified étale locally, where it follows by a straightforward calculation with local coordinates. ∎

#### Lemma 6.2 (cf. [Cla21, Lemma 16.3]).

Suppose $M$ and $N$ are perfect complexes over $X$ that are in duality via a perfect copairing

$$ \mathrm{L}\Omega_{X/S}^{d}[d]=f^{!}\mathcal{O}_{S}\to M\otimes N=\Delta^{*}(M\boxtimes_{S}N). $$

Then $f_{*}M$ and $f_{*}N$ are in duality via the copairing

$$ \mathcal{O}_{S}\to f_{*}M\otimes f_{*}N $$

given as follows: first tensor both sides by $\Delta^{!}\mathcal{O}_{X\times_{S}X}=(f^{!}\mathcal{O}_{S})^{-1}$ to get

$$ \mathcal{O}_{X}\to\Delta^{*}(M\boxtimes_{S}N)\otimes\Delta^{!}\mathcal{O}_{X\times_{S}X}=\Delta^{!}(M\boxtimes_{S}N); $$

then move the $\Delta^{!}$ to the left, apply $(f\times_{S}f)_{*}$ , and finally compose with the canonical map $\mathcal{O}_{S}\to f_{*}\mathcal{O}_{X}$ to get

$$ \mathcal{O}_{S}\to f_{*}\mathcal{O}_{X}\to(f\times_{S}f)_{*}(M\boxtimes_{S}N)=f_{*}M\otimes f_{*}N. $$

#### Proof.

Take a pairing $N\otimes M\to f^{!}\mathcal{O}_{S}$ that forms a duality datum with the copairing. Move $f^{!}$ to the left and use the lax monoidal structure of $f^{*}$ to get

$$ f_{*}N\otimes f_{*}M\to f_{*}(N\otimes M)\to\mathcal{O}_{S}. $$

It suffices to show that this pairing forms a duality datum with the copairing given above. To this end, we consider the composition

$$ f^{!}\mathcal{O}_{S}\otimes M\to(M\otimes N)\otimes M=M\otimes(N\otimes M)\to M\otimes f^{!}\mathcal{O}_{S}. $$

Tensoring $\Delta^{!}\mathcal{O}_{X\times_{S}X}=(f^{!}\mathcal{O}_{S})^{-1}$ , we get

$$ M\to\Delta^{!}(M\boxtimes_{S}(N\otimes M))\to\Delta^{!}(M\boxtimes_{S}f^{!}\mathcal{O}_{S})=M. $$

Moving $\Delta^{!}$ to the left and applying $(f\times_{S}f)_{*}$ , we get

$$ f_{*}M\to f_{*}M\otimes f_{*}(N\otimes M)\to f_{*}M\otimes f_{*}f^{!}\mathcal{O}_{S}\to f_{*}M, $$

where the last map is the counit. Now since we start with a duality datum, the first composition is the map commuting $M$ and $f^{!}\mathcal{O}_{S}$ , so the second and the third compositions are identity maps. Therefore, it suffices to see that the first map above is given by the composition

$$ f_{*}M\to(f_{*}M\otimes f_{*}N)\otimes f_{*}M=f_{*}M\otimes(f_{*}N\otimes f_{*}M)\to f_{*}M\otimes f_{*}(N\otimes M), $$

where the first map is induced by the copairing we constructed. Since we are working with quasicoherent sheaves on $S$ , it suffices to show the statement after restricted along every morphism $U\to S$ and composed with every map $\varphi\colon\mathcal{O}_{U}[n]\to f_{*}M|_{U}$ for every $n\in\mathbb{Z}$ . Restriction commutes with everything here, so we can assume $U=S$ . Then the statement follows from the functorialities of all the above constructions applied to the map $N[n]\to N\otimes M$ induced by $\varphi$ . ∎

Now let $(A,I)$ be a prism and take $S=\spf(\bar{A})$ . To prove the Poincaré duality, we need to produce a copairing map using the syntomic cycle class.

#### Remark 6.3.

Let $R$ be a ring over $\bar{A}$ . Note that the comparison map $\fil^{\bullet}{{\mathbbl{\Delta}}}_{R}\{d\}\to(\fil^{\bullet}{{\mathbbl{\Delta}}}_{R/A}^{(1)})\{d\}$ in [BL22, Construction 5.6.1] is compatible with Frobenius, i.e. the diagram

$$ {\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\fil^{d}{{\mathbbl{\Delta}}}_{R}\{d\}} {\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{{\mathbbl{\Delta}}}_{R}\{d\}} {\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces(\fil^{d}{{\mathbbl{\Delta}}}_{R/A}^{(1)})\{d\}} {\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{{\mathbbl{\Delta}}}_{R/A}\{d\}} {\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{{\mathbbl{\Delta}}}_{R/A}^{(1)}\{d\}} \scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\varphi_{R}\{d\}} \scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\varphi_{R/A}\{d\}} \scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces-\otimes 1} $$

commutes. By Proposition 2.35, this gives rise to a comparison map

$$ \mathbb{Z}_{p}(d)(R)\to\Hom_{{F\text{-}\mathsf{Gauge}}(A,I)}(A,{{\mathbbl{\Delta}}}_{R/A}\{d\}). $$

Also, it is not hard to see from [BL22, Remark 5.5.8] that the diagram

$$ {\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\fil^{d}{{\mathbbl{\Delta}}}_{R}\{d\}} {\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\widehat{\mathrm{L}\Omega^{d}_{R}}[-d]} {\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces(\fil^{d}{{\mathbbl{\Delta}}}_{R/A}^{(1)})\{d\}} {\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\widehat{\mathrm{L}\Omega^{d}_{R/\bar{A}}}[-d]} $$

commutes. Therefore, for a regular immersion $Z\to Y$ of stacks over $\spf(\bar{A})$ of codimension $d$ , the cycle class $\mathrm{Cl}^{\mathrm{syn}}_{Y/X}\in\Omega^{\infty-2d}\mathbb{Z}_{p}(d)(X)$ gives rise to a map $A\to\mathrm{R}\Gamma_{{\mathbbl{\Delta}}}(X/A)\{d\}[2d]$ that sends $1$ to the Hodge cycle class after Hodge specialization.

Recall that $X$ is a stack over $S=\spf(\bar{A})$ , and the map $X\to S$ is representable by algebraic spaces proper smooth of dimension $d$ . Recall by Corollary 2.37 that $\mathrm{R}\Gamma_{{\mathbbl{\Delta}}}(X/A)$ is dualizable in ${F\text{-}\mathsf{Gauge}}(A,I)$ .

#### Theorem 6.4 (Prismatic Poincaré duality).

By Remark 6.3, the syntomic cycle class $\mathrm{Cl}^{\mathrm{syn}}_{\Delta}$ of the relative diagonal $\Delta\colon X\to X\times_{\spf(\bar{A})}X$ induces a map of $F$ -gauges

$$ A\to\mathrm{R}\Gamma_{{\mathbbl{\Delta}}}((X\times_{\spf(\bar{A})}X)/A)\{d\}[2d]=\mathrm{R}\Gamma_{{\mathbbl{\Delta}}}(X/A)\otimes_{A}\mathrm{R}\Gamma_{{\mathbbl{\Delta}}}(X/A)\{d\}[2d]. $$

This map is a perfect copairing, i.e. the dual map

$$ \mathrm{R}\Gamma_{{\mathbbl{\Delta}}}(X/A)^{\vee}\to\mathrm{R}\Gamma_{{\mathbbl{\Delta}}}(X/A)\{d\}[2d] $$

is an isomorphism.

#### Proof.

By Proposition 2.22, it suffices to prove that both the Hodge–Tate and the de Rham specializations of the above map are isomorphisms. By Proposition 2.36, both specializations are complete with only finitely many nonzero graded pieces, so we can pass to the graded pieces, which are the Hodge cohomologies, and the theorem follows from Theorem 6.1 and Remark 6.3. ∎

#### Remark 6.5 (Trace maps).

Theorem 6.4 gives a trace map $\mathrm{R}\Gamma_{{\mathbbl{\Delta}}}(X/A)\{d\}[2d]\to A$ as the dual of the structure map $A\to\mathrm{R}\Gamma_{{\mathbbl{\Delta}}}(X/A)$ , which reduces to the Hodge trace map after specialization. Now if there were a suitably defined dualizable coefficient system $\mathcal{E}$ on $X$ , then the pairing $\mathcal{E}\otimes\mathcal{E}^{\vee}\to\mathcal{O}$ along with the trace map gives a canonical pairing

$$ \mathrm{R}\Gamma_{{\mathbbl{\Delta}}}(X/A,\mathcal{E})\otimes\mathrm{R}\Gamma_{{\mathbbl{\Delta}}}(X/A,\mathcal{E}^{\vee})\{d\}[2d]\to\mathrm{R}\Gamma_{{\mathbbl{\Delta}}}(X/A)\{d\}[2d]\to A. $$

If one worked out the theory of relative $F$ -gauges as sketched in Remark 2.34, then it would be not hard to prove that the pairing is perfect by Hodge specialization; alternatively, one could also see that it is already perfect for $\mathcal{E}$ being a dualizable prismatic crystal by Hodge–Tate specialization, via a careful study of the cohomology along $\mathrm{WCart}_{X/A}^{\mathrm{HT}}\to X$ , cf. [BL22a, Proposition 5.12, Corollary 6.6].

#### Remark 6.6 (Comparisons).

The comparisons of Theorem 6.4 with the duality maps of several other cohomology theories should follow from the uniqueness of cycle classes in Remark 5.28 and Remark 5.29. More specifically:

- • By the proof of Theorem 6.4, it is already clear that the prismatic duality map specializes to the Hodge duality map given by the coherent duality and the de Rham duality map constructed in [Cla21, Lecture 16].

- • For $I=pA$ , Theorem 6.4 recovers the crystalline Poincaré duality in [Ber74, Theorem VII.2.1.3] via [BS22, Theorem 5.2]. Indeed, under the Künneth formula, Berthelot’s pairing map is the composition of the diagonal pullback with the trace map, so by [Ber74, Corollary VII.2.3.2] its dual copairing is the cycle class of the diagonal, which is exactly the copairing here.

- • If one started with a perfect prism $(A,I)$ and a smooth and proper algebraic space over $\spec(\bar{A})$ , rather than such a formal algebraic space over $\spf(\bar{A})$ , then the syntomic cycle class would specialize to the étale one after inverting $p$ , so the prismatic duality map would also specialize to the étale one after inverting $p$ . We are not going into details here, since in future projects, we plan to compare the prismatic Poincaré duality with that of diamonds in [Man22, Theorem 3.10.20].

#### Remark 6.7.

In future projects, we hope to explore generalizations of Theorem 6.4 in the following directions:

- • to general coefficients for the prismatic cohomology as in Remark 6.5.

- • to the absolute prismatic cohomology, or more generally to the coherent duality along the map $X^{{{\mathbbl{\Delta}}}^{\prime\prime}}\to S^{{{\mathbbl{\Delta}}}^{\prime\prime}}$ of prismatizations as in [Dri24].

- • to non-proper maps, i.e. to a 6-functor formalism with a condensed lower shriek as in [Condensed].

- • to non- $p$ -formal schemes, i.e. gluing with similar structure in the étale cohomology, as in [BL22, §8.4].
